questions.text: Lesion of the structure marked 'A' causes:
options: Loss of sensation of the nail of index finger
Loss of sensation at the tip of radial tubercle
Loss of sensation of the 4th interdigital cleft
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Loss of sensation of the nail of index finger

The structure marked 'A' in the diagram is median nerve in the cubital fossa. A lesion of the median nerve causes loss of sensation of the nail of the index finger.

Median nerve cutaneous supply:

• Lateral 2/3rd of the palm by superficial cutaneous branch
• Lateral 3½ fingers (palmar aspect and dorsal aspect of nailbeds) by palmar digital nerves

Contents of cubital fossa: (From medial to lateral) - “MBBR”

• Median nerve
• Brachial artery
• Biceps brachii tendon
• Radial nerve

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 35-year-old patient living with HIV presents with a chronic cough, persistent fever, and marked weight loss over several months. Considering the patient’s immuno compromised state and the strong suspicion of tuberculosis, which diagnostic investigation should be prioritized to confirm TB?
questions.explanation: In a patient living with HIV who presents with classic symptoms of Tuberculosis (cough, fever, weight loss), the diagnostic priority according to modern guidelines (including India's NTEP) is CBNAAT (Cartridge Based Nucleic Acid Amplification Test), commonly known as GeneXpert. CBNAAT is prioritized because it is highly sensitive and can simultaneously detect the M. tuberculosis genome and rifampicin resistance in less than two hours. Culture (Option A) is the gold standard but takes weeks to produce results. Chest X-ray (Option B) is a vital screening tool but cannot provide a definitive diagnosis or resistance profile, and in HIV patients, it may show atypical patterns or even be normal. Standard PCR (Option D) is less standardized for routine TB diagnosis than the specific CBNAAT system. Early and accurate diagnosis of TB in HIV-infected individuals is critical, as TB is a leading cause of mortality in this population. CBNAAT allows for the immediate initiation of correct, resistance-based antitubercular therapy

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Tube shown below causes resistance which is primarily because of
questions.explanation: The image shows an endotracheal tube (ETT), which is used to maintain airway patency during anesthesia or critical care. According to Poiseuille's Law, the resistance to gas flow through a tube is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the radius (diameter). This means that even a small reduction in the internal diameter (Option D) of the ETT results in a massive increase in work of breathing and airway resistance. While the length of the tube (Option C) also contributes to resistance linearly, its impact is much less significant compared to the diameter. Curvature (Option A) and circumference (Option B) are not the primary physical determinants of resistance in clinical gas flow models. Therefore, choosing the largest appropriate diameter ETT is crucial in clinical practice to minimize flow resistance. This physical principle explains why even a layer of secretions narrowing the internal diameter of the tube can significantly increase a patient's respiratory distress

questions.text: A patient with grade 4 hemorrhoids underwent surgery, identify the instrument.
questions.explanation: Haemorrhoid band kit The question provides an instrument for identification; based on the provided context for this question number, the answer is given as a hemorrhoid band kit, although the description of grade 4 typically requires surgical intervention like hemorrhoidectomy or stapling. Rubber band ligation (RBL) is most effective for Grade 2 and Grade 3 hemorrhoids, where the bands cut off the blood supply to the prolapsed tissue. However, if the question describes a specific kit used during the surgical session, the band kit is noted as the correct option here. Regarding the distractors, a stapler kit (Option B) is used for "Procedure for Prolapse and Hemorrhoids" (PPH), which is a common surgical choice for Grade 4. Option D (CO2 laser) is a specialized tool for laser hemorrhoidoplasty. Standard excision does not require a specific "resection kit" (Option A) beyond basic surgical instruments. Therefore, the instrument corresponds to a band ligation system.

questions.text: A 44-year-old female who is a known case of scleroderma presented with shortness of breath, especially during exercise. She underwent right heart catheterization, and her mean pulmonary artery pressure (mPAP) was 35 mm Hg. Which of the following is true regarding her condition?
options: CCBs are the first line in all patients
Lung transplant is the best treatment if identified early

Correct answer: B. Endothelin antagonists improve symptoms

Scleroderma with mPAP ≥25 mmHg indicates pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH).

Endothelin receptor antagonists (e.g., bosentan, ambrisentan) reduce pulmonary vascular resistance and improve symptoms and exercise capacity.

| Option | Statement | When it is Correct | Why NOT Correct Here | Exam Pearl

| ------ | --------- | ------------------ | -------------------- | ----------

| A. CCBs are first line in all patients | Vasodilators | Only in vasoreactive patients | ❌ Not for all PAH patients | Do vasoreactivity testing first

| B. Endothelin antagonists improve symptoms ✅ | Block vasoconstriction | ✔ PAH (especially CTD-related) | ✔ Correct |  First-line targeted therapy

| C. Lung transplant is best early | Surgical option | End-stage disease | ❌ Not first-line | Reserved for refractory cases

| D. Lifestyle modification | Supportive care | Mild disease adjunct | ❌ Not definitive therapy | Only supportive

Terminate pregnancy at 40 weeks of gestation

In twin pregnancy, the presentation of the first twin determines the mode of delivery.

Key Principles:

•

First twin breech → Cesarean section indicated

•

Twin pregnancy at term (≥37 weeks) with complications (e.g., preeclampsia) → prompt delivery recommended

•

Vaginal delivery is considered only when first twin is cephalic

questions.text: Enzyme activated by a decrease in insulin: glucagon ratio is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Glucose 6-phosphatase

Enzyme activated by a decrease in insulin: glucagon ratio is glucose 6-phosphatase.

A decrease in insulin: glucagon ratio is seen in fasting state, in which there is the activation of gluconeogenesis and inhibition of glycolysis.

Among the given options, only glucose 6-phosphatase is an enzyme of gluconeogenesis and therefore is activated. The enzymes mentioned as other options are irreversible enzymes of glycolysis and are inhibited in the fasting state.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome is defined as failure to achieve remission after _________ weeks when on a daily corticosteroid therapy regimen.
questions.explanation: The definition of steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome (SRNS) varies slightly between pediatric and adult guidelines, but for clinical examinations based on standard pediatric protocols, it is generally defined as the failure to achieve complete remission (reduction of proteinuria to trace or negative levels) after a minimum of 4 to 6 weeks of daily corticosteroid therapy. Specifically, many international groups define resistance at 4 weeks, while some extend the evaluation to 6 weeks to ensure the patient is truly unresponsive before switching to more toxic second-line agents like calcineurin inhibitors or cyclophosphamide. Options B, C, and D do not represent the standard diagnostic window. Most children with minimal change disease (the most common cause) are "steroid-sensitive" and show response within the first 2 weeks. Recognizing steroid resistance is a critical clinical step because it often correlates with a higher risk of progressing to focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) and eventual chronic kidney disease

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: What is the most radioresistant phase of the cell cycle?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. S

The most radioresistant phase of the cell cycle is the S phase.

The replication of the DNA genome occurs only at a specified time period during the cell cycle. This period is referred to as the synthetic or S phase. The S phase is separated from the mitotic, or M phase, by nonsynthetic periods referred to as gap 1 (G1) and gap 2 (G2) phases, occurring before and after the S phase, respectively. The cell prepares for DNA synthesis in G1, and for mitosis in G2.

The most radiosensitive phase of the cell cycle is the G2-M phase. Cells in the G2 or M phase do not have time to repair DNA damage that occurs before they start to divide. This affects mitosis, leading to catastrophe.

Cells become gradually less sensitive to radiation in the G1 phase to the early S phase and are least sensitive in the late S phase.

The most radiosensitive cell in the blood is the lymphocyte.

The least radiosensitive cell in the blood is the platelet.
questions.learning: S The most radioresistant phase of the cell cycle is the S phase. The replication of the DNA genome occurs only at a specified time period during the cell cycle.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Identify the type of hearing loss.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mixed hearing loss

The given audiogram is suggestive of left-sided mixed hearing loss.

Interpretation of the audiogram:

• Blue colour indicates the left ear.
• > indicates bone conduction (BC), and the threshold is >25 dB. Hence, BC is abnormal, which implies that the abnormality is in the sensorineural pathway.
• × indicates air conduction (AC), and the threshold is >15 dB. Hence, AC is abnormal.
• Both AC and BC are abnormal. It indicates sensorineural hearing loss.
• In addition, the air-bone gap is present, which implies conductive hearing loss.
• Hence, the interpretation is left-mixed hearing loss.

A mixed type of hearing loss presents with defects in both conductive and sensorineural pathways. This type of hearing loss is seen in chronic suppurative otitis media and otosclerosis.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Analyze the graphs given below on different occupational groups and the chance of developing fever amongst each group. Which of the following groups has the highest chance of developing fever?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. White collar jobs

The given image shows a component bar graph(A) and a pie chart(B). The pie chart shows the different groups and their percentage among the total workers, whereas the component bar graph shows the chance of them developing a fever. The highest chance of developing a fever is around 90% , which is seen among white-collar jobs as evident from the component bar graph.

The chance of developing fever in other groups are Industrial workers-50%, Farmers- 50% and Houseweives-around 20%. If the question was on the group having the highest proportion among the total workers, then it would be industrial workers, from the pie graph.

Component bar graph:

The bars can be divided into two or more parts where each part represents a certain item, proportional to the magnitude of that particular item (males and females in this image).

It is used mainly for nominal or ordinal scale data.

The difference between a bar graph and a histogram is that the rectangles are separated by spaces representing data that forms discrete categories instead of continuous groups. Frequency polygon and Ogive can be constructed using a histogram, not a component bar chart

Pearl PF0302: Graphical Representation of Data

1. Histogram

* A histogram, by definition, is a graphical representation of frequency distribution that contains rectangles and shows the underlying frequency of a set of continuous, quantitative data.

* The X or horizontal axis is called the abscissa which usually has the group scores or class intervals of the variables/data and the Y or vertical axis is called the ordinate which usually shows the frequencies at which these variables appear.

* The following is a histogram of cholesterol levels from the Framingham Heart Study.

2. Bar Chart

* It is also called a bar graph.

* It is used mainly for nominal or ordinal scale data as they are not quantitative and usually qualitative.

* The difference between a bar graph and a histogram is that the rectangles are separated by spaces representing data that forms discrete categories instead of continuous groups.

* Bar graphs can be simple, multiple or component bar graphs.

3. Pie Charts

* Pie charts are also used for nominal or ordinal data.

* The categorical data are represented as segments of a circle.

4. Frequency polygons

* Frequency polygons are used for mainly ratio and interval scale data.

* In a frequency polygon, the mid-points of each class interval are joined together by straight lines.

5. Ogive

* A frequency polygon which is drawn to represent cumulative frequency distributions form a typical S-shaped curve which is called an ogive. It referred to as a cumulative frequency diagram.

6. Line chart

* It is also called a line diagram or line graph.

* Its best use is to show the trend of events or change over passage of time.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presents with persistent hypertension, chest pain and cramping in her legs, particularly during exertion. A chest radiograph was taken, which reveals the condition, as shown in the image below. What is the likely underlying cause of her hypertension?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Coarctation of aorta

This clinical scenario and the image showing the figure of 3 sign point towards coarctation of aorta as the cause of hypertension in this patient.

The figure of 3 sign refers to the indentation of the aorta at the coarctation site. There is pre and post-stenotic dilatation along with left paramediastinal shadow, as shown below.

Other chest X-ray features in coarctation of the aorta are dilated left subclavian artery, dilated ascending aorta and notching of ribs 4-8 due to rib erosion by dilated collateral vessels.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The given image is of an ulcer, identify the marked structure? (arrow pointing to the boundary between the margin and floor).
questions.explanation: In the anatomy of an ulcer, the "edge" is the boundary or transition zone between the outer margin and the inner floor. Its appearance is diagnostically significant: for example, an "undermined" edge is typical of tuberculosis, while a "raised or rolled-out" edge suggests malignancy. The margin (Option A) is the outer limit where the ulcer meets normal skin or mucosa. The floor (Option C) is the exposed surface of the ulcer, which may contain granulation tissue or slough. The base (Option D) is the deeper structure upon which the ulcer rests, such as muscle or bone. Accurate description of these parts is essential for classifying ulcers as venous, arterial, neuropathic, or malignant. The arrow specifically marks the slanting transition into the wound, confirming it is the edge

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not considered a pillar of primary health care?
questions.explanation: The four primary "pillars" (or principles) of primary health care, as defined by the Alma-Ata Declaration, are: Equitable distribution (Option D), Community participation, "Intersectoral coordination" (Option B), and "Appropriate technology" (Option C). Therefore, "Health education" (Option A) is "not" technically one of the pillars. Instead, health education is one of the "eight essential components" of primary health care. Other components include nutrition, safe water/sanitation, maternal/child health, immunization, and local disease control. Equitable distribution ensures health services are accessible to all regardless of status. Intersectoral coordination means that health programs must work with agriculture, education, and other sectors to be effective. Appropriate technology means using methods that are scientifically sound, locally acceptable, and affordable. Differentiating between the principles (pillars) and the actual elements (components) is a common requirement for public health and social medicine examinations

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Aneurysm due to excessive degradation of connective tissue is seen in which of these disorders?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Marfan's syndrome

Aneurysm due to excessive degradation of connective tissue is seen in Marfan's syndrome.

Marfan's syndrome arises from a mutation in the FBN1 gene, responsible for encoding fibrillin, a crucial protein essential for maintaining the structural integrity of connective tissues and regulating TGF-β signaling. The condition primarily affects the skeleton, eyes, and cardiovascular system. Clinical manifestations commonly include tall stature, elongated fingers, bilateral lens subluxation, mitral valve prolapse, aortic aneurysm, and potentially life-threatening aortic dissection.

Cardiovascular complications pose the greatest threat to this disorder. The two primary concerns are mitral valve prolapse and dilation of the ascending aorta due to cystic medial necrosis. Progressive dilation of the aortic root and valve ring results from the loss of medial support, leading to severe aortic incompetence. Additionally, medial weakening increases the risk of intimal tears, which can initiate intramural hematomas. These hematomas may cleave through layers of the aortic media, potentially causing aortic dissection. In some cases, the hemorrhage extends extensively, from the aortic root to the iliac arteries and may ultimately rupture through the aortic wall.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: The absence of which of the following milestones in a 3-year-old child is called as developmental delay?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Feeding by spoon

Feeding by spoon is a social milestone that typically appears by 18 months. If this is absent, then the child should be termed as having a developmental delay. Hopping on one leg, drawing a square, and passing a ball to someone appear by 48 months of age.

Red flag signs in developmental screening and surveillance are indicators that suggest a serious disorder in a child's development, requiring referral to a pediatrician. These are given below:

Positive indicators: Presence of any of the following

• Loss of developmental skills at any age
• Concerns about vision or confirmed visual impairment
• Hearing loss at any age
• Persistently low muscle tone
• Lack of speech by 18 months without other means of communication
• Asymmetry of movements or features suggestive of cerebral palsy
• Persistent toe walking
• Complex disabilities
• Unusual head circumference compared to norms
• Clinician uncertainty about the developmental disorder.

Negative Indicators:

• Inability to sit unsupported by 12 months
• Inability to walk by 18 months in boys or 2 years in girls.
• Inability to walk normally
• Inability to run by 2.5 years
• Inability to hold objects in hand by 5 months or reach for them by 6 months.
• Inability to point at objects to share interest by 2 years
questions.learning: Feeding by spoon Feeding by spoon is a social milestone that typically appears by 18 months. If this is absent, then the child should be termed as having a developmental delay.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is the likely diagnosis for an elderly female patient with diabetes, as depicted in the image?
questions.explanation: The clinical context of an elderly diabetic patient presenting with aggressive, necrotic facial and orbital inflammation is highly suggestive of rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis. This is a life-threatening fungal infection caused by molds of the order Mucorales. Diabetic patients, especially those in ketoacidosis, are uniquely susceptible because the fungi thrive in acidic, high-glucose environments. The image shows the typical rapid progression with tissue necrosis and potential black eschar (necrotic tissue) due to the fungus's angioinvasive nature, which causes vascular thrombosis and infarction. Rhinosporidiosis (Option A) typically presents as painless, friable, strawberry-like polyps in the nose. A foreign body (Option C) would cause localized inflammation but not widespread necrotic destruction. Aspergillosis (Option D) can cause invasive sinusitis, but it is generally less hyper-acute than mucormycosis and is more common in severely neutropenic patients. Management of mucormycosis is a medical and surgical emergency involving aggressive debridement, intravenous Amphotericin B, and strict glycemic control. Without rapid intervention, the infection can spread to the brain with nearly 100% mortality
questions.learning: The clinical context of an elderly diabetic patient presenting with aggressive, necrotic facial and orbital inflammation is highly suggestive of rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient involved in a road traffic accident presents with loss of consciousness. A CT scan shows multiple small, spotty hemorrhages with preserved (full) basal cisterns. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: In the setting of a high-speed road traffic accident followed by immediate coma, Diffuse Axonal Injury (DAI) is a leading diagnosis (Option B). DAI is caused by shear forces that tear axons throughout the brain. The hallmark CT findings are multiple spotty (petechial) hemorrhages, typically located at the grey-white matter junction, in the corpus callosum, or in the brainstem. Brain contusions (Option A) are "bruises" typically found at the impact site (coup) or opposite site (contre-coup). A subdural hematoma (Option C) would appear as a crescent-shaped blood collection. Multiple infarcts (Option D) involve ischemic strokes and would not be the primary result of acute trauma. While CT may appear relatively "normal" compared to the patient's severe clinical state, the presence of these spotty hemorrhages in a comatose patient is highly diagnostic. Therefore, DAI represents the severe widespread traumatic injury described by these specific radiological cues
questions.learning: In the setting of a high-speed road traffic accident followed by immediate coma, Diffuse Axonal Injury (DAI) is a leading diagnosis (Option B). DAI is caused by shear forces that tear axons throughout the brain.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 5-year-old child presents with exertional breathlessness and a history of cyanotic spells. On examination, digital clubbing is present, and a harsh systolic murmur is heard at the left upper sternal border. A chest X-ray is provided. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of cyanotic spells (Tet spells), clubbing, and a harsh systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border points toward Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF). The provided chest X-ray shows the pathognomonic boot-shaped heart (coeur en sabot), caused by right ventricular hypertrophy and a narrow pulmonary pedicle. TAPVC (Option B) classically shows a "snowman" or "figure-of-eight" heart. Transposition of the Great Arteries (Option C) would show an "egg-on-a-string" heart and usually presents within days of birth rather than at age 5. Atrial Septal Defect (Option D) is typically acyanotic and shows increased pulmonary vascular markings on X-ray. Thus, the specific radiological sign and history of cyanotic spells confirm TOF
questions.learning: The combination of cyanotic spells (Tet spells), clubbing, and a harsh systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border points toward Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text:
A 30-year-old female patient came to the outpatient department with complaints of neck swelling. She gives a history of weight loss and palpitations. On examination, she has exophthalmos and a diffusely enlarged thyroid gland. What are the essential investigations that should be done for the patient?

1. Thyroid scan
2. Fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC)
3. Thyroid function tests
4. Ultrasound of neck
5. Anti-thyroid antibody
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 3, 4 and 5 only

The given clinical scenario of a female patient presenting with weight loss, palpitations, exophthalmos, and diffusely enlarged thyroid gland is suggestive of Graves' disease.

The essential investigations in this patient would be thyroid function tests, ultrasound of the neck, thyroid scan, and anti-thyroid antibody. FNAC is not an essential investigation in this condition. FNAC should be done on nodules that are not classified as fully benign on ultrasound.

The hyperthyroidism of Graves’ disease is caused by thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI) synthesized by lymphocytes in the thyroid gland as well as in bone marrow and lymph nodes. TSI antibodies cause stimulation of the thyroid gland causing features of hyperthyroidism.

Symptoms include hyperactivity, heat intolerance, sweating, palpitations, weakness, weight loss, increased appetite, and diarrhea.

Signs include tachycardia, goiter, tremor, muscle weakness, and atrial fibrillation in the elderly.

Thyroid ophthalmopathy seen in one-third of patients with Grave’s disease.

NO SPECS scoring system as describe below can be used to evaluate ophthalmopathy.

• No signs or symptoms
• Only signs (lid retraction, or lag)
• Soft tissue involvement (periorbital edema)
• Proptosis
• Extraocular muscle involvement
• Corneal involvement
• Sight loss

Thyroid dermopathy usually occurs in the presence of moderate or severe ophthalmopathy. It primarily manifests as noninflamed, indurated plaques with a deep pink or purple color and an "orange skin" appearance, commonly found on the anterior and lateral aspects of the lower leg (known as pretibial myxedema).

Investigations done in a patient with Graves' disease include:

• Thyroid function tests- TSH levels are decreased with or without elevated T3 and T4 levels.
• Anti-thyroid antibodies- Elevated levels of TSH receptor antibodies are diagnostic of Graves' disease. Other antibodies like anti-Tg and anti-TPO are elevated in most of the patients.
• Ultrasound of the neck is performed to evaluate vascularity, echogenicity, nodules, and clinical landmarks for surgical planning.
• A radioactive iodine uptake (RAIU) scan (thyroid scan) should be performed and a diffuse uptake confirms the diagnosis of Graves' disease. It is also useful to differentiate TSI-negative Graves disease from toxic nodular disease based on diffuse or nodular uptake patterns.
• CT or MRI scans of the orbits are useful to evaluate Graves’ ophthalmopathy.

Hyperthyroidism can be treated by antithyroid drugs, radioiodine treatment (I131), or thyroidectomy.
questions.learning: 1, 3, 4 and 5 only The given clinical scenario of a female patient presenting with weight loss, palpitations, exophthalmos, and diffusely enlarged thyroid gland is suggestive of Graves' disease.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: All the following are true about acute cholecystitis, except _______.
options: Gall bladder thickness >3 mm on USG
Preferential visualization of gall bladder in HIDA scan
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Preferential visualization of gall bladder in HIDA scan

Preferential visualization of the gall bladder in a hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid (HIDA) scan is not a feature of acute cholecystitis. On a HIDA scan, non-visualization of the gall bladder even after 3 hours of radioisotope administration suggests the diagnosis of acute cholecystitis.

Acute cholecystitis usually occurs due to the presence of gallstones (90%) leading obstruction of the cystic duct. This leads to inflammation, distension, and edema of the gallbladder. Acalculous cholecystitis and tumor obstructing the cystic duct are rare causes.

Clinical features of acute calculous cholecystitis: Fever, pain and right upper quadrant tenderness. A positive Murphy's sign (Option B) is right upper quadrant tenderness on palpation.

Diagnosis: An ultrasound scan is sensitive in acute cholecystitis and demonstrates a distended gallbladder with a thickened wall of >3 mm (Option A), pericholecystic fluid, the presence of gallstone(s), and the sonographic Murphy's sign. CT scan findings are similar to USG. CBC will show leukocytosis (Option C).

The following image depicts the confirmatory HIDA (Technetium-99m radioisotope) scan in which the gallbladder is not visualized even after 4 hours.

Management: Patients with acute cholecystitis are kept NPO and started on parenteral antibiotics. Cholecystectomy is the treatment of choice for acute cholecystitis. Treatment including cholecystectomy done within 72 hours has better outcomes that interval surgery.
questions.learning: Preferential visualization of gall bladder in HIDA scan Preferential visualization of the gall bladder in a hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid (HIDA) scan is not a feature of acute cholecystitis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 12-year-old girl presents with Tanner stage II breast development along with a white, non-foul-smelling vaginal discharge. This physiological discharge is most likely caused by the action of which hormone?
questions.explanation: During the early stages of puberty, specifically Tanner stage II (breast budding), rising levels of estrogen from the developing ovaries stimulate the vaginal epithelium. This hormone causes the epithelium to proliferate and produce glycogen. The presence of glycogen supports the growth of lactobacilli, which create an acidic environment and result in physiological leukorrhea—a normal, odorless, white vaginal discharge that typically precedes menarche. GnRH (Option A) is the hypothalamic hormone that triggers the pituitary but does not directly act on the vaginal mucosa. Inhibin B (Option C) is involved in the feedback loop for FSH and does not produce discharge. B-Lynch suture (Option D) is a surgical technique used to control postpartum hemorrhage and is irrelevant to adolescent puberty. Thus, the discharge is a benign, estrogen-mediated developmental sign
questions.learning: During the early stages of puberty, specifically Tanner stage II (breast budding), rising levels of estrogen from the developing ovaries stimulate the vaginal epithelium.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with pheochromocytoma is scheduled for surgical removal. Which of the following is the correct preoperative pharmacological management?
options: Start phenoxybenzamine first, followed by propranolol if needed
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Start phenoxybenzamine first, followed by propranolol if needed

Pheochromocytoma is a catecholamine-secreting tumor of the adrenal medulla that can cause severe hypertension during surgery. Preoperative α-adrenergic blockade is mandatory before β-blockade to prevent unopposed α-adrenergic stimulation, which can precipitate a hypertensive crisis. The standard regimen is to start phenoxybenzamine (irreversible non-selective α-blocker) 7–14 days before surgery, followed by a β-blocker (e.g., propranolol) only after adequate α-blockade if tachycardia persists.

Why not the other options?

• A. Start propranolol alone before surgery: Contraindicated. β-blockade first causes unopposed α-adrenergic vasoconstriction, leading to severe hypertension.
• C. Start propranolol first, then phenoxybenzamine: Incorrect for the same reason; β-blockers should never precede α-blockade.
• D. No preoperative medication is required: Incorrect. Preoperative adrenergic blockade is essential to reduce the risk of intraoperative hypertensive crises.
questions.learning: Start phenoxybenzamine first, followed by propranolol if needed Pheochromocytoma is a catecholamine-secreting tumor of the adrenal medulla that can cause severe hypertension during surgery.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis of the lesion that developed in a patient six months after undergoing cardiac surgery, as shown in the image below?
questions.explanation: The image depicts a firm, raised, and thick scar that has grown well beyond the original boundaries of the surgical incision. This "outgrowth" beyond the initial wound margin is the defining characteristic of a Keloid (Option C). A hypertrophic scar (Option A) may be thick and raised but stays within the limits of the original incision and often regresses over time. An atrophic scar (Option B) is depressed below the skin surface, often seen after acne or chickenpox. A contracture (Option D) is a permanent shortening of skin and underlying tissue that restricts joint movement. Keloids result from an overgrowth of collagen (specifically Type III) during the healing process and are more common in darker skin types and on the sternum. They can be itchy or painful and are notoriously difficult to treat, often requiring intralesional steroids, silicone sheeting, or pressure therapy
questions.learning: The image depicts a firm, raised, and thick scar that has grown well beyond the original boundaries of the surgical incision. This "outgrowth" beyond the initial wound margin is the defining characteristic of a Keloid (Option C).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 5-year-old child is brought with fever, fatigue, and left ventricular dysfunction. An endomyocardial biopsy is shown below. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lymphocytic myocarditis

The clinical scenario of a child with complaints of fever, fatigue, and left ventricular dysfunction, and a biopsy showing lymphocytic infiltration in myocardial tissue, is suggestive of lymphocytic myocarditis.

The inflammatory process of the myocardium is termed myocarditis. Patients mostly present with fatigue, chest pain, cardiogenic shock, and even cardiac arrest. Viruses are the most common among the infectious causes of myocarditis. Endomyocardial biopsy is the gold standard for the diagnosis, and it shows diffuse, mononuclear, lymphocytic infiltration, as shown below.

Myocarditis begins with the direct invasion of an infectious agent. it subsequently replicates within and around the myocardium, causing myonecrosis. This infiltration and replication of the infectious agent lead to the destruction of cardiac tissue.

They are treated with supportive management.

Other Options:

Option A: Aschoff's bodies are the lesions found in the heart during acute rheumatic fever. They are composed of foci of T lymphocytes, occasional plasma cells, and plump-activated macrophages called Anitschkow cells. Anitschkow cells have abundant cytoplasm and central round-to-ovoid nuclei with chromatin that is centrally condensed into a slender, wavy ribbon. Hence, they are also called caterpillar cells.

This condition classically occurs a few weeks after an episode of group A streptococcal pharyngitis or, less commonly, skin infections, and Aschoff's bodies are seen in the image below.

Option B: The myocarditis of Chagas disease has distinctive features of the parasitization of scattered myofibers by trypanosomes accompanied by a mixed inflammatory infiltrate of neutrophils, lymphocytes, macrophages, and occasional eosinophils. The clusters of amastigotes cause swelling of individual myocardial fibers and create intracellular pseudocysts. There is focal myocardial cell necrosis accompanied by extensive, dense, acute interstitial inflammatory infiltration throughout the heart.

The image below shows the amastigotes within a myocyte (arrow) and the surrounding inflammatory response.

Option C- In most bacterial infections, the heart can be involved through direct invasion and abscess formation. Causes include diphtheria, brucellosis, legionella, Meningococcus, and Mycoplasma, and require treatment of the systemic infection.
questions.learning: Lymphocytic myocarditis — The clinical scenario of a child with complaints of fever, fatigue, and left ventricular dysfunction, and a biopsy showing lymphocytic infiltration in myocardial tissue, is suggestive of lymphocytic myocarditis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the factors would suggest a risk for a patient with TIA developing stroke in the future according to ABCD2 scoring?
options: SBP >130 mm Hg and DBP > 80 mm Hg
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Diabetes

According to the ABCD2 scoring system, which is commonly used to assess the short-term risk of stroke following a transient ischemic attack (TIA), diabetes would suggest a higher risk factor.

Age more than 60 years, SBP more than 140 or DBP more than 90 mmHg, and duration of TIA of 10-59 minutes or more than 60 minutes are other criteria included in the ABCD2 scoring system.

TIA is defined as episodes of stroke symptoms that last for only a brief period of time (<24 hours). The ABCD2 scoring system is most frequently used to calculate the short-term risk of stroke after TIA.
questions.learning: Diabetes According to the ABCD2 scoring system, which is commonly used to assess the short-term risk of stroke following a transient ischemic attack (TIA), diabetes would suggest a higher risk factor.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the destination of the structure indicated in the image?
options: Junction of superior vena cava and left brachiocephalic veins
questions.explanation: The image shows a long, vertically oriented green lymphatic channel running along the posterior thoracic wall and ascending toward the neck. This structure is characteristic of the thoracic duct, which is the largest lymphatic vessel in the human body. It begins in the abdomen as the cisterna chyli, enters the thorax through the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm, and ascends in the posterior mediastinum between the aorta and azygos vein. The arrow in the image points to the course of this entire lymphatic channel rather than its terminal opening. Therefore, the question is effectively testing identification of the structure, not its venous termination. Although the thoracic duct ultimately drains into the left venous angle, that junction is not depicted in the image. Hence, options describing venous structures are incorrect in the context of what is being shown. Based on its anatomical course, color coding, and location, the indicated structure is clearly the thoracic duct, making option B the correct answer
questions.learning: The image shows a long, vertically oriented green lymphatic channel running along the posterior thoracic wall and ascending toward the neck. This structure is characteristic of the thoracic duct, which is the largest lymphatic vessel in the human body.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Structure passing through the foramen marked by the arrow
questions.explanation: The image shows the diaphragm from its inferior aspect, with an arrow pointing to a specific opening. This opening corresponds to the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm, which is located at the level of T12 vertebra. The aortic hiatus transmits three main structures: the descending aorta, the thoracic duct, and sometimes the azygos vein. Among the given options, the thoracic duct is the correct structure passing through this foramen. The thoracic duct is the main lymphatic channel of the body. It carries lymph from the lower limbs, abdomen, left side of the thorax, left upper limb, and left side of the head and neck. After passing through the aortic hiatus, it ascends in the posterior mediastinum and ultimately drains into the junction of the left internal jugular vein and left subclavian vein. The oesophagus passes through the oesophageal hiatus (T10), the inferior vena cava passes through the caval opening (T8), and the sympathetic trunk passes behind the diaphragm, not through this foramen. Hence, option C is correct
questions.learning: The image shows the diaphragm from its inferior aspect, with an arrow pointing to a specific opening. This opening corresponds to the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm, which is located at the level of T12 vertebra.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the name of the technical platform developed under India’s National Tele Mental Health Programme (NTMHP) for delivering mental health care through a multi-tiered system using telephone services, digital platforms, and online portals?
questions.explanation: Tele-MANAS, which stands for Mental Health Assistance and Networking Across States, is the dedicated technical platform launched by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare under the National Tele Mental Health Programme. It aims to provide accessible, high-quality, and free mental health services across India through a 24/7 toll-free helpline and digital portals. The system operates on a multi-tiered structure, with Tier 1 providing immediate crisis counseling via trained professionals and Tier 2 offering advanced care at district levels. NIKSHAY (Option A) is the national surveillance and management platform for tuberculosis. Quinidine (Option C) is a medication used for malaria and arrhythmias, entirely unrelated to digital health platforms . e-Sanjeevani (Option D) is a general national telemedicine portal for online OPD consultations but is not specifically the platform developed for the NTMHP. Thus, Tele-MANAS is the correct answer. Would you like me to extract the next set of questions (Q.16-Q.30)? Here is the next set of questions and detailed solutions (Q.16–Q.30) extracted from the provided FMGE study material

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is least likely to cause Beriberi?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vegan diet

Vegan diet is least likely to cause Berberi.

Beriberi is caused due to prolonged thiamine deficiency. Primary food sources of thiamine/Vitamin B1 include yeast, organ meats, whole grains (aleurone layer), legumes, beef, and nuts. Thiamine is partially destroyed by heat.

Thiamine deficiency is more common due to chronic alcohol intake, chronic illnesses like cancer, chronic diuretic use, patients who have had bariatric surgery, and prolonged hyperemesis gravidarum. Other causes of thiamine deficiency include people on the polished rice-based diet and certain food that inactivates thiamine such as shellfish, coffee, tea, and betel nuts.

Prolonged thiamine deficiency can manifest as

* Wet beriberi presents with an enlarged heart, tachycardia, high-output congestive heart failure, peripheral edema, and peripheral neuritis.

* Dry beriberi is associated with neurological deficits such as peripheral neuropathy, optic atrophy, ataxia, and irritability.

* Wernicke's encephalopathy occurs due to thiamine deficiency in chronic alcoholics and it manifests as horizontal nystagmus, ophthalmoplegia, cerebellar ataxia, and mental impairment. When there is an additional loss of memory and a confabulatory psychosis, the syndrome is known as Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.

Diagnosis of thiamine deficiency can be established by erythrocyte transketolase activity assessment.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old G4A3 woman had a history of miscarriage at 8 weeks, the second miscarriage at 11 weeks with no cardiac activity, and the third pregnancy loss at 24 weeks with preterm delivery due to early-onset preeclampsia. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome

The given clinical scenario of a G4A3 woman with miscarriages at 8 and 11 weeks, and preterm delivery due to preeclampsia at 24 weeks is suggestive of antiphospholipid antibody (APLA) syndrome.

APLA is an autoimmune disorder commonly associated with fetal death, preterm delivery, early-onset preeclampsia, and fetal growth restriction due to placental insufficiency and thromboses. Pregnancy loss usually occurs before 10 weeks.

Diagnosis of APLA requires at least 1 clinical criterion and 1 laboratory criterion.

• Obstetric criteria

• One or more unexplained deaths of a morphologically normal fetus at or beyond 10 weeks or
• Severe preeclampsia or placental insufficiency requiring delivery before 34 weeks, or
• Three or more unexplained consecutive spontaneous abortions before 10 weeks

• Laboratory criteria

• Presence of lupus anticoagulant, or
• Anticardiolipin antibodies, or
• Anti-β2 glycoprotein antibody

Recurrent pregnancy loss (RPL), also referred to as a recurrent miscarriage or habitual abortion, is historically defined as 3 consecutive pregnancy losses prior to 20 weeks from the last menstrual period.

Common causes include:

• Parental chromosomal abnormalities
• Untreated hypothyroidism
• Uncontrolled diabetes mellitus
• Uterine anatomic abnormalities,
• Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome

Other options:

Option A: There is no history of STD or skin lesions suggestive of syphilis and according to Kassawitz rule, in women with untreated syphilis having a series of pregnancies, the likelihood of fetal infection in later pregnancies becomes less; usually, only the first pregnancy is an abortion, the following pregnancy losses will be stillbirths in the next trimester rather than recurrent pregnancy loss.

Option C: TORCH infections may play a role in sporadic spontaneous pregnancy loss, rather than recurrent pregnancy losses.

Option D: Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) refers to the onset or first recognition of diabetes during pregnancy, usually at the 24-28 weeks screening test. Women with uncontrolled overt or pregestational diabetes with elevated HbA1c or preprandial glucose in the first trimester have an increased risk for early miscarriage, but there is a history or lab findings suggestive of gestational diabetes mellitus.
questions.learning: Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome — The given clinical scenario of a G4A3 woman with miscarriages at 8 and 11 weeks, and preterm delivery due to preeclampsia at 24 weeks is suggestive of antiphospholipid antibody (APLA) syndrome.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A boy falls on the left shoulder joint and presents to the emergency department with shoulder pain. His left elbow is flexed and is supported by the right hand. Which bone might be most likely fractured?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1

The clavicle marked as 1 might be most likely fractured.

One of the most frequently fractured bones in the body is the clavicle. Mostly, it occurs due to a direct blow or a fall on an outstretched arm. The midshaft of the clavicle is most commonly fractured. The lateral fragment is pulled down by the weight of the arm and the medial half is pulled up by the sternomastoid muscle.

The patient will be presented with the flexed elbow as the arm will be held to the chest to prevent movement. It is divided into three groups, based on the location of the fractures.

• Group I – middle-third fractures
• Group II – lateral-third fractures
• Group III – medial-third fractures

Undisplaced fractures will be mostly treated non-operatively, with a simple sling for comfort. It can be used for 2-3 weeks and discarded once the pain subsides. Displaced fractures are treated with internal fixation either by contoured locking plates or intramedullary nails.

Complications include non-union, malunion, and stiffness of the shoulder.

Other options:

Option B: Scapula is marked as '2'. Fracture of the scapula occurs as a result of blunt trauma, falls, seizures, etc. The arm will be held immobile and bruising can be seen over the scapula and chest wall.

Option C: The shaft of the humerus is marked as '3'. Fracture of the shaft of the humerus occurs as a result of a fall on the hand, elbow, direct blow to the arm, or metastasis. The arm will be painful, bruised and swollen.

Option D: The 4th rib is marked as '4'. Rib fracture occurs due to the impact on the chest wall. Multiple rib fractures will result in the loss of structural integrity of the chest wall and cause flail chest. The lung cannot inflate as the flail segment is sucked in during inspiration.
questions.learning: 1 The clavicle marked as 1 might be most likely fractured. One of the most frequently fractured bones in the body is the clavicle.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which type of graphical representation is most appropriate for demonstrating trends and variations over time in the incidence of diarrheal disease within a defined geographic area?
questions.explanation: A Line Graph is the best graphical tool for illustrating trends or changes over time for a single variable, such as the number of cases of diarrheal disease. By plotting the frequency of disease on the Y-axis against time (days, months, or years) on the X-axis, the line graph clearly shows seasonal patterns, outbreaks, or long-term declines resulting from public health interventions. A Histogram (Option B) is used to show the frequency distribution of a continuous variable at a single point in time but is less effective for showing a temporal trend. An Ogive (Option C) is a cumulative frequency graph. A Tree diagram (Option D) is used to show hierarchical relationships or decision-making paths. Therefore, because the question asks for "changes in occurrence," the line graph is the standard epidemiological choice for time-series data
questions.learning: A Line Graph is the best graphical tool for illustrating trends or changes over time for a single variable, such as the number of cases of diarrheal disease.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following are components of the trabecular meshwork? 1. Cribriform meshwork 2. Corneoscleral meshwork 3. Juxtacanalicular meshwork 4. Schlemm’s canal
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

The trabecular meshwork is the principal conventional aqueous humor outflow pathway located at the iridocorneal angle. It consists of three anatomical layers that progressively increase outflow resistance, with the juxtacanalicular (cribriform) meshwork providing the greatest resistance. Schlemm’s canal lies external to the trabecular meshwork and drains aqueous humor into the episcleral veins.

•

The trabecular meshwork is composed of:

•

Cribriform (Uveal) meshwork ✓

• Corneoscleral meshwork ✓
• Juxtacanalicular meshwork ✓

4. Schlemm’s canal ✗ is not a component of the trabecular meshwork; it receives aqueous humor after it passes through the meshwork.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which type of radiation is produced using the principle of linear accelerators?
questions.explanation: Linear accelerators (LINACs) are the most common devices used for external beam radiation therapy. They work by accelerating electrons to near light speed and striking a heavy metal target (like tungsten), which results in the production of high-energy X-rays (photons). LINACs can also be configured to deliver electron beams directly. Protons (Option A) are produced in cyclotrons or synchrotrons for specialized proton beam therapy. Gamma rays (Option C) are emitted by the decay of radioactive isotopes like Cobalt-60. Neutrons (Option D) are produced in nuclear reactors or specialized neutron generators. LINACs are favored because they allow for highly precise conformal therapy (like IMRT), targeting the tumor with high-dose X-rays while sparing adjacent healthy organs. Unlike cobalt units, they do not require a radioactive source, making them safer to house and maintain in clinical settings. The ability to vary the X-ray energy allows for the treatment of both superficial and deep-seated tumors

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman presents with fluctuating muscle weakness predominantly involving speech and swallowing. Repetitive nerve stimulation demonstrates a decremental response. Serological testing is negative for acetylcholine receptor (AChR) antibodies. Which other antibody is most likely responsible for her symptoms?
questions.explanation: The patient’s symptoms—fluctuating weakness in speech and swallowing (bulbar symptoms) and a decremental response on nerve stimulation—are typical of Myasthenia Gravis. In patients who are seronegative for AChR antibodies, the Anti-MuSK (Muscle-Specific Kinase) antibody is the most likely culprit. MuSK is essential for clustering AChRs at the neuromuscular junction; its inhibition disrupts signal transmission. Regarding the distractors, Anti-dsDNA (Option A) is a marker for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Anti-TPO (Option C) is associated with autoimmune thyroiditis. Anti-Ro (Option D) is found in Sjogren's syndrome. Because MuSK-positive patients often present with severe bulbar involvement and are negative for the standard AChR test, this antibody specifically matches the patient's clinical and laboratory profile
questions.learning: The patient’s symptoms—fluctuating weakness in speech and swallowing (bulbar symptoms) and a decremental response on nerve stimulation—are typical of Myasthenia Gravis.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 6-year-old boy presents to the psychiatric outpatient department with inattention at school, hyperactivity (excessive talking and difficulty remaining seated), aggressive behavior toward peers, and poor academic performance. Which drug is indicated for the management of this condition?
questions.explanation: The child's symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity (hitting friends, excess talking), and impulsivity (cannot sit still) causing functional impairment in school are classic for Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD). The first-line pharmacological treatment for ADHD in children aged 6 years and older is Methylphenidate, a CNS stimulant. It works by increasing the levels of dopamine and norepinephrine in the prefrontal cortex, helping to improve focus and impulse control. Modafinil (Option B) is used for narcolepsy. Atenolol (Option C) is a beta-blocker. Amitriptyline (Option D) is a tricyclic antidepressant; while sometimes used off-label for ADHD, it is never the first-line choice. Management of ADHD also requires behavioral interventions and parent training. Long-term use of stimulants requires monitoring for side effects like suppressed appetite and growth. Methylphenidate remains the gold-standard treatment for pediatric ADHD
questions.learning: The child's symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity (hitting friends, excess talking), and impulsivity (cannot sit still) causing functional impairment in school are classic for Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A chronic smoker with a 20-year occupational history of working in a cement factory develops mesothelioma. This association is most likely attributable to which exposure?
questions.explanation: Mesothelioma is a malignant tumor of the pleura that is almost exclusively associated with chronic exposure to asbestos fibers. Asbestos is commonly used in construction and cement manufacturing. The inhalation of these fibers leads to chronic pleural inflammation and mutations. Bagassosis (Option A) is caused by exposure to sugar cane dust. Silicosis (Option B) results from inhaling silica dust in industries like sand mining. Coal worker pneumoconiosis (Option D) is caused by long-term coal dust inhalation. While smoking significantly increases the risk of general lung carcinoma in asbestos workers, it is the asbestos exposure itself that is the specific primary cause of mesothelioma. Therefore, given the patient’s occupational history in a cement factory, asbestosis is the underlying causative condition
questions.learning: Mesothelioma is a malignant tumor of the pleura that is almost exclusively associated with chronic exposure to asbestos fibers. Asbestos is commonly used in construction and cement manufacturing.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which one of the following is increased in hypothalamic hamartoma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. GnRH

Hypothalamic hamartoma is caused by increased release of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH).

Hypothalamic hamartoma, a neuronal migration defect, is the most common cause of organic central precocious puberty. The onset of breast development before the age of 8 years in females and the onset of testicular development (>4 mL) before the age of 9 years in males are suggestive of central precocious puberty.

It is a congenital malformation that consists of ectopically located neural tissue characterized by

* Early-onset of puberty

* Seizures associated with unnatural crying or laughing episodes are known as gelastic seizures.

Tuberculous meningitis, tuberous sclerosis, and astrocytomas can also cause central precocious puberty.

Hypothalamic hamartomas are congenital non-progressive lesions in the hypothalamus that occur during foetal development. Two anatomical subtypes are recognised depending on the location of the mass-like lesion. The first type is the intrahypothalamic lesion that connects with the posterior hypothalamus and third ventricle; they appear near the mammillary bodies and are usually associated with gelastic seizures. The second type is the parahypothalamic or pedunculated lesion located near the anterior hypothalamus, tuber cinereum, or pituitary stalk and attaches only to the floor of the third ventricle. It is usually associated with signs of precocious puberty caused by increasing the release of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH). These lesions typically develop a disabling course presenting with multiple seizure types, cognitive decline, and psychiatric symptoms
questions.learning: GnRH Hypothalamic hamartoma is caused by increased release of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH). Hypothalamic hamartoma, a neuronal migration defect, is the most common cause of organic central precocious puberty.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following substances is not considered a micromineral?
questions.explanation: Minerals are divided into macrominerals and microminerals (trace elements) based on the body's daily requirement. Macrominerals are required in amounts greater than 100 mg per day. Calcium is a macromineral (Option A); it is the most abundant mineral in the body, essential for bone structure, muscle contraction, and nerve signaling. Other macrominerals include phosphorus, magnesium, sodium, and potassium. Microminerals (trace elements) are needed in minute amounts, typically less than 15-20 mg per day. Selenium (Option B), iodine (Option C), and copper (Option D) are all classified as microminerals. Iodine is crucial for thyroid hormone synthesis, while selenium and copper act as essential cofactors for various enzymes. Because the body requires significant daily intake of calcium (often 1000 mg or more), it is not a trace element. Therefore, Calcium is the correct answer to this "not" question
questions.learning: Minerals are divided into macrominerals and microminerals (trace elements) based on the body's daily requirement. Macrominerals are required in amounts greater than 100 mg per day.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is correct about CT scan?
options: CT consists of unfiltered x-ray beams
It is the investigation of choice for gallstones
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. CT score of water is 0

The correct statement is that the CT score of water is 0.

On CT, each image consists of a matrix of data points (pixels) that are assigned a number that represents the X-ray attenuation(μ) at that point in the body. CT number is a scaled version of μ that is normalised to the X-ray attenuation of water (μW).

CT = 1000 × (μ/μW − 1)

The resulting numbers are called ‘Hounsfield units’(HU). Due to this normalisation, water is assigned 0 HU, and air is assigned a CT number of −1000 HU.

CT numbers:

• Water = 0 HU
• Solid soft tissues are centred around 0 HU
• Lungs = -1000 HU
• Air = −1000 HU
• Dense cortical bone = +1000 HU
• Acute Blood Clot = 60-90 HU
• Fat = -100 HU

Other options:

Option B: Computed tomography (CT) imaging involves the use of a narrow beam of X-rays that are emitted from a rotating X-ray tube.CT scanners typically use a combination of X-ray beams at different energies and filters to reduce scatter and improve image quality. Therefore, the X-ray beams used in CT imaging are often filtered to enhance image contrast and reduce radiation dose to the patient.

Option C: The investigation of choice for gallstones is an Abdominal ultrasound and not a CT Abdomen. An ultrasound can assess for complications of gallstones, such as inflammation of the gallbladder (cholecystitis) or obstruction of the bile ducts. In cases where ultrasound findings are inconclusive or further characterisation is needed, other imaging modalities such as CT scan or magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) may be used.

Option D: The mSv (millisievert) value for a non-contrast computed tomography (NCCT) scan of the head typically ranges from around 1 to 2 mSv. This radiation dose can vary depending on factors such as the specific CT scanner used, the scanning protocol, and the individual patient characteristics. However, in general, NCCT head scans are associated with relatively low radiation doses compared to other medical imaging procedures.
questions.learning: CT score of water is 0 — The correct statement is that the CT score of water is 0. On CT, each image consists of a matrix of data points (pixels) that are assigned a number that represents the X-ray attenuation(μ) at that point in the body.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Chocolate agar is primarily used for the isolation of which of the following organisms?
questions.explanation: Haemophilus influenzae is a fastidious organism that requires specific growth factors: X (hemin) and V (NAD). These factors are readily available in chocolate agar, which is prepared by heating blood agar to lyse red blood cells and release these nutrients. This organism is a major cause of pediatric meningitis and epiglottitis, particularly strains with the type b capsular polysaccharide. Listeria monocytogenes (Option B) can grow on standard blood agar and does not require lysed cell factors. Streptococcus pneumoniae (Option C) grows best on regular blood agar and requires an enriched carbon dioxide environment rather than heated blood. Escherichia coli (Option D) is a robust gram-negative rod that is typically identified as a lactose fermenter on MacConkey agar rather than requiring specialized chocolate agar. Therefore, chocolate agar is the essential medium for the recovery and diagnosis of H. influenzae in clinical samples
questions.learning: Haemophilus influenzae is a fastidious organism that requires specific growth factors: X (hemin) and V (NAD). These factors are readily available in chocolate agar, which is prepared by heating blood agar to lyse red blood cells and release these nutrients.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: The adult form of echinococcus is seen in which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dog

The adult form of echinococcus is seen in dogs and other canids, which are its definitive hosts.

The larval stage is passed in intermediate hosts such as sheep, cattle, goat, swine, horses, camels, and man. Man acts as an accidental intermediate host (dead end). Human infection follows the ingestion of eggs due to the intimate handling of dogs or by eating raw vegetables or other food contaminated with dog feces.

Note: Humans can become accidental definitive hosts, second intermediate hosts, or paratenic hosts for spirometra. These are cestodes belonging to the Diphyllobothriidae family. They cause a condition called sparagnosis.

The image below shows the life cycle of Echinococcus granulosus.
questions.learning: Dog — The adult form of echinococcus is seen in dogs and other canids, which are its definitive hosts. The larval stage is passed in intermediate hosts such as sheep, cattle, goat, swine, horses, camels, and man.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 26-year-old man presents with a chronic skin lesion that has a rough, scaly surface. Skin biopsy shows marked hyperkeratosis. Based on these clinical and histopathological findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical description of a scaly, rough skin lesion in a young adult is highly suggestive of Psoriasis (Option B). The histopathological finding of marked hyperkeratosis (thickening of the stratum corneum) is a classic feature of psoriasis, along with parakeratosis and acanthosis. Atopic dermatitis (Option A) typically presents as itchy, poorly defined eczematous patches in the flexures, often with a different histological pattern. Pemphigus vulgaris (Option C) and Pemphigus foliaceus (Option D) are autoimmune blistering diseases; they present with fluid-filled vesicles or erosions rather than primary thick scaly plaques. Pemphigus vulgaris specifically involves painful mucosal erosions and deep blisters. Therefore, the specific combination of a chronic scaly plaque and hyperkeratosis on biopsy makes psoriasis the most probable and accurate diagnosis. Psoriasis lesions are typically well-demarcated with silvery scales

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: A 32-year-old man is brought to the emergency department due to progressive confusion and lethargy over the past several hours. The patient has no significant medical history but he has been depressed since a recent breakup with his girlfriend. He works at an automotive repair shop, and one of his coworkers reported seeing the patient consume antifreeze prior to symptom onset. Blood pressure is 110/66 mmHg, pulse is 110/min, and respirations are 24/min. Bilateral costovertebral angles are tender to percussion. Bladder catheterization yields a small amount of bloody urine. Which of the following is most likely to be seen on this patient's arterial blood gas analysis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. pH 7.3, pO2 95, pCO2 24, HCO3 19

Ethylene glycol (antifreeze) poisoning causes high anion gap metabolic acidosis due to metabolism into glycolic and oxalic acids. This leads to:

• ↓ pH (acidemia)
• ↓ HCO₃⁻ (metabolic acidosis)
• Compensatory ↓ pCO₂ from hyperventilation
• Normal PaO₂

Oxalate crystal deposition in kidneys causes flank pain, hematuria, and acute kidney injury.

Thus, ABG shows metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation.
questions.learning: pH 7.3, pO2 95, pCO2 24, HCO3 19 Ethylene glycol (antifreeze) poisoning causes high anion gap metabolic acidosis due to metabolism into glycolic and oxalic acids.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is commonly used for preservation of viscera in toxicology autopsy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Saturated salt solution

A saturated salt solution is used commonly for the preservation of viscera in toxicology autopsy.

Rectified spirit is indicated for most of the poisons, exceptions being alcohol, kerosene, phosphorus, paraldehyde, carbolic acid, acetic acid, etc.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not a component of School Health under Ayushman Bharat Program?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Monthly IFA supplementations

Under the School Health Programme of Ayushman Bharat, services include periodic health check-ups, biannual deworming with albendazole, and menstrual hygiene support, including sanitary napkin distribution.

Iron–folic acid supplementation under this program follows the Weekly Iron and Folic Acid Supplementation (WIFS) strategy, not monthly dosing.

Therefore, monthly IFA supplementation is not a component of School Health under Ayushman Bharat.
questions.learning: Monthly IFA supplementations Under the School Health Programme of Ayushman Bharat, services include periodic health check-ups, biannual deworming with albendazole, and menstrual hygiene support, including sanitary napkin distribution.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient complains of visual blurring which is relieved on its own. Fundus examination showed papilledema. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Amaurosis fugax

Visual blurring in papilledema is called amaurosis fugax

Amaurosis fugax is the transient loss of vision due to an interruption in the blood supply to the retina or brain by emboli or spasms. The onset is abrupt and may follow a falling curtain pattern. The symptoms are relieved upon removal of the insult or the emboli and they recover in the same pattern the vision loss occured.

In papilledema, amaurosis fugax lasts 30-60 seconds. It's usually bilateral but can be unilateral in asymmetric disc edema due to giant cell arteritis or raised intracranial pressure

Other systemic causes can present as amaurosis fugax. Notably, cardiovascular abnormalities like arrhythmias, mitral valve prolapse, venous stasis retinopathies, fibromuscular dysplasia, etc.

Treatment is based on the cause. It's often self-limiting in papilledema. Aspirine or persantine may be used in cases of platelet emboli-induced disease. Severe emboli may require dis-obliteration of the vessels.

Other options:

Option A: Retinal detachment is the separation of retinal epithelium. They may present as visual blurring but is not transient. Fundus examination will show a greyish or whitish tint to the detached portions with evident tears and holes in cases of larger detachments.

Option C: Blindness as per WHO is visual acuity less than 3/60 or corresponding visual field defects in the better eye with the best possible correction.

Option D: Angle-closure glaucoma presents with painful loss of vision with redness. Fundus examination may show hyperemic disc or maybe even normal disc.
questions.learning: Amaurosis fugax Visual blurring in papilledema is called amaurosis fugax Amaurosis fugax is the transient loss of vision due to an interruption in the blood supply to the retina or brain by emboli or spasms.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Sign of effective neonatal resuscitation is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Increased heart rate

An increase in the heart rate is the best sign of effective neonatal resuscitation. The response to neonatal resuscitation at various steps is assessed based on the heart rate.

As soon as a baby is born, the tone, cry, breathing efforts, and respiratory efforts are assessed. If the tone is poor, or if the baby is not breathing, the following measures are done immediately - warming to maintain the normal temperature, proper positioning of the baby's airway, i.e. sniffing position with the head slightly extended, clearing of airway secretions, and tactile stimulation.

After the initial steps of neonatal resuscitation, the heart rate of the baby must be assessed. If the heart rate is < 100 beats per minute (bpm), positive pressure ventilation is provided along with SPO2 monitoring to ensure adequate ventilation.

If the heart rate remains at < 100 bpm, ventilation corrective steps and/or endotracheal intubation have to be considered. The ventilation corrective steps are as follows and can be remembered with the mnemonic MRSOPA.

1. Mask has to be reapplied
2. Reposition head
3. Suction the secretions
4. Open mouth slightly and ventilate
5. Pressure is increased slightly
6. Airway may be changed

If the heart rate is < 60 bpm, chest compressions are initiated over the lower third of the sternum at a rate of 90 compressions/min. The ratio of compressions to ventilation is 3: 1 (90 compressions: 30 breaths).

If the heart rate still remains <60 bpm, despite effective compressions and ventilation, then epinephrine (1:10,000 solution at 0.1–0.3 mL/kg intravenously or 0.5–1 mL/kg intratracheally) should be administered. The dosage can be repeated every 3–5 minutes. Persistent bradycardia may signify inadequate ventilation or severe cardiac compromise.

questions.learning: Increased heart rate — An increase in the heart rate is the best sign of effective neonatal resuscitation. The response to neonatal resuscitation at various steps is assessed based on the heart rate.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 50-year-old diabetic man presents with a progressive increase in pain in his calf, initially after walking a distance of 400m later 200m over the last 6 months. He now prefers to sleep in a seated position by hanging his leg to alleviate pain. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Rest pain

The given clinical scenario describes a case of peripheral arterial disease which has worsened over time. This patient who prefers to sleep in a seated position by hanging his leg to alleviate pain now has rest pain.

Peripheral arterial disease (PAD) presents as intermittent claudication (crampy pain in the muscles). As the disease progresses, claudication distance decreases, and pain occurs even at rest called ischemic rest pain. Rest pain is due to ischemia of the somatic nerves. The pain is exacerbated by lying down or elevation of the foot due to the loss of the gravitational effects on perfusion pressure. It may be lessened by hanging the foot down.

Physical exam findings include atrophied skin, pallor on the raising leg (Buerger's test), nail changes, and decreased peripheral pulses.

The initial investigation done is an ABI. Further investigation is done with Doppler imaging, duplex scan, and digital subtraction angiography. Rest pain is seen when ABI becomes <0.5.

Other options:

Option A: Sciatica - The patient complains of pain radiating down the back of the thigh and calf. Sciatica can either be because of inflammation of the sciatic nerve or because of compression of one of the roots constituting the sciatic nerve

Option B:  Neurogenic claudication occurs with changes in the position of the back such as bending forward and straightening. It takes more time to be relieved by rest (more than 5 minutes). In spinal stenosis, there is an abnormal narrowing of the central canal, the lateral recesses, or the intervertebral foramina to the point where the neural elements are compromised.

Option C: Patients with venous claudication have some form of venous diseases like varicose veins, edema and skin changes due to chronic venous diseases like pigmentation, eczema or ulcers.

Pearl PF1741: Ankle–brachial Pressure Index (ABPI)

The ankle-brachial Pressure Index (ABPI) is the ratio of systolic pressure at the ankle to that in the arm.

The numerator is the highest pressure in the dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial, or peroneal artery and the denominator is the highest brachial systolic pressure.

ABPI Reading
Interpretation

>0.91 < 1.3
Normal

<0.9
Diagnostic of occlusive arterial disease in patients with symptoms of claudication or other signs of ischemia

0.5 to 0.9
Arterial obstruction often associated with claudication

<0.3
Critical limb ischemia (multilevel obstruction i.e any combination of iliac, femoral or tibial vessel disease and may be associated with non-healing ulcerations, ischemic rest pain, or pedal gangrene.

>1.4
Signifies poor compressibility of the arteries. Mostly due to calcification because of increased age, diabetes etc.

Note: A fall in the resting ABPI of more than 20% after exercise is indicative of arterial disease.
questions.learning: Rest pain — The given clinical scenario describes a case of peripheral arterial disease which has worsened over time. This patient who prefers to sleep in a seated position by hanging his leg to alleviate pain now has rest pain.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Hormone degradation as an important mechanism for regulating local concentrations is seen in _________.
options: Degradation of retinoic acid by Cyp26b1 in primordial germ cells of males
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. All of the above

Hormone degradation as an important mechanism for regulating local concentrations is seen in all of the above.

11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase inactivates glucocorticoids in renal tubular cells, preventing actions through the mineralocorticoid receptor.

During development, degradation of retinoic acid by Cyp26b1 prevents the primordial germ cells in the male from entering meiosis, which occurs in the female ovary.

The thyroid hormone deiodinases convert T4 to T3 and can inactivate T3. All the three are hence examples of local hormone degradation being utilized as a method for regulation of hormone concentration locally.
