questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient presents with swelling in MCP joints and his serum uric acid levels were found to be elevated. His physician prescribed a drug which is considered as the first line agent in the management of this condition. What is the mechanism of this drug?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Xanthine oxidase inhibitor

Allopurinol is recommended as the first-line urate-lowering agent in all patients with gout. It is a purine antimetabolite and an inhibitor of xanthine oxidase enzyme.

It prevents the conversion of hypoxanthine and xanthine to uric acid reducing plasma uric acid levels. Allopurinol is also a substrate for xanthine oxidase. The metabolite of allopurinol called oxypurinol is a non-competitive inhibitor of xanthine oxidase.

Febuxostat is a uric acid synthesis inhibitor that acts by inhibiting the enzyme xanthine oxidase and it is indicated in gout management.

Both Febuxostat and Allopurinol are Xanthine Oxidase inhibitors, of which Allopurinol is a hypoxanthine analog.
questions.learning: Xanthine oxidase inhibitor Allopurinol is recommended as the first-line urate-lowering agent in all patients with gout. It is a purine antimetabolite and an inhibitor of xanthine oxidase enzyme.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the characteristic feature seen in ectopic pregnancy? hCG- Human chorionic gonadotropin
options: Ovarian mass with thin layer of endometrium
Empty uterus with adnexal mass and fluid in pelvis
Empty uterus and adnexal mass with ground glass appearance
Trilayer endometrium without an adnexal mass
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Empty uterus with adnexal mass and fluid in pelvis

An empty uterus with an adnexal mass and fluid in pelvis is the sign most suggestive of an ectopic pregnancy.

A pregnancy is considered ectopic if implantation occurs at a site outside the uterine cavity. The majority of ectopic pregnancies occur in the fallopian tube, the ampulla being the most common site.

The most appropriate management for an unruptured ectopic pregnancy is single-dose methotrexate.

Management of ectopic pregnancy:

Expectant management: Ectopic pregnancies measuring <3 cm and with declining beta hCG levels initially <1500 mIU/mL may resolve without intervention and can be managed expectantly.

Medical management with single or multiple-dose methotrexate is preferred if:

* Hemodynamic stability

* Serum beta-hCG ≥1500 mIU/ml and ≤5000 mIU/mL

* Mean sac diameter <3.5cm with no fetal cardiac activity detected on transvaginal ultrasound.

* Patients are willing and able to comply with post-treatment follow-up and have access to emergency medical services within a reasonable time frame in case of a deterioration in the clinical status.

Methotrexate(MTX) can be given as a single IM dose of 50 mg/m2 or as a multiple-dose regimen of 1mg/kg on days 1, 3, 5, and 7.

Surgical management with salpingectomy or salpingostomy is done when:

* Criteria for expectant and medical management are not met

* Gestational sac >3.5 cm

* Fetal cardiac activity present

* Beta hCG > 5000 mIU/mL

* Significant pain and hemoperitoneum

* Failure of expectant or medical management

* Clinical status of patient warrants urgent intervention

* Doubtful compliance with medical management

Milking of the tube through the fimbriae carries a high risk of bleeding, damage to the tube, the persistence of trophoblastic tissue, and recurrence of ectopic pregnancy.

Other Options:

Option A: Ovarian mass with thin layer of endometrium  is suggestive of an ovarian cyst.

Option C: Empty uterus and adnexal mass with ground glass appearance is suggestive of a chocolate cyst/ ovarian endometrioma.

Option D: Trilayer endometrium without an adnexal mass is the physiological state of the uterus.
questions.learning: Empty uterus with adnexal mass and fluid in pelvis — An empty uterus with an adnexal mass and fluid in pelvis is the sign most suggestive of an ectopic pregnancy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 5-year-old child has flexible fingers and can even touch the back of his hand with his wrist extended. The child also demonstrates the sign shown in the image below. On auscultation, a click is heard after S1, followed by a late systolic murmur. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ehlers-Danlos syndrome

The probable diagnosis of the above scenario is Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS) and the image shows Gorlin’s sign which is the ability to touch the tip of the nose with the tip of the tongue. The auscultation finding is of mitral valve prolapse which is a frequent finding in patients with EDS.

The Ehlers–Danlos syndrome (EDS) is a heterogeneous group of heritable connective tissue disorders (HCTDs) characterized by joint hypermobility, skin hyperextensibility, and tissue fragility.

The following diagnostic criteria have been proposed by the 2017 International Classification of the Ehlers–Danlos Syndromes.

Major criteria:

* Skin hyperextensibility and atrophic scarring

* Generalized joint hypermobility (GJH)

Minor criteria:

* Easy bruising

* Soft, doughy skin

* Skin fragility (or traumatic splitting)

* Molluscoid pseudotumors

* Subcutaneous spheroids

* Hernia (or history thereof)

* Epicanthal folds

* Complications of joint hypermobility (e.g., sprains, luxation/ subluxation, pain, flexible flatfoot)

* Family history of a first-degree relative who meets clinical criteria

Minimal diagnostic criteria for classical EDS:

* Major criterion (1): skin hyperextensibility and atrophic scarring

Plus

* Either major criterion (2): GJH

* And/or: at least three minor criteria

Marfan's Syndrome can have joint hypermobility but it is mainly characterised by skeletal abnormalities, including tall stature, long limbs, and arachnodactyly (long, slender fingers).
Given the presence of Gorlin's sign, along with other features like joint hypermobility, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is the probable diagnosis here.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 60-year-old female comes with complaint of unable to bear weight following trivial trauma. X ray of hip and leg is given. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Metastasis

The given scenario of a 60-year-old female with trivial trauma unable to bear weight and X ray findings suggestive of destruction of the hip joint and periarticular bone and shaft of the tibia fracture is most likely due to metastasis.

Its more likely this patient has metastasis because:

• Age: 60-year (old age favors cancer)
• Overall bone denisty is normal

Pathological fractures are fractures that occur in a weakened bone that has structurally changed due to some condition. They occur either spontaneously or due to minor trauma. The features suggestive of a pathological fracture include:

• Pain at the site before the fracture
• Multiple recent fractures
• Elderly patient
• History of primary malignancy
• Unusual fracture pattern (Banana fracture - transverse fracture through an abnormal area of bone, similar to breaking a segment from a banana)

Other Options:

Option A: Brown tumor: Seen in hyperparathyroidism. X-rays show lytic lesions, but this is rare and typically involves long-standing disease in younger patients. Focal osteoblastic activity. Overall bone denisty is low.

Option B: Disseminated TB: Pott’s disease or monoarticular destruction (e.g., hip or spine). Hip joint is usually destroyed and articular surface erosion is present. Disseminated TB rarely causes widespread fractures. Here there is no joint involvement.

Option C: Eosinophilic granulomas: Typically seen in younger individuals (children/young adults). X-rays reveal punched-out lesions, not diffuse destruction.
questions.learning: Metastasis — The given scenario of a 60-year-old female with trivial trauma unable to bear weight and X ray findings suggestive of destruction of the hip joint and periarticular bone and shaft of the tibia fracture is most likely due to metastasis.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a group, the mean blood glucose level is 105 mg/dL with a standard deviation of 10 mg/dL. Assuming a normal distribution, what is the expected range of blood glucose values for approximately 95% of the population? SD-Standard deviation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 85–125 mg/dL

The expected range of blood glucose values for approximately 95% of the population will be 85–125 mg/dL.  For a normal distribution, ~95% of observations lie within ±2 SD of the mean.

To determine the range within two standard deviations in a normal distribution, we use the formula:

Range Mean ±2 × Standard Deviation (SD)

Given data: Mean = 105, Standard Deviation = 10

So, Range  = Mean +/- 2 SD.

Calculation:
Lower limit=105−(2×10)=105−20= 85

Upper limit=105+(2×10)=105+20=125

Hence, the range of blood pressure of 95% of the population will be 85–125 mg/dL.

Pearl PF0301: Normal Distribution

* Normal distribution is the most widely used continuous distribution.

* It is also called bell curve (bell shaped) or Gaussian distribution after a mathematician named Karl Friedrich Gauss.

* The following is an image of three different types of normal distributions.

* Normal distributions are defined by two parameters: the mean and the standard deviation.

* The mean, median and mode are all equal in a normal distribution.

* All normal distributions are symmetric and have bell-shaped density curves with a single peak.

* Exactly half of the values are to the left of the centre and the other half to the right.

* The total area under the curve is 1.

* The density of a normal distribution is more around the centre and less around the tails.

* There is no skew in the curve.

* Looking at the figure below, we can understand the empirical rule of a normal distribution which states that:

* Approximately 68% of the distribution falls within one standard deviations of the mean (mean ± 1 SD).

* Approximately 95% of the distribution falls within two standard deviations of the mean (mean ± 2 SD).

* Approximately 99.7% of the distribution falls within three standard deviations of the mean (mean ± 3 SD).

* Many data like blood pressure, heights, IQ scores, etc. form a normal distribution.

* A standard normal distribution is a normal distribution with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1.
questions.learning: 85–125 mg/dL The expected range of blood glucose values for approximately 95% of the population will be 85–125 mg/dL. For a normal distribution, ~95% of observations lie within ±2 SD of the mean.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is not seen in Meniere's Disease?
questions.explanation: Meniere's disease is an inner ear disorder caused by the excessive accumulation of endolymph (endolymphatic hydrops). It is classically defined by a clinical triad: episodic vertigo (lasting minutes to hours), fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, and low-frequency, roaring tinnitus. Aural fullness or a "blocked ear" sensation is also a frequent accompanying symptom. Ear pain (otalgia), however, is notably absent in uncomplicated Meniere's disease and usually suggests secondary infections or a different diagnosis. Tinnitus (Option A), vertigo (Option B), and ear fullness (Option C) are all hallmarks of the condition. Diagnosis is typically confirmed via audiometry showing low-frequency sensorineural loss, while treatment involves low-sodium diets, diuretics, and vestibular suppressants

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the basis for the formation of omphalocele?
options: Physiological hernia failing to go back
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Physiological hernia failing to go back

Omphalocele is protrusion of abdominal contents through the umbilical ring. It is due to failure of physiological hernia to reduce into the abdominal cavity, which results in non-closure of the umbilical ring. .

An omphalocele may contain stomach, liver, and intestines. And these contents are enclosed in a sac.

Omphalocele is usually associated with other congenital anomalies (e.g., trisomy 13, trisomy 18, or Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome) and with increased levels of α-fetoprotein.

Note: In gastroschisis, there is an absence of a membranous sac and is paraumbilical.
questions.learning: Physiological hernia failing to go back Omphalocele is protrusion of abdominal contents through the umbilical ring. It is due to failure of physiological hernia to reduce into the abdominal cavity, which results in non-closure of the umbilical ring. .

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is incorrect about iron absorption?
options: RBC protophyrin is increased in deficiency
Iron excretion is only through skin, gut and urothelial cells
Body cannot compensate if more than 10 RBC/HPF per day is lost in urine
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ferrireductase convert Fe2+ to Fe 3+

Ferrireductase is an enzyme that converts Fe3+ (ferric iron) to Fe2+ (ferrous iron),  not the other way around. Ferrous is the form of iron that is more readily absorbed in the gut.

Almost all the iron absorption occurs in the duodenum.

Most of the iron in the diet is in the ferric (Fe3+) form, whereas it is the ferrous (Fe2+) form that is absorbed.

Body iron stores are controlled by intestinal absorption as there is no exit to iron from the body. Divalent metal transporter 1 (DMT1) transports non-heme iron into the enterocyte. Iron absorption in the duodenum is regulated by hepcidin release from the liver in response to increases in intrahepatic iron levels. It binds to ferroportin leading to endocytosis and degradation within the enterocyte. This prevents the transfer of iron from enterocyte to plasma resulting in iron trapping within duodenal cells in the form of mucosal ferritin. The trapped iron is lost as these cells are sloughed. The iron transported by ferroportin into the plasma is transferred to other parts with the help of transferrin and stored as serum ferritin and hemosiderin. The image depicting iron absorption and storage is given below:

Other options:

Option B: RBC protoporphyrin is increased in deficiency, increased protoporphyrin levels in red blood cells can indicate iron deficiency or disorders of heme synthesis.

Option C: Iron is primarily excreted through the gut, skin, and urinary tract, but the body generally has very limited mechanisms for iron excretion compared to iron absorption and recycling.

Option D: The body’s iron homeostasis is finely tuned, and a significant loss of red blood cells, such as more than 10 ml per day, can overwhelm the body’s ability to compensate and maintain iron balance.
questions.learning: Ferrireductase convert Fe2+ to Fe 3+ Ferrireductase is an enzyme that converts Fe3+ (ferric iron) to Fe2+ (ferrous iron), not the other way around. Ferrous is the form of iron that is more readily absorbed in the gut.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A woman at 8 weeks of gestation is diagnosed with hyperthyroidism. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment option?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Propylthiouracil

Propylthiouracil is preferred in the first trimester because methimazole/carbimazole are teratogenic and linked to embryopathy.

| Trimester | Drug of Choice | Reason

| --------- | -------------- | ------

| 1st trimester | ⭐ PTU | Less teratogenic

| 2nd & 3rd trimester | Methimazole | Less hepatotoxic

PTU also reduces peripheral T4→T3 conversion, helping rapid control of thyrotoxicosis. After the first trimester, therapy is often switched to methimazole due to PTU hepatotoxicity risk.

| Drug | Mechanism

| ---- | ---------

| PTU | ↓ T3/T4 synthesis + ↓ T4 → T3 conversion

| Methimazole | ↓ T3/T4 synthesis only

Methimazole causes teratogenic effects:

| Defect | Description

| ------ | -----------

| Aplasia cutis | Absence of scalp skin

| Choanal atresia | Nasal blockage

| Esophageal atresia | Feeding difficulty

Radioactive iodine is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 10-year-old child is brought to the clinic for routine immunization. According to the National Immunization Schedule, which vaccine is administered at this age?
questions.explanation: According to the National Immunization Schedule of India, the standard vaccine administered to children when they reach 10 years of age is the Tetanus and adult Diphtheria (Td) booster (previously ). A subsequent dose of Td is given at 16 years of age. BCG (Option B) is given at birth to protect against severe forms of tuberculosis. DTP (Option D) is given as primary doses in infancy and boosters at 16–24 months and 5–6 years of age. MMR (Option C) is not part of the standard national schedule, although the Measles-Rubella (MR) vaccine is given at 9 and 16–24 months. The Td booster is critical for maintaining long-term immunity against tetanus, especially as older children become more active and prone to injuries. It also helps maintain immunity against diphtheria in the adolescent and adult population. Clinicians must ensure that this often-missed booster is provided during school health visits or regular clinic check-ups
questions.learning: According to the National Immunization Schedule of India, the standard vaccine administered to children when they reach 10 years of age is the Tetanus and adult Diphtheria (Td) booster (previously ).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A person wants to study about the relationship between smoking and lung cancer, so he collects data about people diseased with lung cancer from government hospitals and the number of cigarette packets sold at the same time period. Which type of study is this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ecological

The type of study described is an ecological study as the unit of study is the population. The number of cigarette packets sold at the same time is data about the population.

Option A: The unit of study in a cross-sectional study is an individual.

Option C: There is no experiment done here. Hence, it is not experimental study.

Option D: Quasi-experiments are nonrandomized, pre-post intervention studies done when it is not feasible or ethical to conduct a randomized controlled trial. The unit of study is therefore patients or individuals and not population.
questions.learning: Ecological — The type of study described is an ecological study as the unit of study is the population. The number of cigarette packets sold at the same time is data about the population.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following sensory receptors are responsible for tactile discrimination?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Meissner’s corpuscle

Meissner’s Corpuscles are responsible for discriminative touch.

Meissner’s corpuscles are encapsulated receptors found in the dermis of the non-hairy skin, most commonly on the fingertips, lips, and other locations where tactile discrimination is very good. Their field of reception is very small and hence used for two-point discrimination. These are rapidly adapting receptors that encode

• Point discrimination
• Precise location
• Tapping
• Flutter

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with ocular pain, redness, and blurred vision. On slit-lamp examination, the pupil is shown in the image. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Posterior synechiae due to anterior uveitis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Posterior synechiae due to anterior uveitis

Posterior synechiae are adhesions between the posterior surface of the iris and the anterior lens capsule, most commonly resulting from anterior uveitis (iritis/iridocyclitis). These adhesions produce an irregular, distorted ("festooned") pupil that responds poorly to light and dilating agents. If circumferential (360°), they may cause seclusio pupillae, leading to iris bombe and secondary angle-closure glaucoma.

Why not the other options?

• B. Acute angle-closure glaucoma – Typically presents with a mid-dilated, vertically oval, fixed pupil, not an irregular pupil due to iris–lens adhesions.
• C. Adie’s tonic pupil – Characterized by a large, regular pupil with poor light reaction but preserved slow constriction during near response (light-near dissociation). There are no synechiae.
• D. Oculomotor nerve palsy – Causes a dilated, fixed pupil associated with ptosis and ophthalmoplegia, but the pupil remains round, not irregular.

High-yield pearl

• Irregular pupil → Think posterior synechiae (anterior uveitis).

Differentiate common pupillary abnormalities:

| Condition | Characteristic pupil

| --------- | --------------------

| Anterior uveitis | Irregular, constricted pupil due to posterior synechiae

| Acute angle-closure glaucoma | Mid-dilated, fixed, often vertically oval pupil

| Adie’s tonic pupil | Large, regular pupil with light-near dissociation

| Oculomotor nerve palsy | Dilated, fixed, round pupil with ptosis and "down-and-out" eye
questions.learning: Posterior synechiae due to anterior uveitis Posterior synechiae are adhesions between the posterior surface of the iris and the anterior lens capsule, most commonly resulting from anterior uveitis (iritis/iridocyclitis).

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A patient receiving the antipsychotic haloperidol develops acute dystonia. What is the next best step in management?
questions.explanation: Acute dystonia (involuntary muscle contractions, such as torticollis or oculogyric crisis) is a common and distressing extrapyramidal side effect of high-potency first-generation antipsychotics like Haloperidol. The next best step and standard acute treatment is the administration of an anticholinergic agent, such as Benztropine or Procyclidine, which rapidly reverses the muscle spasm. Fluphenazine (Option C) is another high-potency antipsychotic that would likely worsen the dystonia. Increasing the dose of haloperidol (Option D) is strictly contraindicated and would exacerbate the condition. Changing to clozapine (Option B) is a long-term strategy for refractory patients but is not the immediate treatment for an acute dystonic episode. After reversing the dystonia, the overall treatment plan should be reviewed, often by switching the patient to an atypical antipsychotic with lower extrapyramidal risk. Bedside recognition and rapid pharmacological reversal are essential for patient comfort and safety
questions.learning: Acute dystonia (involuntary muscle contractions, such as torticollis or oculogyric crisis) is a common and distressing extrapyramidal side effect of high-potency first-generation antipsychotics like Haloperidol.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 40-year-old patient accidentally swallowed a fish bone and presented with choking. On examination, the bone was found to be impacted in the esophagus at the level of T4 vertebra. Which of the following structures is responsible for the obstruction at this level?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Arch of aorta

The esophagus has physiological constrictions, one of which occurs at the T4 vertebral level due to the arch of aorta crossing anterior to the esophagus.

This site is a common location for foreign body impaction, especially fish bones.

The cricopharyngeal junction lies at C6, the left bronchus crosses at T5–T6, and the diaphragm constriction is at T10.
questions.learning: Arch of aorta — The esophagus has physiological constrictions, one of which occurs at the T4 vertebral level due to the arch of aorta crossing anterior to the esophagus.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 50-year-old man presents with episodic headaches, excessive sweating, and palpitations, and imaging shows a small mass in the left adrenal gland. Which investigation would best confirm the suspected diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The triad of recurrent headaches, sweating (diaphoresis), and palpitations in the presence of an adrenal mass is highly suggestive of a pheochromocytoma. Pheochromocytoma is a catecholamine-secreting tumor that typically arises from the adrenal medulla. Vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) is a major metabolic end-product of catecholamines (epinephrine and norepinephrine) excreted in the urine. Therefore, measuring 24-hour urinary VMA levels is a standard confirmatory test for this condition. Blood or urine 5-HIAA (Option B) is used to diagnose carcinoid syndrome, which presents with flushing and diarrhea. Urine myoglobin (Option C) is a marker for rhabdomyolysis. Stool trypsin (Option D) is used to evaluate pancreatic exocrine function in cystic fibrosis. Consequently, because VMA levels directly reflect the excessive catecholamine production characteristic of pheochromocytoma, this is the most appropriate test for confirmation
questions.learning: The triad of recurrent headaches, sweating (diaphoresis), and palpitations in the presence of an adrenal mass is highly suggestive of a pheochromocytoma.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 3-year-old male is brought into the OPD by his mother. She complains that his left eyelid is constantly drooping. Physical examination reveals that the eyeball is abducted and depressed in its primary position. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 3rd nerve palsy

The clinical scenario is suggestive of oculomotor nerve palsy (3rd nerve palsy).

In primary gaze, the patient's left eye has deviated down and out. There is also profound ptosis due to the weakness of the levator muscle. Due to the involvement of the superior rectus and medial rectus, elevation and adduction will be impaired. Abduction and depression in the primary position (down and out) due to unopposed action of the lateral rectus and superior oblique muscles. All of these findings indicate left oculomotor nerve palsy.

The signs of left oculomotor nerve palsy are summarised in the image attached below.

In trochlear nerve palsy (4th nerve palsy), the superior oblique is affected, causing:

* The weakness of depression: Mainly seen when the eye is adducted (depression during abducted position is a function of the Inferior rectus)

* Weakness of abduction

* Failure of intorsion: cause of diplopia.

In abducens nerve palsy (6th nerve palsy), the lateral rectus is affected. Due to the involvement of only the lateral rectus, abduction will be impaired.

In facial nerve palsy (7th nerve palsy), there is facial weakness.
questions.learning: 3rd nerve palsy The clinical scenario is suggestive of oculomotor nerve palsy (3rd nerve palsy). In primary gaze, the patient's left eye has deviated down and out.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text:
A patient with varicose veins comes with complaints of eczema over the same region. What is the stage of the clinical classification according to the CEAP guidelines?

CEAP - Clinical-Etiology-Anatomy-Pathophysiology classification of chronic venous disorders
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. C4a

A patient with varicose veins and overlying eczema is classified as C4a under CEAP guidelines.

The Clinical-Etiology-Anatomy-Pathophysiology (CEAP) classification system is used to classify chronic lower extremity venous disease.

The clinical class of C4 under CEAP includes changes in skin and subcutaneous tissue secondary to chronic venous disease. It is further classified as follows:

• C4a - Pigmentation or eczema
• C4b - Lipodermatosclerosis or atrophie blanche
• C4c - Corona phlebectatica

Image A shows tortuous dilated veins - C2, image B shows atrophie blanche - C4b, and image C shows fan-shaped telangiectasia - C4c.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 15-year-old girl presents with itchy lesions on her arm as shown. Her family history is positive for asthma. What could be the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Atopic dermatitis

The clinical scenario depicting pruritic lesions at a flexural site along with a family history of atopy (asthma) is suggestive of atopic dermatitis (AD) or atopic eczema (AE). The scratch marks and excoriations shown in the image are due to pruritis, which is the hallmark feature of AD.

AD is a chronic relapsing inflammatory condition. It presents with erythematous macules, papules and vesicles that often start in early childhood, usually less than 2 years old. The lesions later become excoriated and lichenified. It is frequently associated with dryness of the skin and secondary infections. In infancy, the lesions initially appear on face (sparing the napkin area) and later on extensor aspect of knees and elbows as the child starts crawling. In later childhood and in adults, the principal site of involvement is flexures.

The filaggrin monomers in keratinocytes in the epidermis bind and aggregate keratin bundles and intermediate filaments to form the epidermal barrier. Any damage/dysfunction of this barrier is associated with an increased risk of developing AD. Damage to this barrier can be due to environmental factors (detergents, hard water, UV light) or local inflammatory reactions. Dysfunction of the barrier can be due to genetic mutation of the FLG gene leading to reduced filaggrin production or local immunomodulatory effects leading to reduced filaggrin expression.

Other options:

Option A: Seborrheic dermatitis is a chronic inflammatory skin condition characterized by erythema, pruritus, scaling, flaking, or crusting of the skin. It is often associated with Malasezzia fungal infection. A milder form of seborrheic dermatitis of the scalp is commonly known as dandruff.

Option C: Allergic contact dermatitis (ACD) is an inflammatory condition caused due to a delayed hypersensitivity reaction (Type 4 hypersensitivity) to a specific allergen that comes into direct contact with the skin.Patients usually present with pruritus, erythema, swelling, papules, and papulovesicles. Some common allergens include nickel (found in artificial jewelry), PPD/Para phenylene diamine (in hair dye), chromate (in cement), rubber or latex, cosmetics, etc. Patch test (image below) is used for the diagnosis of ACD.

Option D: Erysipelas is a bacterial skin infection caused by Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Streptococcus) characterized by raised, erythematous sharply demarcated rapidly spreading skin lesions, along with systemic symptoms like fever and chills. The skin may also have a peau d'orange or orange peel-like appearance.
questions.learning: Atopic dermatitis — The clinical scenario depicting pruritic lesions at a flexural site along with a family history of atopy (asthma) is suggestive of atopic dermatitis (AD) or atopic eczema (AE).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 20-year-old male presents with acute epigastric pain and fever. He has a past history of cholelithiasis. On examination, abdominal guarding and rigidity present. His serum amylase, lipase are raised and patient has leucocytosis. What is true regarding his condition?
options: Serum amylase remains elevated even after 30 days of resolution of acute pancreatitis
Serum lipase is more specific than serum amylase
Increase in the level of serum lipase is directly proportional to the severity
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Serum lipase is more specific than serum amylase

The patient presents with features suggestive of acute pancreatitis (epigastric pain, fever, history of cholelithiasis, guarding/rigidity, raised serum amylase and lipase, and leukocytosis). For acute pancreatitis, serum lipase is more specific than serum amylase.

Lipase has a higher specificity for diagnosing acute pancreatitis, as elevated amylase can occur in other conditions such as salivary gland disorders, intestinal obstruction, or renal failure. Lipase also remains elevated longer than amylase.

The diagnostic criteria for acute pancreatitis require at least two of the following three features:

1. Characteristic Abdominal Pain:
Acute onset of severe epigastric pain, often radiating to the back.
Pain may worsen after eating and is associated with nausea and vomiting.
2. Serum Lipase and/or Amylase Elevation:
At least 3 times the upper limit of normal (ULN).
Lipase is preferred due to its higher specificity and longer half-life.
3. Imaging Findings:
Characteristic findings of pancreatitis on imaging (CT scan, MRI, or ultrasound), such as:
Pancreatic enlargement
Peripancreatic fluid collections
Inflammatory changes in and around the pancreas

Other Options:

Option A: Amylase levels normalize within 3-5 days after an episode of acute pancreatitis.

Option C: Hypocalcemia is more commonly observed, due to fat saponification in severe cases.

Option D: The degree of elevation of serum lipase does not correlate with the severity of acute pancreatitis. Severity is assessed using clinical scores like Ranson's criteria, APACHE II, or CT severity index.
questions.learning: Serum lipase is more specific than serum amylase — The patient presents with features suggestive of acute pancreatitis (epigastric pain, fever, history of cholelithiasis, guarding/rigidity, raised serum amylase and lipase, and leukocytosis).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following viruses spreads predominantly through water?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. HAV (Hepatitis A Virus)

Hepatitis A virus spreads by the fecal–oral route, classically through contaminated water and food. It causes acute, self-limited hepatitis and is linked to poor sanitation and outbreaks. In contrast, HBV, HCV, and HDV are transmitted parenterally via blood or body fluids. Waterborne transmission is a key epidemiologic hallmark of HAV.

| Feature | HAV | HBV | HCV | HDV | HEV

| ------- | --- | --- | --- | --- | ---

| Transmission | Feco-oral | Blood/sexual | Blood | Blood | Feco-oral

| Chronicity | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ (high) | ✅ | ❌ (except pregnancy severe)

| Envelope | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ❌

| Vaccine | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | (via HBV) | ❌

| Special note | Waterborne outbreaks | Vertical transmission | Silent chronic | Needs HBV | Severe in pregnancy

• HAV & HEV = Enterically transmitted
• HBV, HCV, HDV = Parenteral
• HAV:

• No carrier state
• No chronic hepatitis
• Lifelong immunity after infection
questions.learning: HAV (Hepatitis — A Virus) Hepatitis A virus spreads by the fecal–oral route, classically through contaminated water and food. It causes acute, self-limited hepatitis and is linked to poor sanitation and outbreaks.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Early cord clamping is done in which of the following cases?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Non-vigorous baby

Early cord clamping will be done in the case of a non-vigorous baby.

Early cord clamping is performed within the first 60 seconds after birth, typically when the newborn requires urgent resuscitation. A non-vigorous baby, characterised by poor respiratory effort, low muscle tone, or a heart rate below 100 beats per minute, necessitates immediate intervention, making ECC necessary.

Indications for early cord clamping include:

* Babies needing immediate resuscitation: In emergencies, rapid neonatal stabilisation takes precedence, and delayed cord clamping (DCC) may not be possible.

* Fetal hydrops

* Maternal or placental complications: Situations such as placental abruption or postpartum hemorrhage may require early clamping to ensure maternal safety.

Delayed cord clamping involves waiting for a minimum of 1-3 minutes after birth before clamping the umbilical cord. It is recommended for both term and preterm babies as part of standard delivery care.

Benefits of DCC:

* In term infants, delayed umbilical cord clamping leads to higher haemoglobin levels at birth, improved iron stores during the first few months of life, and a reduced risk of neonatal anaemia.

* In preterm infants, delayed cord clamping is associated with lower rates of intraventricular haemorrhage and necrotising enterocolitis, as well as a decreased need for blood transfusions.
questions.learning: Non-vigorous baby Early cord clamping will be done in the case of a non-vigorous baby. Early cord clamping is performed within the first 60 seconds after birth, typically when the newborn requires urgent resuscitation.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is true regarding an increase in Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR)?
options: Increase in the resistance of the afferent arteriole
Decrease in the resistance of the efferent arteriole
Increase in Bowman's capsule hydrostatic pressure
questions.explanation: The Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) is determined by the balance of Starling forces across the glomerular capillaries. An increase in renal perfusion (blood flow to the kidney) increases the hydrostatic pressure within the glomerular capillaries, which directly leads to an increase in GFR. Increasing the resistance of the afferent arteriole (Option A) would decrease flow and pressure, thus decreasing GFR. Decreasing the resistance of the efferent arteriole (Option B) allows blood to exit the glomerulus more easily, lowering the filtration pressure and decreasing GFR. Increasing Bowman's capsule hydrostatic pressure (Option C)—which might happen in a urinary tract obstruction—opposes filtration and decreases GFR. In essence, GFR is increased by anything that "pushes" more fluid out of the blood and into the capsule, primarily high glomerular capillary pressure. This pressure is regulated by the relative constriction or dilation of the afferent and efferent arterioles, a process known as renal autoregulation

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the statements below accurately describes p53?
options: It increases telomere length in the liver.
It is stable by preventing genome mutation.
It retains the telomerase enzyme in the nucleus
questions.explanation: The p53 protein is widely known as the "guardian of the genome." Its primary function is to maintain cellular and genetic stability by preventing genome mutation. When DNA damage is detected, p53 halts the cell cycle at the G1/S checkpoint to allow for repair. If the damage is too severe, p53 triggers apoptosis (programmed cell death) to prevent the propagation of mutated cells. Loss or mutation of the TP53 gene is found in more than 50% of all human cancers. Options A and D refer to the function of telomerase, which maintains the ends of chromosomes. Option B is incorrect as p53 is a transcription factor that regulates gene expression rather than a polymerase that synthesizes RNA directly. By acting as a critical tumor suppressor, p53 ensures that cells with damaged DNA do not divide. Understanding the p53 pathway is fundamental to modern oncology and the study of cellular responses to stress and carcinogens
questions.learning: The p53 protein is widely known as the "guardian of the genome." Its primary function is to maintain cellular and genetic stability by preventing genome mutation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient is brought to the casualty following a road traffic accident. He is tachypneic and uses accessory neck muscles for respiration. His BP is 90/60 mm Hg. On percussion, the right chest is hyper-resonant. On auscultation, breath sounds could not be heard on the right chest. An urgent chest X-ray is done. What is the next best step of management?
options: Tube thoracostomy at 5th intercostal space anterior to mid-axillary line
Needle decompression at 5th intercostal space anterior to mid-axillary line
Needle decompression at 5th intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line
Needle decompression at 2nd intercostal space anterior to mid-axillary line
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Needle decompression at 5th intercostal space anterior to mid-axillary line

The above patient with hemodynamic instability, tachypnea and hyper-resonant sounds on percussion with absent breath sounds on auscultation along with the radiolucency and mediastinal shift on X-ray is suggestive of tension pneumothorax. Immediate management is done with needle decompression or needle thoracostomy i.e. insertion of a wide-bore needle in the 5th ICS anterior to the midaxillary line.

Tension pneumothorax is a life-threatening emergency when air leaks from the lungs into the pleural cavity and cannot escape. This leads to compression of the lung field with mediastinal shift and collapse of lung parenchyma. This can be diagnosed clinically with high index of suspicion and immediate decompression with wide bore needle in the 5th intercostal space should be done.

Definitive management - tube thoracostomy or chest tube insertion in the 5th ICS in the triangle of safety.

Triangle of safety:

The boundaries are

* Anteriorly - lateral border of the pectoralis major

* Posteriorly- latissimus dorsi

* Inferiorly- a line perpendicular to the nipple going to the back

For pediatric patients, needle decompression is done at the midclavicular line in the 2nd intercostal space.

The images below show the triangle of safety and technique of chest drain insertion.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis in a patient who presents with recurrent vomiting followed by hematemesis after excessive alcohol consumption?
questions.explanation: The clinical history of recurrent vomiting followed by hematemesis (vomiting blood) shortly after heavy alcohol use is pathognomonic for Mallory-Weiss syndrome. This condition involves non-transmural mucosal lacerations at the gastroesophageal junction, caused by the sudden increase in intra-abdominal pressure during forceful retching. Esophageal carcinoma (Option B) typically presents with progressive dysphagia and weight loss in older adults rather than acute alcohol-related hematemesis. Achalasia cardia (Option C) is a motility disorder characterized by a "bird's beak" appearance on barium swallow and chronic difficulty swallowing. Boerhaave's syndrome (Option D) is a much more severe condition involving transmural rupture of the esophagus, often presenting with excruciating chest pain, shock, and subcutaneous emphysema rather than simple hematemesis. Most Mallory-Weiss tears are self-limiting and heal within a few days with supportive care, though severe bleeding may require endoscopic intervention. Therefore, based on the specific temporal relationship with alcohol and vomiting, Mallory-Weiss is the correct diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical history of recurrent vomiting followed by hematemesis (vomiting blood) shortly after heavy alcohol use is pathognomonic for Mallory-Weiss syndrome.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which antihypertensive drug is contraindicated in pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Enalapril, an Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme (ACE) inhibitor, is strictly contraindicated in pregnancy due to its severe teratogenic effects. It blocks the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, which is vital for fetal renal development. Exposure, particularly in the second and third trimesters, can cause fetal renal dysgenesis, leading to oligohydramnios and Potter sequence (lung hypoplasia and limb deformities). Methyldopa (Option A) is a preferred, safe choice for chronic hypertension in pregnancy. Labetalol (Option B) is commonly used for preeclampsia and hypertensive emergencies. Nifedipine (Option D) is a calcium channel blocker that is also considered safe for managing pregnancy-associated hypertension. Other ACE inhibitor risks include hypocalvaria (skull hypoplasia) and neonatal renal failure. Therefore, ACE inhibitors must be discontinued immediately when pregnancy is planned or confirmed to protect the fetus
questions.learning: Enalapril, an Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme (ACE) inhibitor, is strictly contraindicated in pregnancy due to its severe teratogenic effects. It blocks the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, which is vital for fetal renal development.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The probable diagnosis based on the below clinical image of the breast is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mondor's disease

The image shows a thrombosed subcutaneous cord attached to the skin of the breast which is the pathognomic feature of Mondor's Disease.

Mondor’s disease is the thrombophlebitis of the superficial veins of the breast and anterior chest wall. It may also occur in the arm or penis. On raising the arm, the skin over the chest gets stretched and a narrow, shallow groove alongside the cord is seen. It is treated by restricting arm movements and usually subsides within a few months without recurrence, complications, or deformity.

The differential diagnosis to be considered is lymphatic permeation from an occult carcinoma of the breast.

Other options:

Option A: Paget’s disease is a type of ductal carcinoma in situ arising from the nipple and commonly presents as nipple erosion.

Option B: Zuska’s disease, also called recurrent periductal mastitis, is a condition of recurrent retroareolar infections and abscesses. Smoking has been implicated as a risk factor for this condition. Managed symptomatically by antibiotics coupled with incision and drainage as necessary.

Option D: Tietze’s syndrome refers to the benign inflammation of one or more costal cartilages.
questions.learning: Mondor's disease — The image shows a thrombosed subcutaneous cord attached to the skin of the breast which is the pathognomic feature of Mondor's Disease.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 23-year-old woman presents with acute right lower abdominal pain for 4 hours, with tenderness at McBurney’s point. Which investigation is most appropriate to confirm a diagnosis of appendicitis?
questions.explanation: While acute appendicitis is often a clinical diagnosis based on history and tenderness at McBurney's point, a CT Scan of the abdomen (ideally with contrast) is currently the most accurate and "best suited" investigation to confirm the diagnosis (Option A) . It has high sensitivity and specificity for identifying an inflamed appendix, periappendiceal fat stranding, or an appendicolith. A plain X-ray (Option B) is rarely useful and may only show non-specific signs. Serum ESR (Option C) is a non-specific marker of inflammation that does not provide localized diagnostic information. MRI (Option D) is highly accurate but is generally reserved as a second-line option for pregnant patients or children to avoid ionizing radiation. Therefore, for a 23-year-old non-pregnant female, the CT scan remains the definitive gold standard imaging modality. It allows for prompt surgical planning and helps rule out other pelvic pathologies like ovarian torsion
questions.learning: While acute appendicitis is often a clinical diagnosis based on history and tenderness at McBurney's point, a CT Scan of the abdomen (ideally with contrast) is currently the most accurate and "best suited" investigation to confirm the diagnosis (Option A) .

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis for this condition?
questions.explanation: The clinical triad of miosis (constricted pupil), mild ptosis (drooping eyelid), and anhidrosis (loss of sweating) on one side of the face is diagnostic of Horner syndrome. This syndrome results from a lesion in the sympathetic nerve pathway from the hypothalamus to the eye. The pupil remains small in dim lighting (dilation lag) because the sympathetic dilator muscle is paralyzed. Adie's tonic pupil (Option A) presents with a dilated pupil that reacts slowly to light. A blind eye (Option C) would show an afferent pupillary defect but not ptosis or anhidrosis. An Argyll Robertson pupil (Option D) is characterized by bilateral small pupils that accommodate but do not react to light, often associated with neurosyphilis. Because the patient exhibits the complete classic triad of sympathetic failure, Horner syndrome is the definitive diagnosis. Further investigation is required to locate the lesion along the first, second, or third-order neurons
questions.learning: The clinical triad of miosis (constricted pupil), mild ptosis (drooping eyelid), and anhidrosis (loss of sweating) on one side of the face is diagnostic of Horner syndrome.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Deamination of methylated cytosine forms which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Thymine

Deamination of methylated cytosine forms thymine.

Deamination is the removal of an amino group(NH2) from a chemical compound. Enzymes that catalyze this reaction are called deaminases. Deamination of 5-methylcytosine forms thymine.

Other significant deaminations are given below:

• Deamination of adenosine forms inosine. This is a metabolic step involved in uric acid formation by purine catabolism. It is mediated by the enzyme adenosine deaminase (ADA). ADA deficiency leads to sparse or defective T cells and B cells and patients suffer from Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID).
• Deamination of cytosine leads to uracil formation - The production of apolipoprotein B-48 (apoB-48) in the intestine is the result of RNA editing in the intestine. This involves post-transcriptional deamination of cytosine to uracil by enzyme cytidine deaminase. This converts sense codon (CAA) in the mRNA to nonsense codon (UAA)at a single specific site. This edited mRNA translates to apoB-48.
• Deamination of guanine forms xanthine. This is a metabolic step involved in uric acid formation by purine catabolism.
questions.learning: Thymine Deamination of methylated cytosine forms thymine. Deamination is the removal of an amino group(NH2) from a chemical compound.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 45-year-old male with a history of smoking and NSAID use presents with multiple episodes of hematemesis and melena. He is pale and hypotensive. After stabilization, an upper GI endoscopy reveals erosion of a posterior duodenal ulcer in the first part of the duodenum with an active spurt. Which artery is most commonly responsible for this finding?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Gastro-duodenal artery

A posterior duodenal ulcer can erode into the gastroduodenal artery (GDA), leading to massive upper gastrointestinal bleeding, presenting as hematemesis, melena, hypotension, and shock. This is a surgical emergency if bleeding cannot be controlled endoscopically.

• The first part (D1) of the duodenum lies directly anterior to the gastroduodenal artery.
• A posteriorly penetrating duodenal ulcer erodes the artery, causing profuse arterial hemorrhage.

Why not the other options?

• B. Left gastroepiploic artery: Runs along the greater curvature of the stomach.
• C. Right gastroepiploic artery: Supplies the greater curvature; not related to posterior D1 ulcers.
• D. Splenic artery: Related to the pancreas and posterior stomach, not the first part of the duodenum.
questions.learning: Gastro-duodenal artery — A posterior duodenal ulcer can erode into the gastroduodenal artery (GDA), leading to massive upper gastrointestinal bleeding, presenting as hematemesis, melena, hypotension, and shock.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following ion channels in peripheral chemoreceptors is oxygen-sensitive?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. K+

Potassium channels in the peripheral chemoreceptors are oxygen-sensitive.

Type I glomus cells (carotid and aortic body) have O2-sensitive K+ channels, whose conductance is reduced in proportion to the degree of hypoxia.

This reduces the K+ efflux, depolarizing the cell and causing Ca2+ inﬂux.

Hypoxia induces vasoconstriction by inhibition of oxygen-sensitive potassium channels in pulmonary vascular smooth muscle cell membranes. This leads to depolarization of the cell membrane and activation of calcium channels causing the influx of calcium ions. The Ca2+ influx triggers action potentials and consequent excitation of the afferent nerve endings and constriction of small arteries and arterioles.

When the concentration of O2 in the alveoli decreases below normal the adjacent blood vessels constrict. This effect is opposite to the effect observed in systemic vessels, which dilate rather than constrict in response to low O2 levels.

This is because the low oxygen concentrations can :

* Stimulate the release of or increase sensitivity to vasoconstrictor substances such as endothelin or reactive oxygen species.

* Decrease the release of vasodilators such as nitric oxide from the lung.
questions.learning: K+ Potassium channels in the peripheral chemoreceptors are oxygen-sensitive. Type I glomus cells (carotid and aortic body) have O2-sensitive K+ channels, whose conductance is reduced in proportion to the degree of hypoxia.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following features is most helpful in identifying a nasal discharge as cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) rhinorrhea?
questions.explanation: The "Halo sign" (or double-ring sign) is a classic bedside test used to identify CSF rhinorrhea. When blood-stained nasal discharge is dropped onto a piece of filter paper or a handkerchief, the blood remains in the center while the clear CSF migrates further to the periphery, forming a clear ring or "halo" around the central blood spot. The Handkerchief sign (Option B) refers to the fact that CSF does not stiffen a handkerchief upon drying, unlike nasal mucus. Schwartz sign (Option C) is a reddish hue on the tympanic membrane seen in otosclerosis. Phelps sign (Option D) is a radiological sign associated with glomus tumors. For a 23-year-old male with potential head trauma and nasal discharge, the presence of the halo sign on a handkerchief provides immediate clinical evidence of a dural tear. Definitive diagnosis usually requires testing for beta-2 transferrin

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Identify the vitamin which when deficient can lead to neonatal seizures.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pyridoxine

Pyridoxine deficiency can cause refractory seizures in the neonatal period and infancy.

Pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (P5P) is the active form of pyridoxine and functions as a cofactor for enzymes involved in neurotransmitter synthesis, amino acid metabolism, and glycogen metabolism. Intracellular P5P deficiency in the brain can lead to a seizure disorder that does not respond to typical anticonvulsant medications but shows a response to pyridoxine.

Antiquitin deficiency is the most common cause of pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy (due to mutations in the ALDH7A1 alleles)

They primarily present with generalized seizures in the early days of life. The seizures can be of various types, recurrent focal motor seizures, generalized tonic seizures, and myoclonus. Additional manifestations may include dystonia, respiratory distress, abdominal distention with vomiting, hepatomegaly, hypoglycemia, and hypothermia.

Increased α-aminoadipic semialdehyde and pipecolic acid levels are observed in the CSF, plasma, and urine. Treatment with vitamin B6 (50-100 mg/day) shows significant improvement in seizures. Life-long therapy is needed.

Other options:

Option B: Thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency causes beriberi.

Option C: Riboflavin (vitamin B2) deficiency causes glossitis, cheilosis, keratitis, and corneal vascularization.

Option D: Pantothenic acid (vitamin B5) deficiency causes burning feet syndrome.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the primary factor responsible for the demographic burden?
questions.explanation: The "demographic burden" typically refers to the socio-economic strain placed on the working-age population (usually 15-64 years) to support the non-working segments. In modern demographic transitions, the most significant and growing factor is the increased old age dependency ratio. As life expectancy increases and birth rates decline (demographic aging), there are more elderly individuals requiring healthcare and pensions relative to the fewer workers available to fund these systems. While an increased young age dependency (Option B) also creates a burden, it is often seen as a temporary "investment" in future productivity. Decreased dependency ratios (Options A and C) actually represent a "demographic dividend" or relief rather than a burden. Therefore, the long-term structural burden associated with an aging population is the primary concern described by this demographic term
questions.learning: The "demographic burden" typically refers to the socio-economic strain placed on the working-age population (usually 15-64 years) to support the non-working segments.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A doctor received a summons from the criminal court to provide evidence as an expert witness, but two days earlier, he had also received a summons from the civil court. What should the doctor do in this situation?
options: Attend the summons for the criminal case
Attend the summons in the civil court
Attend the court for the summons received first and inform the other court accordingly.
Inform both the courts and wait
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Attend the summons for the criminal case

When a doctor receives a summons from the civil and criminal courts, priority should be given to attending the summons for the criminal case first.

A summons is a document compelling the attendance of a witness in a Court of law under penalty, on a particular day, time, and to give evidence.

Priority of summons

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presents with fever after returning from a trip to a forested area. On examination, a black eschar is observed on the abdomen. What is the most likely diagnosis, and what is the drug of choice for its treatment?
questions.explanation: The presence of fever and a characteristic black eschar (the necrotic site of the mite bite) following a forest trip is pathognomonic for Scrub Typhus. This bacterial infection is caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi and is transmitted to humans via chigger mites. The standard treatment and drug of choice for rickettsial infections like scrub typhus is Doxycycline. Penicillin (Option A) is ineffective against these intracellular organisms. Ceftriaxone (Option C) is used for various bacterial infections like typhoid or meningitis but not for rickettsial diseases. Artesunate (Option D) is an antimalarial used for severe P. falciparum malaria. Given the forest exposure and the presence of the eschar, scrub typhus managed with doxycycline is the most accurate clinical diagnosis and treatment plan
questions.learning: The presence of fever and a characteristic black eschar (the necrotic site of the mite bite) following a forest trip is pathognomonic for Scrub Typhus.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 24-year old male patient presents with anemia. His father and paternal aunt had a similar illness that was treated successfully by splenectomy. His peripheral blood smear is similar to that shown in the illustration below. Which of the following additional abnormalities is expected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Howell-Jolly bodies

The above image showing spherocytes present on the peripheral blood smear and, along with the history, strongly suggest a diagnosis of hereditary spherocytosis (HS). The presence of Howell-Jolly bodies is an additional abnormality which can be expected here.

It is an autosomal dominant inheritance disorder. It is due to defective ankyrin, band 3, spectrin, or band 4.2 proteins causing a defect in the red cell membrane. This causes red cells to shed membrane vesicles and transform into spherocytes. The non-deformable spherocytes get trapped in the splenic cords and are phagocytosed by macrophages.

* Most common mode of inheritance of HS: Autosomal dominant

* Most common gene mutation in autosomal dominant HS: Ankyrin > Band 3

Clinical presentation:

The patients usually present with anemia, gall stones, splenomegaly, and jaundice but the age of presentation varies with the severity of the disease. They might also have a family history.

Aplastic crisis might occur where red cell production comes to a halt due to parvovirus infection. This lasts for 1 to 2 weeks which is usually the time required for the immune system to clear the virus. Blood transfusions may be needed during this period.

Morphology :

* The most common finding is spherocytosis, which presents as small, dark-staining (hyperchromic) red cells without the central zone of pallor but this is not specific to HS.

* Features seen in HS are :

* Reticulocytosis- increased reticulocyte count

* Howell-Jolly bodies- dense basophilic nuclear remnants in the RBCs.

* Marrow erythroid hyperplasia

* Hemosiderosis

* Splenomegaly as a result of congested Billroth cords and increased phagocytes.

Diagnosis:

Based on family history, peripheral smear findings, and laboratory investigations an adequate diagnosis is made. Increased osmotic fragility is seen in majority of the cases. They also show an increased MCHC (mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration) due to cellular dehydration.

Note- Heinz bodies: Undeterred oxidation of hemoglobin in the RBCs leads to the formation of denatured precipitates known as Heinz bodies. These bodies damage the RBC membrane. When these RBCs pass through the splenic cords, macrophages pluck out these precipitates, giving them the characteristic appearance of bite cells. They are seen in cases of chemical poisoning, drug toxicity, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, or the presence of unstable hemoglobin (e.g. hemoglobin Köln)

Below image shows Heinz bodies and bite cells.
questions.learning: Howell-Jolly bodies — The above image showing spherocytes present on the peripheral blood smear and, along with the history, strongly suggest a diagnosis of hereditary spherocytosis (HS).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the best imaging study for diagnosis of cerebral infarct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Diffusion weighted MRI

Diffusion-weighted MRI is the most sensitive investigation for diagnosis of cerebral ischemia.  It is particularly useful for identifying acute ischemic changes in the brain due to its ability to detect diffusion restriction of water molecules in the brain tissue.

Diffusion restriction: hyperintense on DWI and hypointense on ADC.

●       Diffusion restriction is seen with:

1.     Acute stroke

2.     Hypercellular tumors

3.     Abscess

4.     Epidermoid cyst

5.     Keratin-Craniopharyngioma/ Cholesteatoma

Other Options:

Option A: FLAIR MRI: Fluid-Attenuated Inversion Recovery (FLAIR) MRI is useful for identifying older infarcts and chronic changes but is less sensitive in the acute phase of a stroke.

Option B: Non-contrast CT: While commonly used for initial assessment due to its availability and speed, it is less sensitive in the early stages of a stroke, often not showing changes until several hours post-onset.

Option D: СECT (Contrast-Enhanced CT): Typically used to assess for complications or other causes of symptoms but not as sensitive as DWI for early detection of cerebral infarcts.

Educational Objective

Diffusion-weighted MRI is the optimal choice for early detection of cerebral infarcts, making it an indispensable tool in acute stroke management. Its ability to show diffusion restriction provides critical information that can influence therapeutic decisions.
questions.learning: Diffusion weighted MRI Diffusion-weighted MRI is the most sensitive investigation for diagnosis of cerebral ischemia. It is particularly useful for identifying acute ischemic changes in the brain due to its ability to detect diffusion restriction of water…

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Human papillomavirus (HPV) is most commonly associated with which of the following carcinoma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Oropharyngeal carcinoma

Human papillomavirus (HPV), especially type 16, is most strongly associated with oropharyngeal carcinoma, particularly involving the tonsil and base of tongue.

·         HPV-related cancers arise from oropharyngeal lymphoid tissue

·         Mechanism: Viral oncoproteins E6 and E7 inactivate p53 and Rb tumor suppressor genes

·  Epidemiology:

o    Often seen in younger patients

o    Less association with smoking/alcohol compared to other head & neck cancers

·   Prognosis: Better prognosis than HPV-negative tumors

Why not other options:

·   Nasopharyngeal carcinoma: Associated with Epstein–Barr virus (EBV)

·   Laryngeal carcinoma: Strongly linked to smoking and alcohol

·  Hypopharyngeal carcinoma: Also related to tobacco and alcohol, not HPV
questions.learning: Oropharyngeal carcinoma Human papillomavirus (HPV), especially type 16, is most strongly associated with oropharyngeal carcinoma, particularly involving the tonsil and base of tongue. · HPV-related cancers arise from oropharyngeal lymphoid tissue ·…

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child with recurrent episodes of cough and cold is diagnosed with an acyanotic congenital heart disease suggestive of a ventricular septal defect (VSD). Which type of murmur is most commonly heard?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pansystolic

Ventricular septal defect (VSD) is the most common congenital heart disease and classically produces a harsh pansystolic (holosystolic) murmur, best heard at the left lower sternal border due to left-to-right shunting across the ventricular septum.

Key clinical features:

• Small VSD: Loud, harsh pansystolic murmur with a palpable thrill.
• Large VSD: Softer murmur (due to equalization of ventricular pressures), recurrent respiratory infections, failure to thrive, and signs of congestive heart failure.

Exam Pearl:

• VSD → Pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border.
• Large left-to-right shunts may produce an apical mid-diastolic flow murmur due to increased mitral inflow, but the characteristic murmur of VSD remains the pansystolic murmur.
• Untreated large VSDs can progress to pulmonary hypertension and Eisenmenger syndrome, resulting in reversal of the shunt (right-to-left) and cyanosis.
questions.learning: Pansystolic Ventricular septal defect (VSD) is the most common congenital heart disease and classically produces a harsh pansystolic (holosystolic) murmur, best heard at the left lower sternal border due to left-to-right shunting across the ventricular septum.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the embryological cause of this anomaly?
options: Failure of fusion of metanephric duct
questions.explanation: The anomaly shown is a unicornuate uterus, which results from the developmental failure of one paramesonephric (Müllerian) duct. Normally, the two paramesonephric ducts must fuse at the midline to form the uterus, cervix, and upper vagina. If one duct fails to develop or fuse properly with its counterpart, it results in a single-sided uterine cavity, often accompanied by a small rudimentary horn. Non-fusion of the mesonephric ducts (Option A) would affect male reproductive anatomy, such as the vas deferens. "Metanephric duct" (Option C) is an incorrect term, as the metanephros forms the kidneys, not the uterus. Complete agenesis (Option D), known as Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser syndrome, would result in the total absence of the uterus and upper vagina. Therefore, the partial failure of Müllerian duct development is the correct embryological cause
questions.learning: The anomaly shown is a unicornuate uterus, which results from the developmental failure of one paramesonephric (Müllerian) duct. Normally, the two paramesonephric ducts must fuse at the midline to form the uterus, cervix, and upper vagina.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient post-tonsillectomy in the recovery room starts bleeding from the operative site. On examination, blood clots are seen. What will be your immediate management?
options: Shift to OT, remove the clots, and cauterize/ligate the vessel
Shift to OT, start IV antibiotics, and pack the tonsillar fossa
Give anticoagulants, repeated gargling, and wait for 24 hours
Do blood transfusion and wait and watch
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Shift to OT, remove the clots, and cauterize/ligate the vessel

The given clinical picture suggests reactionary hemorrhage post-tonsillectomy. The immediate management is to shift the patient to OT, remove the clots, and cauterize/ligate the bleeding vessel.

Hemorrhage is a common complication of tonsillectomy. It can be primary, reactionary, or secondary.

Primary hemorrhage occurs at the time of operation. It can be controlled by pressure, ligation, or electrocoagulation of the bleeding vessels.

Reactionary hemorrhage occurs within 24 hours. It may be due to improper clipping action of the superior constrictor muscle.

The tonsillar artery perforates the superior constrictor and ramifies in the tonsil. Therefore, the presence of a clot can hinder the clipping action of the superior constrictor muscle, leading to hemorrhage. Slippage of ligature, or blood pressure returning to normal are other causes.

It is managed by removing the clot and application of pressure or vasoconstrictor. Ligation or electrocoagulation of the bleeding vessels is done under anesthesia if the above measures fail.

The image below shows the relation between the superior constrictor muscle and the tonsillar artery at the tonsillar bed.

Secondary hemorrhage is usually seen between the 5th to 10th postoperative day, due to sepsis and premature separation of the membrane. Clots are removed, IV antibiotics are given and the bleeding vessel is electrocoagulated or ligated if bleeding continues.
questions.learning: Shift to OT, remove the clots, and cauterize/ligate the vessel The given clinical picture suggests reactionary hemorrhage post-tonsillectomy. The immediate management is to shift the patient to OT, remove the clots, and cauterize/ligate the bleeding vessel.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text:
True regarding POAG:

A. Abnormality of the trabecular meshwork is seen on gonioscopy
B. Family members are likely to develop steroid responsiveness.
C. Dilatation of the pupil is associated with exacerbation of IOP
D. First degree relatives are at 1% increased risk of POAG
E. Visual field defect can exist with normal C:D ratio
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. B and E only

In primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG), family members are likely to develop steroid responsiveness (statement B) and visual field defect can exist with a normal C:D ratio (statement E).

Statement A: Gonioscopy cannot visualize the specific abnormalities that occur in the trabecular meshwork in POAG. Gonioscopy diagnoses POAG because of the visibility of all the structures of the angle of the anterior chamber in contrast to the non-visibility of different structures in angle closure glaucoma.

Statement C: Primary angle-closure glaucoma is associated with exacerbation of IOP with pupillary dilatation and not POAG.

Statement D: There is a 10% increased risk of POAG in siblings and a 4% increased risk in children of patients with POAG.

POAG also known as chronic simple glaucoma of adult-onset is characterized by the presence of any 2 of the following 3 categories of changes:

• Increased intraocular pressure:

• IOP >21mmHg on more than one occasion, and/or
• Circadian variation in IOP of >8 mmHg, or
• Asymmetry in IOP > 5 mmHg between both eyes

• Optic nerve head changes suggestive of glaucomatous damage. These may include one or more of the following changes:

• Vertically oval cup
• Cup-disc (C:D) ratio > 0.6 (average cup: disc ratio 0.3-0.4)
• Asymmetry in C:D ratio > 0.2 between both eyes.
• Narrowing, notching, or pallor of the neuroretinal rim.
• Disc haemorrhages
• Nasal shifting of retinal vessels-Bayonetting sign
• Lamellar dot sign

• Visual field changes - isopter contraction, barring of blind spot, paracentral scotoma, Seidel's scotoma, Bjerrum's scotoma, double arcuate scotoma, and Roenne's central nasal step.

A patient presenting with just raised IOP and visual field defects with normal optic nerve head findings such as a normal C:D ratio can still be diagnosed as POAG (statement E).
questions.learning: B and E only — In primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG), family members are likely to develop steroid responsiveness (statement B) and visual field defect can exist with a normal C:D ratio (statement E).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient had a pulmonary mass which shows IHC staining with TTF-1 as shown in the image. What is the likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Adenocarcinoma lung

TTF-1 positivity is characteristic of primary lung adenocarcinoma, reflecting origin from type II pneumocytes or Clara cells.

• Thyroid Transcription Factor-1
• Nuclear transcription factor
• Expressed in:

• Lung adenocarcinoma
• Small cell carcinoma

Squamous cell carcinoma is TTF-1 negative, while small cell carcinoma can be TTF-1 positive but shows neuroendocrine markers and different morphology.

Thus, TTF-1 staining in a pulmonary mass most strongly supports adenocarcinoma of the lung.

| Option | Tumor Type | TTF-1 Status | When it is Correct | Why NOT Correct Here | Exam Pearl

| ------ | ---------- | ------------ | ------------------ | -------------------- | ----------

| A. Squamous cell carcinoma | Central tumor | ❌ Negative | Keratin pearls, smoking | ❌ TTF-1 negative | p40, CK5/6 positive

| B. Adenocarcinoma ✅ | Peripheral tumor | ✔ Positive | ✔ Most common lung cancer | ✔ Correct |  TTF-1 hallmark

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A poor farmer with a history of successive crop failure develops progressive spastic paraparesis, signs of upper motor neuron paralysis, and gait instability. Name the toxin responsible for this condition.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Beta-oxalyl-amino-alanine

The clinical picture describes neurolathyrism, a chronic neurological disorder seen in populations consuming Lathyrus sativus (khesari dal) during periods of famine or crop failure.

The causative neurotoxin is β-oxalyl-amino-alanine (BOAA), which leads to upper motor neuron damage and progressive spastic paraparesis.

BOAA acts as a neurotoxic excitatory amino acid.

Effects:

• Degeneration of upper motor neurons
• Damage to corticospinal tract
• Progressive spastic paralysis of lower limbs

Importantly:

• Sensory system remains normal
• Bladder control usually preserved

This condition is classically associated with poverty, drought, and dietary dependence on a single pulse, distinguishing it from mycotoxin-related illnesses.
questions.learning: Beta-oxalyl-amino-alanine — The clinical picture describes neurolathyrism, a chronic neurological disorder seen in populations consuming Lathyrus sativus (khesari dal) during periods of famine or crop failure.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 52-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with a palpable breast lump. Targeted breast ultrasound shows a hypoechoic lesion with angular margins and significant asymmetry compared with surrounding parenchyma. Which of the following ultrasound findings is NOT typically associated with malignant breast lesions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Posterior acoustic enhancement

Malignant breast lesions on ultrasound typically show suspicious features such as:

• Irregular or angular margins

• Poorly circumscribed/spiculated borders

• Hypoechoic solid mass

• Architectural distortion and asymmetry

• Posterior acoustic shadowing (due to dense fibrous stroma)

Posterior acoustic enhancement is more commonly seen in benign lesions (e.g., cysts, fibroadenomas) because sound waves pass easily through fluid or uniform tissue, producing increased echoes behind the lesion.
questions.learning: Posterior acoustic enhancement Malignant breast lesions on ultrasound typically show suspicious features such as: • Irregular or angular margins • Poorly circumscribed/spiculated borders • Hypoechoic solid mass • Architectural distortion and asymmetry •…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with symmetrical flaccid weakness of the lower limbs along with absence of spinal cord reflexes. This clinical presentation is suggestive of which condition?
questions.explanation: The symptoms of symmetric lower limb flaccidity and areflexia (no cord reflex) are characteristic of Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS). GBS is an acute, autoimmune polyradiculoneuropathy that causes demyelination of peripheral nerves. It typically presents as a "ground-to-brain" ascending paralysis, beginning with weakness in the legs. Multiple sclerosis (Option B) is a central nervous system disorder that usually presents with upper motor neuron signs like spasticity and hyperreflexia. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (Option C) involves both upper and lower motor neuron signs but typically presents with asymmetric onset and fasciculations. Spinal cord injury (Option D) usually presents with a clear sensory and motor level and, after the initial shock phase, leads to spasticity rather than persistent flaccidity. Thus, the rapid onset of symmetric flaccid paralysis and absent reflexes is a clinical hallmark of the peripheral nerve involvement seen in GBS
questions.learning: The symptoms of symmetric lower limb flaccidity and areflexia (no cord reflex) are characteristic of Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS). GBS is an acute, autoimmune polyradiculoneuropathy that causes demyelination of peripheral nerves.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is altered in thyroid profile throughout pregnancy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Total T3 level

Total T3 levels are altered throughout pregnancy.

Total T3 and total T4 increase due to stimulation of thyroid tissue by hCG (α-subunit of hCG is similar to TSH) during the early period of gestation. However, there is no change in free T3 and T4 due to an increase in thyroid-binding globulin (TBG).

This leads to a transient fall in TSH (but remains in the normal range) during the early weeks of gestation. The level of TSH becomes normal during the second and third trimesters.

Unchanged

FSH (Follicle-stimulating hormone)
TSH

Prolactin
DHEAS (Di-hydro epiandrosterone)
ADH (Anti-  diuretic hormone)

Total T3, T4

Aldosterone

Testosterone, Androstenedione, and cortisol
