questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the indication of this procedure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Keratoconus

The given image shows the placement of Intacs, which is done for keratoconus.

Keratoconus or conical cornea is a non-inflammatory condition of the axial cornea. Central or paracentral thinning of the cornea and apical protrusion of the anterior cornea are pathognomonic. This is attributed to mucopolysaccharide and collagen tissue synthesis defects.

Clinical features of the condition include defective vision, which develops due to progressive myopia and irregular astigmatism. Light sensitivity and ocular irritation may also be present. Complications include acute hydrops due to rupture of Descemet's membrane.

Slit-lamp examination reveals Fleischer's ring at the base of the cone formed. Deep, vertical stromal striae (Vogt lines) that disappear on external pressure are characteristic. Retinoscopy shows a yawning reflex.

The image below shows Munson's sign i.e. bulging of the lower lid on looking down.

The severity of the condition is graded based on keratometry. Corneal topography is a diagnostic modality with the highest sensitivity for early cases.

Intacs or intracorneal ring segments are useful in moderate cases, due to their flattening effect. Rigid gas permeable contact lenses, corneal collagen cross-linking with riboflavin, and keratoplasty are the other treatment modalities.

Other options:

Option B - Vogt's limbal girdle is a degenerative corneal disease that is more commonly seen in women aged ≥40 years. A white crescentic limbal band can be seen at 9 and/or 3 'o'clock position, more frequently on the nasal side. In type I, a swiss-cheese hole pattern with a clear zone separating it from the scleral margin can be observed. Type II is more common and lacks a clear zone and holes.

Option C - Keratoglobus is a familial disorder, marked by thinning and hemispherical protrusion of the entire cornea. It can be congenital or acquired. Globular protrusion is seen here, in contrast to the conical ectasia seen in keratoconus. Intrastromal ring segments and cross-linking can be used for management.

Option D - Corneal dystrophy is used to describe a group of non-inflammatory conditions, with bilateral opacification of the cornea with no vascularisation. These are divided into epithelial, Bowman layer, stromal, Descemet membrane, and endothelial dystrophies. Most conditions have genetic abnormalities.
questions.learning: Keratoconus — The given image shows the placement of Intacs, which is done for keratoconus. Keratoconus or conical cornea is a non-inflammatory condition of the axial cornea.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not a part of case-control studies?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Follow up

Among the given options, follow-up is not a part of case-control studies.

Case-Control Studies are also called retrospective studies. This study proceeds from effect to cause and is done after the exposure and outcome have occurred. They focus on diseases or health problems that have already developed. They are less time-consuming and have no risk of attrition because they do not require follow-up.

There are four basic steps in conducting a case-control study:

• Selection of cases and controls
• Matching- This is done to ensure comparability between cases and controls. Controls are selected such that they are similar to cases with respect to certain pertinent selected variables that influence the disease outcome.
• Measurement of exposure - This is obtained by interviews, questionnaires, or study of the past records of cases.
• Analysis in the form of exposure rates, risk ratio, and odds ratio.

Odds Ratio (OR) calculated from a case-control study, is a measure of the strength of the association between risk factor and outcome.

Note: Follow-up is a part of cohort studies. The elements in cohort studies include selecting study subjects, obtaining data on exposure, selecting comparison groups, follow up and analysis.
questions.learning: Follow up Among the given options, follow-up is not a part of case-control studies. Case-Control Studies are also called retrospective studies.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Gold standard investigation for endometriosis?
questions.explanation: Laparoscopy is universally recognized as the gold-standard investigation for the diagnosis of endometriosis. It allows for direct visualization of the characteristic "powder-burn" or "mulberry" lesions on the peritoneal surfaces and pelvic organs. Ideally, suspicious areas are biopsied for Histopathological Examination (HPE, Option A), which provides the definitive proof of endometrial glands and stroma; however, the procedure of laparoscopy itself is the diagnostic standard. Ultrasound (Option C) and MRI (Option D) are valuable for identifying deep infiltrating endometriosis or an "endometrioma" (chocolate cyst) in the ovary, but they are not sensitive enough to rule out superficial peritoneal disease. Endometriosis classically presents with the triad of dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and dyschezia, often leading to chronic pelvic pain and infertility. During laparoscopy, the stage of the disease is assigned based on the American Society for Reproductive Medicine (ASRM) classification, which guides subsequent medical or surgical management
questions.learning: Laparoscopy is universally recognized as the gold-standard investigation for the diagnosis of endometriosis. It allows for direct visualization of the characteristic "powder-burn" or "mulberry" lesions on the peritoneal surfaces and pelvic organs.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The statement, “Health is a dynamic equilibrium between man and environment and disease a maladjustment of the human organism to environment” explains which one of the following concepts of health?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ecological

The ecological concept of health defines health as a dynamic equilibrium between the individual and the environment. Disease occurs when this balance is disturbed, leading to maladjustment between the human organism and its environment. This concept emphasizes the interaction of host, agent, and environment, which forms the basis of modern epidemiology.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A.  Biomedical concept:

• Defines health as the absence of disease.
• Focuses on biological causes and medical treatment, largely ignoring social and environmental factors.

• C. Psychosocial concept: Emphasizes the influence of psychological, social, cultural, economic, and political factors on health.
• D. Holistic concept: Integrates physical, mental, social, environmental, and spiritual well-being, representing the broadest concept of health.
questions.learning: Ecological — The ecological concept of health defines health as a dynamic equilibrium between the individual and the environment. Disease occurs when this balance is disturbed, leading to maladjustment between the human organism and its environment.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A teenager is brought to the OPD with history of amenorrhea. On examination, she is short statured, has a webbed neck, low hairline at the back of the neck. Further examination revealed widely spaced nipples. Karyotyping in this patient would reveal which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 45 X0

This patient most likely has turner's syndrome, with 45 XO.

Turner's syndrome is a chromosomal abnormality with partial or complete monosomy of the X chromosome (45+XO). In Turner's syndrome, gonadal dysgenesis causes primary ovarian failure that is hypogonadism. The clinical picture of amenorrhea, short stature, webbed neck, low hairline at the back of the neck, widely spaced nipples, and lack of secondary sexual characteristics is seen in Turner's syndrome.

Important features associated with Turner's syndrome: (mnemonic: See A Baby CLOWN Here)

* Short stature, Short fourth metacarpal, Sensorineural hearing loss, Shield chest

* Amenorrhea (primary), infertility

* Barr body absent

* Cardiac defects, Cubitus valgus, Congenital lymphedema

* L: Learning disabilities

* Ovaries underdeveloped (streak ovaries), Gonadoblastoma (increased risk if Y chromosome material is present)

* Webbed neck

* Nipples widely spaced

* Horseshoe kidneys

The image below shows webbed neck.

Option D - 47 XXY: Klinefelter's syndrome occurs in males with a 47 XXY karyotype and is associated with testicular dysfunction and male infertility.
questions.learning: 45 X0 This patient most likely has turner's syndrome, with 45 XO. Turner's syndrome is a chromosomal abnormality with partial or complete monosomy of the X chromosome (45+XO).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following microorganisms cannot be grown on artificial culture media?
questions.explanation: Mycobacterium leprae, the causative agent of leprosy, is an obligate intracellular pathogen. A hallmark of this organism is its total inability to grow on any artificial or cell-free culture media. For experimental purposes, it is cultivated in animal models, such as the footpads of mice or the nine-banded armadillo. Staphylococcus aureus (Option B) grows easily on standard media like blood agar. Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Option C) is slow-growing but cultivable on Löwenstein-Jensen (LJ) media. Streptococcus pneumoniae (Option D) is fastidious but grows on enriched media. The failure of M. leprae to grow in vitro is attributed to its massive gene decay, having lost many essential metabolic pathways. Therefore, it remains the classic example of a bacterium that cannot be cultured using standard microbiological techniques
questions.learning: Mycobacterium leprae, the causative agent of leprosy, is an obligate intracellular pathogen. A hallmark of this organism is its total inability to grow on any artificial or cell-free culture media.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Among the direct causes of maternal mortality during or shortly after labor and delivery, which is the most common contributor to maternal deaths?
questions.explanation: In the context of global health and obstetric care, Hemorrhage (specifically Postpartum Hemorrhage or PPH) remains the most prevalent and leading direct cause of maternal mortality worldwide. PPH can occur rapidly after delivery and is often defined as blood loss exceeding 500 ml following vaginal birth or 1000 ml after a cesarean section. While Anemia (Option D) is a major indirect cause and a significant risk factor that exacerbates the effects of blood loss, it is not the primary direct mechanism of death. Embolism (Option A), including amniotic fluid embolism or pulmonary embolism, and pre-existing Heart Disease (Option B) are significant contributors but occur with much lower frequency than hemorrhage. Effective management of PPH involves active management of the third stage of labor, use of uterotonics like oxytocin, and timely surgical intervention if medical therapy fails. Reducing deaths from hemorrhage is a cornerstone of global initiatives aimed at achieving Sustainable Development Goal targets for maternal health
questions.learning: In the context of global health and obstetric care, Hemorrhage (specifically Postpartum Hemorrhage or PPH) remains the most prevalent and leading direct cause of maternal mortality worldwide.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The upstroke of action potential (phase 0) in the sinoatrial node is due to ______________ ?
options: Sodium influx via voltage gated sodium channels
Influx of both sodium and calcium
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Calcium currents only

The upstroke of action potential (phase 0) in the sinoatrial node is due to calcium currents only. It occurs due to the influx of Ca2+ ions by the opening of voltage-gated L-type channels.

The action potential of the SA node differs from that of the atria, ventricles, and Purkinje fibres in the following ways: (1) In the absence of neural input, the SA node demonstrates automaticity and the ability to produce its own action potentials. (2) It has an unstable resting membrane potential. (3) It has no sustained plateau.

The resting membrane potential (RMP) of the SA node is -55 to -60 millivolts. Phases of this potential are:

• Phase 0 (Upstroke wave)-  This is due to the influx of Ca2+ ions by the opening of voltage-gated L-type channels.
• Phase 3 (Downstroke wave)- This is due to the efflux of K+ leading to repolarization. (Option C)
• Phase 4 (Prepotential)- Because of ongoing K+ efflux, hyperpolarization sets in. This makes the channel more permeable to Na+ ions and since these Na+ channels are activated during hyperpolarization they are referred to as funny currents (Ih/ If). They form the first half of the pre-potential. The second half of the prepotential is completed by the opening of the voltage-gated T-(transient) type Ca2+ channel. The slope of Phase 4 in the SA node determines the heart rate.
questions.learning: Calcium currents only — The upstroke of action potential (phase 0) in the sinoatrial node is due to calcium currents only. It occurs due to the influx of Ca2+ ions by the opening of voltage-gated L-type channels.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 42-year-old labourer developed a sudden, severe and persistent headache, accompanied by vomiting and neck pain. He was evaluated at the nearest hospital where an emergency computed tomography was negative for stroke. Which one of the following investigations is best to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lumbar puncture after 12 hours

The presentation is highly suggestive of subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH): sudden, severe “thunderclap” headache with vomiting and neck pain/meningism. A CT scan may be negative, particularly when performed after the early period. In a patient with persistent clinical suspicion and a negative CT, lumbar puncture can demonstrate RBCs and xanthochromia in the CSF.

The question specifically specifies LP after 12 hours, which is important because xanthochromia becomes detectable several hours after the hemorrhage.

Why not the others?

• A. EEG: Used to evaluate seizures/epileptiform activity; does not confirm SAH.
• B. Carotid Doppler: Evaluates carotid stenosis; not useful for diagnosing SAH.
• D. Upper GI endoscopy: Has no role in evaluating thunderclap headache.
questions.learning: Lumbar puncture after 12 hours — The presentation is highly suggestive of subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH): sudden, severe “thunderclap” headache with vomiting and neck pain/meningism.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which hormones are produced from the zones labelled in the image given?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. A-aldosterone, B-cortisol, C-androgens, D-epinephrine

Option D is the correct option. This is a section through an adrenal gland showing both the medulla and the zones of the cortex. Following are the zones of the cortex and medulla, and the hormones they secrete.

A – Zona Glomerulosa  – secretes mineralocorticoids (aldosterone)

B – Zona Fasciculata  – secretes glucocorticoids (cortisol, corticosterone)

C – Zona Reticularis –  secretes androgens (dehydroepiandrosterone)

D – Adrenal Medulla – Produces Catecholamines: Norepinephrine, Epinephrine, and Dopamine

On histological examination, the different layers are identified as:

• Outer zona glomerulosa - small, compact cells
• Central zona fasciculata - larger lipid-rich cells arranged in radial columns
• Inner zona reticularis - pigmented, compact cells
• Adrenal medulla - thin layer of large chromaffin cells
questions.learning: A-aldosterone, B-cortisol, C-androgens, D-epinephrine Option D is the correct option. This is a section through an adrenal gland showing both the medulla and the zones of the cortex.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The treatment of paucibacillary leprosy consists of MDT (which comprises rifampicin, dapsone, and clofazimine). The latest recommended regimen is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 3 drug therapy for 6 months

The latest recommendation is 3 drug therapy for 6 months to treat paucibacillary (PB) leprosy by WHO. The regimen consists of rifampicin, dapsone, and clofazimine.

Meanwhile, multibacillary (MB) leprosy is treated using the same 3 drugs for a duration of 12 months. While the NLEP guidelines earlier mentioned a 2-drug MDT for PB leprosy, the National Strategic Plan and Roadmap for Leprosy (2023-2027) now recommends a uniform MDT of 3 drugs for both PB and MB leprosy.

Note: The central government has approved a new treatment regimen for paucibacillary (PB) leprosy. The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has introduced a 3-drug regimen for PB leprosy instead of a 2-drug regimen. This revised drug regimen will be applicable in India from April 1, 2025.
questions.learning: 3 drug therapy for 6 months The latest recommendation is 3 drug therapy for 6 months to treat paucibacillary (PB) leprosy by WHO. The regimen consists of rifampicin, dapsone, and clofazimine.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A child with normal IQ and learning skills for his age is weak in mathematics reasoning. Despite being tutored by a private tutor for 1 year, the child showed no improvement. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Specific learning disorder

Based on the clinical scenario, the most likely diagnosis for a child who has normal IQ and learning skills for their age but is weak in mathematical reasoning despite one year of tutoring is a specific learning disorder in mathematics, also known as dyscalculia.

Dyscalculia is a specific learning disorder that affects an individual's ability to understand and work with numbers. It is similar to dyslexia but specifically related to mathematical skills. Children with dyscalculia may have difficulty understanding number concepts, memorizing basic arithmetic facts, and comprehending mathematical symbols and operations.

The learning difficulties begin during school-age years but may not become fully manifest until the demands increase as in a test or exam and are not better accounted for by intellectual disabilities, uncorrected visual or auditory acuity, other mental or neurological disorders, psychosocial adversity, lack of proficiency in the language of academic instruction, or inadequate educational instruction.

The four diagnostic criteria are to be met based on a clinical synthesis of the individual's history (developmental, medical,family, educational), school reports, and psychoeducational assessment.

Note: Dyscalculia is an alternative term used to refer to a pattern of difficulties characterized by problems processing numerical information, learning arithmetic facts, and performing accurate or fluent calculations.
questions.learning: Specific learning disorder — Based on the clinical scenario, the most likely diagnosis for a child who has normal IQ and learning skills for their age but is weak in mathematical reasoning despite one year of tutoring is a specific learning disorder in…

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Wobble hypothesis explains which of the following concepts of the genetic code?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Degeneracy

The wobble hypothesis explains the degeneracy of the genetic code.

The wobble hypothesis states that codon-anticodon pairing follows the traditional Watson–Crick rules (G pairs with C and A pairs with U) for the first two bases of the codon but can be less stringent for the third/last base. It has been observed that a tRNA can recognize more than one codon for a specific amino acid, especially in the last nucleotide of the codon triplet. This is referred to as degeneracy and its mechanism can be explained by the wobble hypothesis.

The first base of the anticodon moves to permit nontraditional pairing with the last base of the codon. This movement is called wobble and is possible because the first base of the anticodon is not as spatially defined as the other two bases. Due to the wobbling, 61 tRNA species are not required to read the 61 codons.

For example, three codons for glycine—GGU, GGC, and GGA—can form a base pair from one anticodon, 3′ CCI 5′ ie, I, inosine, can base pair with U, C, and A, as shown in the diagram below.

Other options:

Option A: The genetic code is universal because it is the same for all living organisms.

Option B: The genetic code is unambiguous because each codon is specific for only one amino acid. Example: GGA only codes for Glycine.

Option D: The genetic code is non-punctuated. This means that once the reading commences at a specific start codon, it is continuous and is read continuously as triplets until a stop codon is reached without stopping.
questions.learning: Degeneracy — The wobble hypothesis explains the degeneracy of the genetic code. The wobble hypothesis states that codon-anticodon pairing follows the traditional Watson–Crick rules (G pairs with C and A pairs with U) for the first two bases of the codon…

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following abnormalities is a child with a single palmer transverse crease and low-set ears most likely to have?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Aneuploidy

A child with a single palmar transverse crease and low-set ears is most likely to have Down syndrome and it is a type of aneuploidy.

Down Syndrome is a type of aneuploidy. It occurs due to the presence of an extra copy of chromosome 21 (trisomy 21), leading to a total of 47 chromosomes instead of the normal 46. This chromosomal abnormality causes the characteristic physical features, developmental delays, and health issues associated with the condition.

Mechanism:

* Majority of cases -  meiotic nondisjunction (95%) of chromosome 21 in the ovum

* Rarely - (4%) Robertsonian translocation (option D) of the long arm of chromosome 21 to another acrocentric chromosome (e.g., 22 or 14)

* Mosaic pattern: 1% (option A)

Clinical features of Down’s syndrome include (Mnemonic: I C A PROBLEM Somewhere), intellectual disability/Incurved or short fifth finger with clinodactyly, congenital heart disease, acute megakaryoblastic leukaemia/Alzheimer's disease/Atlantoaxial instability/Atresia of the duodenum, protruding tongue, round face, occiput flat/Open wide fontanelle/Open mouth, brachycephalic/Brush field's spots, low (depressed) nasal bridge, epicanthal fold/Ears low set and dysplastic, mongoloid slant (oblique palpebral fissure), simian palmar crease and wider gap between first and second toes.

The most common cause of intestinal obstruction in Down syndrome is duodenal atresia (double-bubble sign). Children with Down's syndrome have an increased risk of developing leukaemias, including acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) and acute myeloid leukaemia (AML). AML is more common during the first 3 years of life. The most common AML associated with Down Syndrome is acute megakaryoblastic leukaemia. The most common haematological manifestation of Down syndrome is transient abnormal myelopoiesis (TAM). Brushfield's spots are whitish speckling on the iris seen in light-skinned people as shown in the image below.

Other options:

Option A: Gonadal mosaicism is a mutation that occurs only in egg or sperm cells and the individual will be phenotypically normal. These individuals with gonadal mosaicism can transmit the disease-causing mutation to the offspring through their mutated gametes.
questions.learning: Aneuploidy — A child with a single palmar transverse crease and low-set ears is most likely to have Down syndrome and it is a type of aneuploidy. Down Syndrome is a type of aneuploidy.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 14-year-old male has been diagnosed with a condition due to a DNA repair gene defect. He is having hyperpigmentation on the skin and high risk for the development of skin cancers as per the physician. Which of the following mechanisms is likely to be defective in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Nucleotide Excision Repair defect

The above given clinical findings is suggestive of xeroderma pigmentosum. Xeroderma pigmentosum is an example of defective DNA nucleotide excision repair where there is an inability to repair DNA pyrimidine dimers caused by UV exposure.

Xeroderma Pigmentosum (XP) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by defective DNA repair mechanisms. This defect makes affected individuals highly sensitive to ultraviolet radiation. They also show increased vulnerability to various carcinogenic agents.

Important clinical features are:

Intense cutaneous photosensitivity, xerosis, poikiloderma, actinic keratosis, acute burning under minimal sun exposure, erythemas, hyperpigmented lentiginous macules, and malignant lesions in sun-exposed areas, including basocellular carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and melanoma.

The final diagnosis of XP can be confirmed by special laboratory tests by examining the DNA damage repair in cells from cultures exposed to ultraviolet radiation. The most common tests are skin biopsy and culture of skin fibroblasts.

There is no cure for XP. Treatment consists of minimizing exposure to sunlight and regular dermatological care, as well as surgery for recurrent tumors excision. Patients should be followed up every 3 months.

Genetic counseling is important in a family that has an affected child and is considering having more children.

Other options:

Option A: Nonhomologous End Joining Repair, is involved in repairing double-stranded DNA breaks and is not directly associated with the repair of UV-induced DNA damage.

Option C: DNA Base Excision Repair, primarily addresses small DNA lesions, such as those caused by oxidative damage, rather than the bulky lesions induced by UV radiation.

Option D: DNA Mismatch Repair (MMR) is a cellular mechanism that corrects errors that occur during DNA replication, such as mismatched nucleotides or small insertions or deletions. MMR plays a crucial role in maintaining the integrity of the genome and preventing the accumulation of mutations. However, in the scenario described, where a 14-year-old male has hyperpigmentation on the skin and an increased risk of skin cancers, a DNA Mismatch Repair defect is not the most likely mechanism involved.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a community, there were 550 births in a year out of which 50 were stillbirths. There were 09 deaths among newborns during 0-7 days of life. An additional 41 deaths occurred during 8-28 days of life. Calculate the Early Neonatal Mortality rate for the given community.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 18

Early Neonatal Mortality Rate (ENMR) is defined as the number of deaths during 0–7 days of life per 1,000 live births.

In this question:

• Early neonatal deaths = 9
• Late neonatal deaths = 41

Live births = Total births − Stillbirths = 550 − 50 = 500.

Early neonatal deaths = 9.

ENMR = (9 ÷ 500) × 1,000 = 18 per 1,000 live births.
questions.learning: 18 Early Neonatal Mortality Rate (ENMR) is defined as the number of deaths during 0–7 days of life per 1,000 live births. In this question: • Early neonatal deaths = 9 • Late neonatal deaths = 41 Live births = Total births − Stillbirths = 550 − 50 = 500.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A skull shows: • Mesaticephalic cephalic index • Prominent brow ridges • Narrow nasal aperture • Sharp nasal sill • High bridge nose The race is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Caucasoid

The skull features described are characteristic of the Caucasoid race. A mesaticephalic skull, prominent brow ridges, narrow nasal aperture, sharp nasal sill, and a high nasal bridge are classic anthropological markers of Caucasoid skulls. The sharp nasal sill and narrow nasal opening are especially important discriminators, as they reflect well-developed nasal bones adapted to colder climates.

A. Mongoloid: Typically shows a rounder skull, flatter face, and less prominent nasal bridge.

B. Negroid: Has a broad nasal aperture with a guttered nasal sill and prognathism.

D. Australoid: Shows robust features with wide nasal aperture and less sharp nasal sill.
questions.learning: Caucasoid — The skull features described are characteristic of the Caucasoid race. A mesaticephalic skull, prominent brow ridges, narrow nasal aperture, sharp nasal sill, and a high nasal bridge are classic anthropological markers of Caucasoid skulls.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: You discover that there is evidence of cardiac malformation in a fetus during a routine USG scan at 16 weeks. What is the minimum level of fasting blood sugar at which you can suspect overt diabetes?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 126 mg/dL

Overt diabetes is when fasting blood sugar is ≥ 126 mg/dl. Overt diabetics are women who are known to have diabetes before pregnancy.

A patient is said to have overt diabetes if:

• Fasting blood sugar ≥ 126 mg/dL
• A random blood sugar of ≥ 200 mg/dL
• HbA1c of ≥ 6.5%

The maternal complication of diabetes:

• increased Miscarriage and preterm labor.
• increased incidence of preeclampsia
• polyhydramnios
• prolongation of labor due to shoulder dystocia, operative interference, and cephalo-pelvic disproportion.

Fetal and Neonatal complications of diabetes:

• fetal macrosomia (birth weight > 4kg)
• congenital malformations - Musculoskeletal, urogenital, and CNS anomalies.
questions.learning: 126 mg/dL Overt diabetes is when fasting blood sugar is ≥ 126 mg/dl. Overt diabetics are women who are known to have diabetes before pregnancy.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Serotonin is also known as?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 5 hydroxytryptamine

Serotonin is also known as 5 hydroxy-tryptamine, and it is a monoamine neurotransmitter. Serotonin is produced by hydroxylation of tryptophan and subsequent decarboxylation. It is a potent vasoconstrictor and stimulator of smooth muscle contraction.

Clinical correlation:

In carcinoid syndrome, excessive levels of serotonin is produced which causes flushing, diarrhea, wheezing, damage to the tricuspid valve, etc. The levels of 5-OH indole acetic acid (serotonin metabolite) is elevated in the urine.
questions.learning: 5 hydroxytryptamine Serotonin is also known as 5 hydroxy-tryptamine, and it is a monoamine neurotransmitter. Serotonin is produced by hydroxylation of tryptophan and subsequent decarboxylation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is not used for protein precipitation?
options: Change in pH other than isoelectric pH
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Change in pH other than isoelectric pH

Protein precipitation occurs most efficiently at the isoelectric pH (pI), where the net charge on the protein is zero, minimizing electrostatic repulsion and promoting aggregation. Changing the pH away from the isoelectric point increases the net charge on proteins, enhancing solubility rather than causing precipitation. Hence, pH changes other than pI are not useful for protein precipitation.

Why other options are incorrect:

A. Heavy metals: Form insoluble complexes with proteins, causing precipitation.

B. Organic solvents: Reduce hydration shell and dielectric constant, leading to precipitation.

D. Trichloroacetic acid: A strong acid commonly used to precipitate proteins by denaturation.
questions.learning: Change in pH other than isoelectric pH Protein precipitation occurs most efficiently at the isoelectric pH (pI), where the net charge on the protein is zero, minimizing electrostatic repulsion and promoting aggregation.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 70-year-old patient presented with cough, fatiguability, and weight loss. He was diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) on bronchoscopy. The resected specimen had a hilar lymph node that was 1cm in size and showed a black pigment. What is the black pigment likely to be?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anthracotic pigment

The black-colored pigment in the hilar lymph node of the resected bronchoscopic specimen is likely to be an anthracotic pigment.

The black color is due to the deposition of carbon particles. The inhaled carbon particles are engulfed by the lung macrophages and then transported to the hilar lymph nodes. This accumulates and causes the blackening of the lung tissues or anthracosis.

It is commonly seen in people who work in environments where there is high air pollution with carbon particles, such as coal mines. It is also the most common exogenous pigment found in the human body as a result of air pollution in urban areas. The aggregates of the carbon dust may induce fibroblastic reaction or emphysema that may lead to a condition called coal worker's pneumoconiosis.

The following image shows anthracosis with deposition of black carbon particles, within the cytoplasm of macrophages.

Option B: Melanin is brown-black in color which occurs as a result of oxidation of tyrosine in melanocytes, as shown in the following histopathology of a lymph node.

Option C: Lipochrome or lipofuscin (brown lipid) is seen as a yellow-brown pigment in histopathological sections of the liver and heart of normal aging patients, patients with severe malnutrition, and cancer cachexia. It is derived through lipid peroxidation and indicates free radical injury and lipid peroxidation. The following image shows a cardiac myocyte with fine yellow-brown lipofuscin granules in the perinuclear region.

Option D: Hemosiderin is a hemoglobin-derived golden-yellow colored pigment seen in conditions associated with iron overload such as hemochromatosis. The following image shows extensive intra-alveolar hemosiderin deposition following pulmonary hemorrhage.
questions.learning: Anthracotic pigment — The black-colored pigment in the hilar lymph node of the resected bronchoscopic specimen is likely to be an anthracotic pigment. The black color is due to the deposition of carbon particles.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with guttate lesions in one eye and bullous keratopathy in the other eye. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Fuchs endothelial dystrophy

Fuchs endothelial dystrophy is a progressive disorder of the corneal endothelium characterized by guttata formation and eventual stromal and epithelial edema leading to bullous keratopathy.

Key clinical progression:

• Early stage:

• Guttate lesions (corneal guttata) on Descemet’s membrane

• Late stage:

• Endothelial failure → corneal edema
• Formation of bullae (bullous keratopathy) → pain, decreased vision

Pathophysiology:

• Loss of endothelial cells → impaired corneal deturgescence (fluid pump function)
• Leads to fluid accumulation in cornea

Why not others:

• Interstitial keratitis: Stromal inflammation, not endothelial dystrophy
• Viral corneal ulcer: Epithelial defect, dendritic pattern
• Keratoconjunctivitis: Surface inflammation, no guttata
questions.learning: Fuchs endothelial dystrophy Fuchs endothelial dystrophy is a progressive disorder of the corneal endothelium characterized by guttata formation and eventual stromal and epithelial edema leading to bullous keratopathy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 50-year-old man presents with 6 kg weight loss over three months and difficulty swallowing. His history includes treatment for esophageal cancer one year ago. What is the most likely explanation for his current symptoms?
questions.explanation: In a patient with a prior history of esophageal cancer who presents with significant weight loss and new-onset dysphagia (difficulty swallowing) within a year of treatment, Esophageal cancer recurrence must be the first and most likely differential diagnosis. Malignant recurrence often presents with rapidly progressive dysphagia, initially for solids and then liquids, accompanied by systemic signs like cachexia. Fibrosis (Option B) can occur post-radiation but is less likely to cause a massive 6 kg weight loss in just three months. Achalasia cardia (Option C) typically presents in younger patients and is a motility disorder, not a late-onset sequel of cancer treatment. GERD (Option D) causes heartburn and regurgitation but is not a primary cause of profound weight loss and obstructive dysphagia. Management requires an urgent Upper Gastrointestinal Endoscopy (UGIE) with biopsies and a CT or PET scan for restaging. Unfortunately, the prognosis for recurrent esophageal malignancy is generally poor, and management often shifts toward palliative care interventions
questions.learning: In a patient with a prior history of esophageal cancer who presents with significant weight loss and new-onset dysphagia (difficulty swallowing) within a year of treatment, Esophageal cancer recurrence must be the first and most likely differential diagnosis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which hormone is secreted by the structure indicated by the arrow?
questions.explanation: The arrow in the image points to the zona fasciculata, the middle layer of the adrenal cortex. This layer is characterized by large, pale-staining cells (spongiocytes) arranged in straight cords, due to abundant lipid content. These features help distinguish it from the darker outer zona glomerulosa and inner zona reticularis. The zona fasciculata primarily secretes glucocorticoids, especially cortisol, which plays an important role in: 1. Metabolism (gluconeogenesis, glycogen storage) 2. Stress response 3. Immune modulation Why other options are incorrect: (B) DHEA: Produced by the zona reticularis (inner cortical layer), not the fasciculata. (C) Androgens: Also secreted by the zona reticularis, not the middle layer. (D) Mineralocorticoid: Produced by the zona glomerulosa (outermost layer), responsible for aldosterone secretion. Since the marked region is zona fasciculata, the correct answer is glucocorticoid (cortisol)
questions.learning: The arrow in the image points to the zona fasciculata, the middle layer of the adrenal cortex. This layer is characterized by large, pale-staining cells (spongiocytes) arranged in straight cords, due to abundant lipid content.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Auspitz sign is seen in ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Psoriasis vulgaris

Auspitz sign is a characteristic feature seen in psoriasis.

The presence of silvery-white scaly lesions on the extensor aspect of the elbows and knee is a characteristic feature seen in psoriasis. The condition can be diagnosed clinically by demonstrating the Auspitz sign.

Demonstration of Auspitz Sign:

If superficial silvery scales are removed by scratching (grattage), then the scales come off attached together, as if one has scratched on a wax candle (wax candle scales).

Subsequently, a thin membrane, known as Bulkeley membrane, is seen.

Removal of Bulkeley membrane, reveals classical pinpoint bleeding known as Auspitz sign.

Auspitz sign is due to the elongated vessels in the dermal papilla, together with the thinning of supra papillary epidermis.

Silvery-white scales on the extensor aspect of the elbow seen in psoriasis are portrayed in the picture below:
questions.learning: Psoriasis vulgaris Auspitz sign is a characteristic feature seen in psoriasis. The presence of silvery-white scaly lesions on the extensor aspect of the elbows and knee is a characteristic feature seen in psoriasis.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 40 year old female with no comorbidities complaints of swelling in both her legs which was acute in onset . She also gives a history of loose stools. Her family members too has similar symptoms. On examination there was no signs of inflammation in both the legs. Detailed history revealed that mustard oil is a staple part of their diet . Which of the following substance is responsible for her condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sanguinarine

The clinical presentation is suggestive of epidemic dropsy and Sanguinarine is the toxic compound responsible for this.

Epidemic Dropsy: Contamination of mustard oil with argemone oil.

* Toxic compound: Sanguinarine

* Mechanism of action : Sanguinarine interfers with the oxidation of pyruvic acid which inturn accumulates in the blood and causes symptoms.

* Clinical presentation :The patient presents with sudden onset, non inflammatory swelling of bilateral legs which is often associated with diarrhoea. Some patients can develop glaucoma. Dyspnea, cardiac failure and death can occur in later stages.

* Mortality rate - 5-50%

Tests to detect argemone oil:

* Nitric acid test

* Paper chromatography: most sensitive(can detect very low concentration of argemone oil)

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What condition causes the skull appearance as in the given radiograph?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hyperparathyroidism

The given X-ray of the skull shows multiple radiolucent lytic lesions, typical of the salt and pepper appearance (pepperpot appearance). This is seen in hyperparathyroidism.

In hyperparathyroidism, there is resorption of the trabecular bone of the skull (which causes the radiolucent areas) in combination with cystic areas of osteopenia. There is also a loss of definition between the inner and outer tables of the skull.

Other options:

Option B: In multiple myeloma, multiple well-defined "punched out" lytic lesions exist.

Option C: Untreated hyperthyroidism for several years can lead to osteoporosis of bones.

Option D: In Paget's disease, the pelvis, spine, skull, and proximal long bones are most frequently affected. Radiological skull changes include:

• Osteoporosis circumscripta: Large, well-defined lytic lesion
• Cotton wool appearance: Mixed lytic and sclerotic lesions of the skull
• Diploic widening: Both inner and outer calvarial tables are involved, with the former usually more extensively affected
• Tam o'Shanter sign: Frontal bone enlargement, with the appearance of the skull falling over the facial bones, like a Tam o'Shanter hat
questions.learning: Hyperparathyroidism — The given X-ray of the skull shows multiple radiolucent lytic lesions, typical of the salt and pepper appearance (pepperpot appearance).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following can alter the gene expression by methylation and acetylation but not change the gene sequence?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Epigenetics

Epigenetics is defined as heritable changes in gene expression that are not caused by alteration in gene sequence.
It means “above genetics” and refers to the fact that gene regulatory mechanisms do not change the underlying regulated DNA sequence, but rather simply the expression patterns of the DNA.

Epigenetic mechanisms play a key role in establishment, maintenance, and reversibility of transcriptional states. A key feature is that the controlled transcriptional on/off states can be maintained through multiple rounds of cell division. This observation indicates there must be robust mechanisms to maintain and stably propagate these epigenetic states.

Histone Methylation Mostly Makes DNA Mute.
Histone Acetylation: Relaxes DNA coiling, allowing for transcription. Histone Acetylation makes DNA Active.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: In which of the subsequent circumstances is macrocytic anemia observed?
questions.explanation: Macrocytic anemia is defined by a mean corpuscular volume (MCV) greater than 100 fL. Among the options, liver disease is a well-recognized cause of non-megaloblastic macrocytic anemia. The macrocytosis in liver disease is often due to the deposition of excess cholesterol and phospholipids on the red cell membrane, which increases its surface area, or sometimes due to concomitant alcohol use. Thalassemia (Option A) and sideroblastic anemia (Option C) are classically microcytic anemias, characterized by an MCV less than 80 fL. Anemia of chronic disease (Option B) is typically normocytic but can sometimes be microcytic; it is virtually never macrocytic. Therefore, while Vitamin B12 and folate deficiencies are the most common causes of macrocytosis, liver disease is the only correct option provided that results in an elevated MCV. Consequently, liver disease is the correct clinical association
questions.learning: Macrocytic anemia is defined by a mean corpuscular volume (MCV) greater than 100 fL. Among the options, liver disease is a well-recognized cause of non-megaloblastic macrocytic anemia.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 30-year-old man is brought after a road traffic accident with deformity of the left lower limb. The limb is positioned in flexion, abduction, and external rotation, with apparent lengthening. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The specific posture of the affected limb is the key to differentiating hip dislocations. An anterior hip dislocation (Option B) classically presents with the leg held in abduction, external rotation, and flexion, which results in "apparent lengthening" of the limb. This is much rarer than a posterior dislocation (Option A), which presents with the opposite posture: adduction, internal rotation, and flexion, with apparent shortening. Intertrochanteric (Option C) and femoral neck fractures (Option D) also cause external rotation but would present with true shortening and no abduction . Anterior dislocations can be "obturator" (more flexion) or "pubic" (more extension). Management requires urgent closed reduction under general anesthesia to prevent avascular necrosis of the femoral head. Because the patient demonstrates the unique "abducted and externally rotated" posture, anterior dislocation is the only accurate diagnosis

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman is admitted to the emergency department after an accidental burn. She has burns involving her right upper limb, the entire right lower limb, and the entire anterior and posterior abdomen. Using the Rule of Nines, what is the estimated total body surface area (TBSA) affected by burns?
questions.explanation: The Wallace Rule of Nines is used to estimate the total body surface area (TBSA) burned in adults. Applying it step by step: 1. Right upper limb = 9% 2. Entire right lower limb = 18% 3. Anterior abdomen = 9% 4. (Anterior trunk is 18%; abdomen represents half of it) Posterior abdomen = 9% (Posterior trunk is 18%; abdomen represents half of it) Total TBSA burned: 9% + 18% + 9% + 9% = 45% Therefore, the estimated burned TBSA is 45%, making Option (A) correct. Why others are incorrect: 28% underestimates by excluding major areas. 60% and 70% overestimate by incorrectly counting full trunk or extra limbs. Accurate TBSA estimation is crucial for fluid resuscitation, commonly calculated using the Parkland formula: Half is given in the first 8 hours, and the rest over the next 16 hours. Incorrect estimation can lead to fluid overload or hypovolemic shock

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the primary location of the Thermogenin protein?
questions.explanation: Thermogenin, also known as Uncoupling Protein 1 (UCP1), is a specialized protein found in the inner mitochondrial membrane of brown adipose tissue. Its primary function is non-shivering thermogenesis, a process vital for maintaining body temperature in neonates and hibernating animals. Thermogenin works by allowing protons to leak across the inner mitochondrial membrane, bypassing ATP synthase. This collapses the proton gradient, and instead of producing ATP, the energy is released directly as heat. The Golgi complex (Option A), Endoplasmic reticulum (Option B), and Nucleus (Option D) do not contain thermogenin or participate in this specific uncoupling of the electron transport chain. Because thermogenin’s physiological role is strictly tied to the uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation, which occurs only in the mitochondria, its localization is definitively mitochondrial

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Anuj has been diagnosed with diphtheria and is being treated in the ward. His 3-year-old brother, Ajay who lives in the same house has received vaccination against diphtheria about 16 months back. What is the next best step for the management of the younger sibling, Ajay?
options: Nothing as the child is already exposed
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Erythromycin only

In the given clinical scenario, a 3-year-old child is likely to have received the 4th dose (1st booster) of the diphtheria vaccine between 16–24 months of age according to National Immunization Schedule (i.e., 16 months ago). Since he has received a booster dose within 5 years, only erythromycin is indicated in case of close contact with the diphtheria patient.

All household contacts with diphtheria patients should be closely monitored for 7 days. Culture should be taken from both the throat and nose. All contacts should receive antibiotic prophylaxis (benzathine penicillin G or erythromycin), regardless of immunization status.

Children who have not received a booster dose of the diphtheria toxoid vaccine within 5 years should be given the vaccine in an age-appropriate form. Children who have not yet received their 4th dose should be vaccinated accordingly.

If fewer than three doses of diphtheria toxoid have been given, or vaccination history is unknown, an immediate dose of diphtheria toxoid should be given and the primary series completed according to the current schedule.

Asymptomatic carriers of diphtheria are treated with antimicrobial prophylaxis for a period of 10-14 days. If an individual has not received a booster dose of diphtheria toxoid within 1 year, an age-appropriate preparation of the vaccine should be administered promptly.

Droplet precautions (respiratory colonization) or contact precautions (cutaneous colonization) of cases and carriers are maintained until two consecutive negative cultures (collected 24 hours apart) are obtained after cessation of therapy.
questions.learning: Erythromycin only — In the given clinical scenario, a 3-year-old child is likely to have received the 4th dose (1st booster) of the diphtheria vaccine between 16–24 months of age according to National Immunization Schedule (i.e., 16 months ago).

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 28-year-old dentist presents with painful grouped vesicular lesions on the distal phalanx of her right index finger. She reports a burning sensation followed by the appearance of fluid-filled blisters that ruptured into shallow ulcers. She denies systemic symptoms. Which of the following is the most likely condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Herpetic whitlow

The given clinical vignette of a dentist with fluid-filled, painful grouped vesicular lesions, with a burning sensation on the distal phalanx of a dentist, is suggestive of herpetic whitlow infection.

Clinical features include painful, deep vesicles at the site of inoculation (in this case, the fingertips), which coalesce to form large bullae or a honeycomb appearance, which is most commonly contracted by dental workers and medical workers exposed to oral secretions. Fever and constitutional symptoms are mild. HSV-1 and HSV-2 can cause this condition.

Whitlow can lead to necrosis of the distal 4/5th of the terminal phalanx. It does not cause necrosis of the entire phalanx because the proximal 1/5th escapes, as in this part, the artery does not cross the fibrous septa.The pulp space of fingers contains subcutaneous fat arranged in tight compartments. These compartments are formed by fibrous septa extending from the skin to the periosteum of the terminal phalanx.

Diagnosis of herpes simplex virus:

* Most sensitive test- HSV DNA- PCR (can differentiate between HSV 1 and 2)

* Most definitive test- virus isolation using human diploid fibroblast in which cytopathic changes can be observed as early as 24 - 48 hours.

* Microscopy - Tzanck smear, which is a rapid, diagnostic method, shows Tzanck cells. These are multinucleated giant cells with faceted nuclei and homogenously stained ground-glass chromatin. Intranuclear type A inclusion bodies may also be seen.

The image given below shows Tzanck cells:

The image below shows the characteristic lesions of herpetic whitlow (The presence of vesicles and cloudy blisters at the pulp of fingers)

Topical acyclovir therapy can be initiated in cases of primary herpetic whitlow. Primary HSV infection at multiple sites and recurrent herpetic whitlow require oral acyclovir therapy. Intravenous acyclovir is recommended in immunocompromised patients.

Other options:

Option A: Molluscum contagiosum is a common, self-limiting viral disease of the skin caused by the molluscum contagiosum virus(MCV), which is classified within the poxvirus family. Usually, it occurs as scattered lesions on discrete areas of the body, appearing as shiny, pearly white, umbilicated papules(shown below).

Option B: Paronychia refers to an infection of the proximal & lateral nail folds. It results from the disruption of the protective barrier between the nail and the nail fold, introducing pathogens and predisposing the area to infection. Most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus(shown below).

Option C: Verruca vulgaris or common wart is caused by human papilloma virus 2 (HPV-2), but is also closely related to types 27 and 57 as well as types 1 and 4. These present as firm papules with a rough, horny surface and are most commonly situated on the backs of the hands and fingers, and in children, frequently on the knees, though they may occur anywhere on the skin.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A hypertensive patient presents with an irregularly irregular pulse and a loud P2 on auscultation. Upon examination of the Jugular Venous Pressure (JVP), which finding is most likely to be observed in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Absent a wave

An irregularly irregular pulse indicates atrial fibrillation.

| Wave | Cause

| ---- | -----

| a wave | Atrial contraction

| c wave | Tricuspid valve bulging

| v wave | Venous filling of atrium

| x descent | Atrial relaxation

| y descent | Ventricular filling

In AF, atrial contraction is absent, leading to loss of the ‘a’ wave in JVP.

A loud P2 suggests associated pulmonary hypertension.

Cannon waves occur with AV dissociation, not atrial fibrillation.

B) Cannon a wave

Occurs when atria contract against a closed tricuspid valve.

Seen in:

• Complete heart block
• AV dissociation

C) Rapid x descent

Seen in conditions like cardiac tamponade.

D) Rapid y descent

Seen in constrictive pericarditis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 27-year-old primigravida at 20 weeks' gestation is diagnosed with rheumatic mitral stenosis. Echocardiography shows a mitral valve area of 1.2 cm². She experiences mild exertional dyspnea (NYHA Class II) but has no pulmonary edema, atrial fibrillation, or features of heart failure. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Continue medical management with regular antenatal follow-up
Elective mitral valve replacement during pregnancy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Continue medical management with regular antenatal follow-up

Pregnancy increases:

• Blood volume by 40–50%
• Cardiac output by 30–50%
• Heart rate

These physiological changes can worsen mitral stenosis by increasing left atrial pressure and the risk of pulmonary congestion.

However, this patient is:

• NYHA Class II
• Hemodynamically stable
• Has no heart failure or pulmonary edema

Therefore, conservative (medical) management with close maternal and fetal surveillance is appropriate.

Management includes:

• Regular antenatal and cardiology follow-up
• Activity modification
• Salt restriction if needed
• Beta-blockers (e.g., metoprolol) if symptomatic tachycardia develops
• Diuretics if pulmonary congestion occurs
• Anticoagulation only if atrial fibrillation or another indication is present

Why not the other options?

• A. Immediate percutaneous balloon mitral valvotomy (PBMV): Reserved for severe symptomatic mitral stenosis (NYHA III/IV) or patients with pulmonary edema or refractory symptoms despite optimal medical therapy. It is not indicated in a stable NYHA II patient.
• C. Elective mitral valve replacement during pregnancy: Open-heart surgery during pregnancy carries significant maternal and fetal risks and is reserved for patients in whom PBMV is not feasible and who have life-threatening disease.
• D. Termination of pregnancy: Not indicated. Most women with NYHA Class I–II mitral stenosis can continue pregnancy with appropriate multidisciplinary care.

High-yield pearl

Management of mitral stenosis in pregnancy

| Clinical status | Recommended management

| --------------- | ----------------------

| NYHA I–II, stable | Medical management + close antenatal follow-up

| NYHA III–IV or pulmonary edema despite medical therapy | Percutaneous balloon mitral valvotomy (preferably in the 2nd trimester)

| Severe disease not amenable to PBMV | Cardiac surgery only if life-saving

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which among the following are hepatobiliary flukes (trematodes)? 1. Clonorchis sinensis 2. Mansonella perstans 3. Fasciola hepatica 4. Opisthorchis felineus Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 3 and 4

Hepatobiliary flukes are trematodes that primarily infect the liver and biliary tree, causing cholangitis, biliary obstruction, and chronic hepatobiliary disease. The important human hepatobiliary flukes are Clonorchis sinensis, Fasciola hepatica, and Opisthorchis felineus.

Why is C correct?

• 1. Clonorchis sinensis✅: Chinese liver fluke infecting the intrahepatic bile ducts.
• 3. Fasciola hepatica✅: Sheep liver fluke infecting the liver and biliary tract.
• 4. Opisthorchis felineus✅: A liver fluke causing opisthorchiasis with biliary involvement.

Incorrect option:

• 2. Mansonella perstans❌: A filarial nematode, not a trematode; causes mansonellosis.
questions.learning: 1, 3 and 4 Hepatobiliary flukes are trematodes that primarily infect the liver and biliary tree, causing cholangitis, biliary obstruction, and chronic hepatobiliary disease.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following MRI imaging techniques is shown in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. T2 MRI

The MRI shows CSF as bright/hyperintense while white matter is dark and grey matter is white, hence this is a T2 weighted MRI image.

T1 weighted image

* It is one of the basic MRI pulse sequences.

* The difference in the appearance of various tissues is due to their different T1 relaxation times.

* CSF has a long T1 time and appears dark.

T2 weighted images:

* It is also a basic MRI pulse sequence.

* It is based on the T2 relaxation time of the tissues.

* CSF appears bright in these images.

Short tau inversion recovery(STIR):

* It is a form of inversion recovery sequence.

* It is used to selectively null signals from fat.

* The imaging sequence is identified by observing the fat tissues and fluid-filled spaces.

* Fluids like CSF appear bright and fat appears dark.

Fluid attenuated inversion recovery(FLAIR):

* It is also a form of inversion recovery sequence.

* It is used to selectively null signals from fluids.

* Fluids like CSF appear dark and pathological processes appear bright.

* It would appear as a fluid suppressed T2 image.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: 26-year P1L1 presents with abdominal pain. She has a past history of rheumatic heart disease for which she has undergone mitral valve replacement surgery and is on the oral tablet warfarin 3mg OD. On examination, an abdominal mass corresponding to 14 weeks was felt. On USG, an 8*6 cm unilocular cyst with a reticular pattern was observed in the left ovary. What is the next line of management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Repeat USG after 6-12 weeks

The USG findings of a unilocular cyst with reticular pattern indicate a functional hemorrhagic cyst. Hence, the next line of management is to repeat USG after 6-12 weeks.

Although the cyst size is >7 cm, invasive treatments are not suitable immediately because of her current use of warfarin which needs time to be tapered. Also, as most functional cysts resolve spontaneously over time, repeat USG might show a decrease in cyst size.

Management of ovarian cysts in reproductive age and perimenopausal women is mentioned in the table below:

Size
Management

< 5cm
Wait & watch; no additional treatment required

5cm - 7cm
Follow up with serial TVS in 6-12 weeks; if cyst persists continue TVS on yearly basis

> 7cm
MRI pelvis; surgical evaluation

Other Options:

Option A: Measure CA-125: In this case, it might not be the best first step because CA-125 is not specific and its level can be influenced by multiple factors. Additionally, the cyst described here is more likely to be benign (reticular pattern suggesting blood), such as a functional ovarian cyst or follicular cyst.

Option C: Surgical Intervention: Surgical intervention may be required if there are signs of torsion, rupture, or malignancy. However, with a simple, unilocular cyst without these features, surgery is usually not warranted immediately, especially as the patient is on warfarin and needs to be tapered. This approach would be more appropriate if the cyst showed signs of complications or did not resolve after monitoring.

Option D: MRI Pelvis: An MRI can offer more detailed imaging if there is concern about the nature of the cyst, but it is typically reserved for complicated cysts (e.g., solid components, suspicious features). It's not the first-line investigation in this case.
questions.learning: Repeat USG after 6-12 weeks — The USG findings of a unilocular cyst with reticular pattern indicate a functional hemorrhagic cyst. Hence, the next line of management is to repeat USG after 6-12 weeks.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient has different refractive powers in each eye, with +5 D in one eye and +1 D in the other. What diagnosis does this suggest?
questions.explanation: The presence of a significant difference in refractive power between the two eyes, such as +5D and +1D, is known as anisometropia. This disparity causes the brain to receive two images of different sizes or clarity, which it cannot easily fuse. Over time, the brain may suppress the image from the eye with the higher refractive error to avoid double vision, leading to anisometropic amblyopia (lazy eye). While "refractive errors" (Option A) is a broad category, it does not specifically address the difference between eyes or the resulting visual deficit. Amblyopia (Option B) is the general term for reduced vision in one eye, but "anisometropic amblyopia" is the most specific diagnosis describing the cause in this scenario. Malingering (Option D) refers to the intentional faking of visual symptoms for secondary gain and is not a medical refractive diagnosis. Early screening and correction with glasses or contact lenses, often followed by patching the stronger eye, are critical to restoring normal vision development
questions.learning: The presence of a significant difference in refractive power between the two eyes, such as +5D and +1D, is known as anisometropia. This disparity causes the brain to receive two images of different sizes or clarity, which it cannot easily fuse.

questions.explanation:

The prothrombin time (PT) assay is done to assesses the function of the proteins in the extrinsic pathway- Factors VII, X, V, II, and fibrinogen.

Factor VIII, IX, and XI participate in the intrinsic pathway of coagulation.

Factor VIII is a protein involved in the intrinsic pathway and its function is assessed by the partial thromboplastin time (PTT) assay.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 22-year-old man with 2 days of fever, cough, sore throat, and runny nose comes to the OPD. Lung sounds are clear to auscultation. A nasopharyngeal swab is obtained. Naked viral particles are seen, and purified RNA molecules are extracted from these particles. Once introduced into human cells, the purified RNA molecules induce viral protein synthesis and viral genome replication. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Rhinovirus

Rhinovirus is the most common cause of the common cold, presenting with fever, sore throat, cough, and rhinorrhea with usually normal lung examination.

Rhinovirus is a non-enveloped (naked), positive-sense single-stranded RNA virus. Its RNA acts directly as mRNA, so when introduced into host cells it can immediately initiate viral protein synthesis and genome replication.

Why not other options:

A. HIV: Enveloped retrovirus with two copies of +ssRNA that requires reverse transcriptase to form DNA before protein synthesis.

B. Influenza virus type A: Enveloped, negative-sense RNA virus; its RNA cannot directly act as mRNA and requires viral RNA polymerase.

C. Respiratory syncytial virus: Enveloped, negative-sense RNA virus; RNA must first be transcribed to mRNA.
questions.learning: Rhinovirus Rhinovirus is the most common cause of the common cold, presenting with fever, sore throat, cough, and rhinorrhea with usually normal lung examination.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is not a classical symptom of acute appendicitis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Constipation

Acute appendicitis classically presents with periumbilical visceral pain that later shifts to the right iliac fossa (McBurney’s point). The classical symptoms are:

• Anorexia (most consistent symptom)
• Periumbilical colicky pain migrating to the right iliac fossa
• Nausea and vomiting (usually after the onset of pain)

Constipation is not a classical symptom. Patients may have constipation or diarrhea, but neither is a characteristic feature.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: The Duffy antigen system serves as receptor for which one of the following protozoal parasites?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Plasmodium vivax

The Duffy antigen (Duffy antigen receptor for chemokines, DARC/Fy antigen) on red blood cells acts as the receptor for Plasmodium vivax, allowing the parasite to invade erythrocytes. Individuals who are Duffy antigen-negative [Fy(a−b−)] are naturally resistant to P. vivax infection.

Why not the other options?

• A. Giardia lamblia: Infects the small intestine; does not use the Duffy antigen.
• C. Entamoeba histolytica: Invades the colon and liver; no relation to the Duffy antigen.
• D. Balantidium coli: A ciliated protozoan causing colitis; does not invade RBCs.
questions.learning: Plasmodium vivax — The Duffy antigen (Duffy antigen receptor for chemokines, DARC/Fy antigen) on red blood cells acts as the receptor for Plasmodium vivax, allowing the parasite to invade erythrocytes.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements accurately describes Ayushman Bharat in this context?
options: Umbrella scheme includes Pradhan Mantri Jan Aarogya Yojna and sub centres
Benefit to 40% of poor and vulnerable population
Covers only tertiary health care centers
Cashless, paperless service by only government hospitals
questions.explanation: Ayushman Bharat - Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PM-JAY) is a flagship health insurance scheme designed to provide financial protection to the bottom 40% of India's poor and vulnerable population. It offers an annual health cover of ` 5 lakhs per family for secondary and tertiary care hospitalization. Option A is partially correct but the scheme actually includes "Health and Wellness Centres" rather than just standard sub-centres. Option C is incorrect as it covers both secondary and tertiary care. Option D is incorrect because the cashless, paperless service is provided at both government and empanelled private hospitals. The scheme is a major step toward Universal Health Coverage in India, aiming to reduce out-of-pocket expenditures that often lead to poverty. Therefore, the defining demographic reach of the scheme is the protection of the most vulnerable 40% of the citizenry
questions.learning: Ayushman Bharat - Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PM-JAY) is a flagship health insurance scheme designed to provide financial protection to the bottom 40% of India's poor and vulnerable population.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Feeding is done through the given method. Which of the following is not a complication of this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Aspiration pneumonia

The given image shows a central line. Pneumothorax, osteoporosis, and refeeding syndrome are likely complications in patients receiving total parenteral nutrition through a central line. Aspiration pneumonia is more common in enteral feeding and can be prevented by placing the patient in a semi-recumbent position while feeding.

Complications of enteral nutrition are as follows:

1. Tube-related (most common): Malposition, displacement, blockage, breakage/leakage, local complications (e.g. erosion of skin/mucosa)
2. Gastrointestinal: Diarrhoea, bloating, nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, aspiration, constipation
3. Metabolic/biochemical: Electrolyte disorders, vitamin, mineral, and trace element deficiencies, drug interactions
4. Infective: Exogenous (handling contamination) and endogenous (patient)

Other options:

Option A: Refeeding syndrome is a significant metabolic complication of both parenteral and enteral feeding. It occurs days after feeding is commenced in patients who have been severely malnourished. The major pathological process is hypophosphatemia which causes fluid and electrolyte shifts between the intra- and extracellular compartments.

Option B: Osteoporosis and osteomalacia are complications of long-term parenteral nutrition and may lead to fractures or kidney stones. Calcium, phosphate, vitamin D supplementation, and bisphosphonates can help prevent as well as treat this complication.

Option C: Pneumothorax is the most common complication of line insertion and most commonly occurs during the insertion of subclavian lines. It is managed by insertion of a chest drain.
questions.learning: Aspiration pneumonia — The given image shows a central line. Pneumothorax, osteoporosis, and refeeding syndrome are likely complications in patients receiving total parenteral nutrition through a central line.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A bronchial asthma patient on inhalational steroids presented with white patchy lesions on the tongue and buccal mucosa. What is the drug that can be used to treat this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Clotrimazole

The given clinical scenario of white patchy lesions on the tongue and buccal mucosa in a patient using inhalational steroids is oral candidiasis. The drug that can be used for the treatment is clotrimazole.

MDI results in the deposition of steroids in the oropharyngeal space, which can cause cough, dysphonia, and oropharyngeal candidiasis.

Clotrimazole is a topical imidazole used in the treatment of tinea infections like ringworm. It is particularly used for the treatment of vaginitis as a once-daily application because of its long-lasting residual effect.

For oral candidiasis, 10 mg troche of clotrimazole is allowed to dissolve in the mouth 3-4 times a day. Alternatively, lotion or gel is applied and swirled in the mouth for as long as possible. Side effects are local irritation and a burning sensation.

Other options:

Option B: Griseofulvin acts by inhibiting microtubule assembly, disrupting the fungal cell division. It is mainly used against dermatophytes and is the drug of choice for tinea capitis in children. It is not effective against Candida.

Option C: Terbinafine acts by inhibiting epoxidation of fungal squalene that reduces ergosterol biosynthesis. It is helpful for treating nail onychomycosis and tinea capitis.

Option D: Flucytosine acts by inhibiting fungal DNA synthesis. It is used exclusively in combination with amphotericin B for cryptococcal meningitis.
questions.learning: Clotrimazole — The given clinical scenario of white patchy lesions on the tongue and buccal mucosa in a patient using inhalational steroids is oral candidiasis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following drug must always be available for emergency use in labor ward if a patient is on opioid analgesic?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Naloxone

Naloxone is a narcotic antagonist capable of reversing respiratory depression induced by opioid narcotics.

It acts by displacing the narcotic from specific receptors in the central nervous system.

Naloxone:

It is a competitive antagonist on all types of opioid receptors.  It is devoid of any kind of agonistic activity even at high doses. Injected intravenously (0.4–0.8 mg) it promptly antagonizes all actions of morphine: analgesia is gone, respiration is not only normalized but stimulated—probably due to sudden sensitization of the respiratory centre to the retained CO2, or it may be a manifestation of acute withdrawal; pupils dilate. However, sedation is less completely reversed.

Naloxone is inactive orally because of high first-pass metabolism in the liver. Injected i.v. it acts in 2–3 min. The primary pathway of metabolism is glucuronidation. Plasma t½ is 1 hour in adults and 3 hours in newborns. Duration of action is 1–3 hrs.

Adverse effects of naloxone are uncommon, and may include a rise in BP and pulmonary edema; Naloxone 0.4 mg i.v. precipitates morphine withdrawal in dependent subjects: the syndrome lasting 2–3 hours.

Uses of naloxone:

• drug of choice for morphine poisoning (0.4–0.8 mg i.v. every 2–3 min: max 10 mg)
• reversing neonatal asphyxia due to opioid use during labour (10 µg/kg in the cord)
• treat the overdose with other opioids and agonist-antagonists (except buprenorphine)
• to reverse respiratory depression due to intraoperative use of opioids: 0.1–0.2 mg i.v. (this dose usually preserves analgesia in the postoperative period)
• tried as an adjunct to intraspinal opioid analgesia: reverses respiratory depression without abolishing pain relief

Naloxone is contraindicated in newborns of narcotic-addicted mothers as it can lead to neonatal abstinence syndrome (NAS).

NAS is a drug-withdrawal syndrome that most commonly follows in-utero exposure to maternal opioids. It also can complicate exposure to alcohol or benzodiazepines. The syndrome shows hypertonia, autonomic instability, irritability, poor sucking reflex, and seizures. Care includes close observation and pharmacotherapy with morphine and methadone. Naloxone is not recommended as it can precipitate withdrawal symptoms.
questions.learning: Naloxone Naloxone is a narcotic antagonist capable of reversing respiratory depression induced by opioid narcotics. It acts by displacing the narcotic from specific receptors in the central nervous system.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: According to NACO guidelines, when an HIV-positive patient receives counseling and screening for tuberculosis at an ICTC clinic, which level of prevention is being implemented?
questions.explanation: According to NACO guidelines, HIV care includes both preventive counseling and active screening for opportunistic infections like tuberculosis (TB). Primary prevention is represented by counseling, where the patient is educated about TB symptoms, transmission, adherence to treatment, and risk reduction. Since HIV patients are at high risk of developing TB, this counseling helps prevent occurrence or worsening of disease, thus falling under primary prevention. Secondary prevention is represented by screening for TB, which aims at early detection and prompt treatment. Identifying TB at an early stage in HIV-positive individuals reduces complications, transmission, and mortality. Why other options are incomplete: (A) Primordial → Deals with prevention of risk factors before they appear (B) Primary → Only covers counseling, not screening (C) Secondary → Only covers screening, ignores counseling component
