questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A person who met with an accident, and suffered from a skull fracture presents with the following finding. Identify this clinical finding.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Battle sign

The given image shows ecchymosis over the retro auricular and mastoid area suggestive of Battle's sign. It is typically seen in fractures of the middle cranial fossa following head trauma. Battle sign is prominent when there is a fracture of the petrous temporal bone.

Other options:

Option B: Bezold abscess is a complication of acute otomastoiditis where the infection/pus breaks through the thin medial side of the tip of the mastoid and presents as a swelling in the upper part of the neck.

Option C: Acute mastoiditis is used to refer to an acute infection that spreads from the mucosa lining the mastoid air cells to involve the bony walls of the mastoid air cell system. Mastoiditis presents as retro-auricular redness and swelling which is painful.

The image below shows a smooth ironed-out mastoid with erythema seen in acute mastoiditis.

Option D: The Griesinger sign refers to edema of the postauricular soft tissues overlying the mastoid process as a result of thrombosis of the mastoid emissary vein seen in sagittal sinus thrombosis. It is a complication of acute otomastoiditis.
questions.learning: Battle sign — The given image shows ecchymosis over the retro auricular and mastoid area suggestive of Battle's sign. It is typically seen in fractures of the middle cranial fossa following head trauma.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: In a patient on mechanical ventilation and placed in prone position which of the following about PEEP is true?
options: Prevents atelectasis of lung and alveolar collapse
Increases venous return and thus maintains cardiac output
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Prevents atelectasis of lung and alveolar collapse

PEEP helps keep alveoli open and prevents atelectasis, especially beneficial in prone-positioned ventilated patients. It improves oxygenation by maintaining functional residual capacity, while the other options are incorrect: PEEP does not reduce CO₂, does not lower inspiratory pressures, and typically reduces venous return.
questions.learning: Prevents atelectasis of lung and alveolar collapse PEEP helps keep alveoli open and prevents atelectasis, especially beneficial in prone-positioned ventilated patients.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: The following finding was found in an autopsy. Identity the weapon.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Bullet

The given image shows a well-defined punched-out hole in the inner table of the skull. Hence, it could most probably be an entry wound produced by a bullet.

Entry wound: The initial contact of the missile punches a clean hole through the outer table of the skull. Where the bullet emerges internally, the inner table is then unsupported and a cone-shaped plug is detached, forming a crater that is appreciably larger than the external hole.

Bevelling: inner table
Punched out hole: outer table

Exit wound: If the bullet traverses the cranium and penetrates the opposite side, then the same pattern occurs, but this time with the small hole on the inner table and the crater on the outside.

Bevelling: outer table
Punched out hole: inner table

The sequence of bullet injuries is given by Puppe’s rule.

Puppe’s rule: It is possible to determine the sequence of injuries in skull fractures caused by blunt injuries to the head because the second fracture ends at the point where a break in cohesion is already present. The fracture lines created by every other shot extend only up to the fractured lines produced by the previous shot without continuing over them. Even though this rule is true for all blunt injuries to the skull, it is of particular importance in gunshot wounds.

Other options :

Option B: Hammer: When a hammer is used, the fracture is circular or in the shape of an arc of a circle. The diameter of the fracture is the same as the striking surface. There are generally no radiating linear fractures. A depressed fracture is caused by blows from a heavy weapon with a small striking surface. It is also called a signature fracture as the pattern of fracture resembles the weapon or object used.

The following is an image of a depressed fracture:

Option C: Iron Rod: An irregular missile such as an iron rod would produce several irregular lacerated wounds, and the exit wounds are larger than the entrance wounds.

The following is an image of the famous 3D model of Phineas Gage's skull, who survived a workplace injury of a tamping iron rod through his skull.
questions.learning: Bullet — The given image shows a well-defined punched-out hole in the inner table of the skull. Hence, it could most probably be an entry wound produced by a bullet.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Based on the image shown, identify the most appropriate anatomical level for performing a tracheostomy.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Site 4

Tracheostomy is typically performed between the 2nd and 4th tracheal rings, usually below the thyroid isthmus, to establish a definitive surgical airway while minimizing injury to the cricoid cartilage, vocal cords, and major vessels.

Why not the other sites?

• Site 1: Corresponds to the thyrohyoid membrane; not used for tracheostomy.
• Site 2: Corresponds to the cricothyroid membrane; used for emergency cricothyroidotomy, not tracheostomy.
• Site 3: At the level of the 1st tracheal ring/cricoid cartilage; avoided due to the risk of subglottic stenosis and cricoid injury.
• Site 4: Correct site for elective tracheostomy (between the 2nd–4th tracheal rings).
questions.learning: Site 4 Tracheostomy is typically performed between the 2nd and 4th tracheal rings, usually below the thyroid isthmus, to establish a definitive surgical airway while minimizing injury to the cricoid cartilage, vocal cords, and major vessels.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following intravenous anesthetics functions as an NMDA receptor antagonist?
questions.explanation: Ketamine is a unique intravenous anesthetic that works as a non-competitive antagonist at the N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor. It produces a state of "dissociative anesthesia," where the patient appears awake but is detached from their environment and unresponsive to pain. Ketamine is prized for providing intense analgesia and maintaining respiratory drive and blood pressure, making it ideal for trauma or field medicine. Propofol (Option B) and Thiopentone (Option C) primarily function through the enhancement of GABA-A receptors to produce sedation. Midazolam (Option D) is a benzodiazepine that also acts on GABA receptors. Ketamine's primary drawbacks include emergence delirium and vivid dreams, which are often mitigated by combining it with a benzodiazepine. It is also being increasingly used at sub-anesthetic doses for the management of chronic pain and treatment-resistant depression

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A person who has committed a criminal offense was caught by the police and later brought to a criminal court. The court directs the police to transfer the case to juvenile courts if it is proved that the accused is ___years old.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 17

The trial of any juvenile (<18 years) of age is done as per the juvenile justice act.

* According to the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2000, juvenile means a boy or girl who has not completed 18 years of age. They are tried in juvenile courts and not punished with death or imprisonment. They however may be sent to remand home, asked to pay fine

* Recent update: Parliament of India passed the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act - 2015 which came into effect on 15th January 2016. It states that juveniles in conflict with the law in the age group of 16–18, involved in Heinous Offences, can be tried as adults.

* Heinous offenses are those which are punishable with imprisonment of seven years or more if done by adults.

The common carotid artery pulse is taken at the level of the cricoid cartilage.

The common carotid artery pulse is assessed at the level of the neck, typically just lateral to the trachea, where the artery can be palpated against the sternocleidomastoid muscle.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What could be the cause of sudden painless loss of vision?
questions.explanation: Central Serous Retinopathy (CSR) typically presents as a sudden, painless blurring of vision or the appearance of a dark spot (scotoma) in the center of the visual field. It is caused by the accumulation of subretinal fluid in the macula, often associated with stress. Chemical injuries (Option A) are extremely painful and cause immediate structural damage. Acute congestive glaucoma (Option B) and acute iridocyclitis (Option C) are both characterized by severe eye pain, redness, and photophobia. Other major causes of painless sudden vision loss include Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO) and Central Retinal Vein Occlusion (CRVO). Since CSR involves a simple fluid shift without acute inflammation or mechanical destruction, it is the only painless option listed. Most cases of CSR resolve spontaneously, although monitoring is necessary to prevent permanent photoreceptor damage
questions.learning: Central Serous Retinopathy (CSR) typically presents as a sudden, painless blurring of vision or the appearance of a dark spot (scotoma) in the center of the visual field.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presented with fever, dyspnea, palpitations, and tachycardia. The echocardiography revealed vegetation in the septal leaflets. Tissue sections from them reveal the following findings as shown in the image. What is the most likely implicated agent?
options: Pigmented septate hyphae at 90 degrees, Mucormycosis
Right angle branching septate hyphae, Fusarium
Acute angle branching septate hyphae, Aspergillus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Acute angle branching septate hyphae, Aspergillus

The given clinical vignette is suggestive of infective cardiac valvulitis with mycotic vegetation. The histopathological slide shows fungal hyphae of Aspergillus species with non-pigmented, narrow, septate, hyphae with branching at 45o (acute angle).

Invasive aspergillosis is an opportunistic infection seen in the immunosuppressed hosts. Aspergillus has a tendency to invade blood vessels. Thus, widespread hematogenous dissemination with involvement of the heart valves and brain is common. Aspergillus form fruiting bodies and septate filaments, 5 to 10 µm thick, branching at acute angles (40 degrees). Aspergillus hyphae without the distinct fruiting body cannot be distinguished from Pseudallescheria boydii and Fusarium spp. by morphology alone.

Rhinocerebral Aspergillus infection in immunosuppressed individuals resembles that caused by Mucormycoses (e.g., Mucor spp., Rhizopus spp.). (Option-A) Mucormycetes form broad ribbon-like non-septate or sparsely septate pigmented hyphae of variable width (6 to 50 µm) with frequent right-angle branching, distinct from Aspergillus hyphae.

Option B: Disseminated fusariosis differs from disseminated aspergillosis as the former presents with nodular or necrotic painful skin lesions are extremely common with fusariosis. No such history is given in the clinical stem. The organism is difficult to differentiate from Aspergillus species in tissues; thus, identification with culture is imperative.

Option C: Rhizopus shows aseptate hyphae with sporangium and sporangiophores. It is similar in appearance to that of mucormycosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Among the extra intestinal manifestations of Crohn’s disease, which one of the following is related to the disease activity?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Eye complications (Iritis/Uveitis)

• Extraintestinal manifestations (EIMs) occur in 25–40% of patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Some manifestations parallel intestinal disease activity, while others occur independently.
• Eye manifestations (episcleritis, iritis, uveitis) are commonly associated with active Crohn’s disease and may improve with treatment of the intestinal inflammation.

Why not other options?

• B. Renal calculi

• Not related to disease activity.
• Occur due to hyperoxaluria from ileal disease or resection.

• C. Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC)

• Usually independent of bowel disease activity.
• More commonly associated with ulcerative colitis than Crohn’s disease.

• D. Chronic active hepatitis:

• Not directly related to Crohn’s disease activity.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 28-year-old trekker ascends rapidly from sea level to a high-altitude base camp at 4,500 meters. Over the next several days, his body undergoes physiological acclimatization. Which of the following changes is most directly responsible for the early rightward compensation that helps maintain tissue oxygen delivery despite a falling arterial PO2?
options: Decreased 2,3-BPG levels, increasing hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen
Hyperventilation-driven respiratory alkalosis, causing a leftward shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve, followed by renal compensation
Increased renal erythropoietin secretion, causing an immediate rise in hemoglobin concentration within hours
Decreased 2,3-BPG levels and a leftward-shifted curve, improving oxygen loading in the lungs at the cost of tissue unloading
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hyperventilation-driven respiratory alkalosis, causing a leftward shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve, followed by renal compensation

• The earliest acclimatization response to high altitude hypoxia is hyperventilation, triggered by peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid bodies) sensing the fall in arterial PO2. This hyperventilation causes a respiratory alkalosis (low PaCO2, high pH), which initially shifts the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve to the left (increasing hemoglobin's affinity for O2, favoring better loading in the relatively hypoxic alveoli) — though this transiently impairs O2 unloading at the tissues.
• Over subsequent days, renal compensation (bicarbonate excretion) corrects the pH, while a separate, slightly delayed adaptation occurs: increased red cell 2,3-BPG production, which shifts the curve back to the right, restoring better tissue oxygen unloading despite low PaO2.
• Option A (Decreased 2,3-BPG levels, increasing hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen) and Option D (Decreased 2,3-BPG levels and a leftward-shifted curve, improving oxygen loading in the lungs at the cost of tissue unloading) incorrectly state that 2,3-BPG decreases with altitude (it actually increases).
• Option C (Increased renal erythropoietin secretion, causing an immediate rise in hemoglobin concentration within hours) is incorrect because erythropoietin-driven increases in red cell mass/hemoglobin take days to weeks to manifest significantly, not hours — making it a later, not early, compensatory mechanism.

Quick reference — Time course of high-altitude acclimatization:

| Mechanism | Onset | Effect

| --------- | ----- | ------

| Hyperventilation (chemoreceptor-driven) | Minutes–hours | ↓ PaCO2, respiratory alkalosis, ↑ PaO2

| Renal bicarbonate excretion | Days | Corrects pH toward normal, permits further hyperventilation

| ↑ 2,3-BPG in RBCs | Days | Rightward shift of O2-Hb curve, improves tissue O2 unloading

| ↑ Erythropoietin → ↑RBC mass | Days to weeks | ↑ Hemoglobin concentration, ↑O2-carrying capacity

| ↑ Pulmonary vasoconstriction (hypoxic) | Hours–days | Can contribute to high-altitude pulmonary edema if excessive

| ↑ 2,3-DPG, ↑capillary density, ↑ mitochondria (chronic) | Weeks–months | Long-term tissue-level adaptation

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Which of the following best describes paradoxical suicide?
options: Suicide occuring at the time when the patient starts to recover
Suicide after taking low dose of drug
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Suicide occuring at the time when the patient starts to recover

Paradoxical suicide is defined as suicide which occurs when the patient begins to recover from the depression

• This is because, when the patient is in depression, though he/she has the suicidal thoughts cannot act on it due to lack of energy.
• As the patient begins to recover from depression, patients gain energy to put their suicidal thoughts into action.

It is called paradoxical, as one might expect that the risk of suicide reduces as the patient starts to recover, but on contrary to that, the risk of suicide is increased during the recovery phase.

questions.text: What is the name of the procedure shown in the image that was performed on the patient?

Endotracheal intubation (Option A) involves passing a tube through the mouth or nose into the trachea and would not be visible on the external surface of the neck. Needle cricothyroidotomy (Option B) is an emergency procedure involving a small needle through the cricothyroid membrane, used only for temporary oxygenation. questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 55-year-old man presents with hematuria and a mass in the left kidney on a CECT scan, as shown below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Renal cell carcinoma

The history of an elderly male presenting with painless hematuria, renal mass, and an axial renal cortical phase CECT image showing renal lesions with irregular enhancement is suggestive of renal cell carcinoma (RCC).

Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is the most common malignant tumor of the kidney. It usually occurs in the age group 50–70 years and macroscopic hematuria is seen in about 60% of the cases. It usually presents with painless gross hematuria, flank pain, or painless flank mass.

Contrast-enhanced CT is the investigation of choice for RCC. On CT, small lesions enhance homogeneously, whereas larger lesions have irregular enhancement due to areas of necrosis. The clear cell subtype may show much stronger enhancement is a differential for angiomyolipoma. Still, it is essential to note that macroscopic fat is almost always associated with ossification or calcification.

T1-weighted MRI is often heterogeneous due to necrosis, hemorrhage, and solid components. T2-weighted MRI is hyperdense for clear cell RCC and hypodense for papillary RCC. Thus, a T2-weighted MRI can be used for histological diagnosis. Contrast-enhanced MRI is the investigation of choice for detecting vascular invasion of RCC.

Other options:

Renal angiomyolipoma: Angiomyolipomas are benign tumors that occur sporadically or in association with tuberous sclerosis. The mean age of presentation is 43 years, and there is a female predilection. CT findings show cortical lesions that demonstrate macroscopic fat (less than -20 HU) and absence of ossification or calcification.

Renal oncocytoma: They are relatively benign in nature and usually present in the 6th to 7th decade. An important point regarding this tumor is its similarity with RCC, and hence, it is very difficult to differentiate between them preoperatively. A sharp central stellate scar may be seen in one-third of the cases. But RCC may also show this stellate scar appearance in some cases.

Renal cyst: It is a broader term that includes the cystic lesions of the kidney. They can be simple cysts that are benign. Complex or complicated cystic lesions needs evaluation and can be malignant. Bosniak classification of renal cysts is given above.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient with known hypertension presents to the emergency department with palpitations and breathlessness and is diagnosed with hypertensive encephalopathy, with a blood pressure of 220/140 mmHg. What is the most appropriate initial drug to administer?
questions.explanation: This patient is in a hypertensive emergency, defined by severely elevated blood pressure (220/140 mmHg) associated with acute end-organ damage (hypertensive encephalopathy). Immediate management requires controlled reduction of blood pressure using intravenous medications. Nicardipine, a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, is a preferred agent due to its predictable pharmacokinetics, ease of titration, and effectiveness in hypertensive crises. Phentolamine (Option A) is specifically indicated for catecholamine-mediated crises, such as pheochromocytoma. Mannitol (Option C) is an osmotic diuretic used to lower intracranial pressure but is not a primary antihypertensive. Prazosin (Option D) is an oral alpha-blocker used for chronic management, not for the acute parenteral stabilization required in an emergency. The goal in these cases is typically to reduce the mean arterial pressure by no more than 25% within the first hour to prevent cerebral ischemia
questions.learning: This patient is in a hypertensive emergency, defined by severely elevated blood pressure (220/140 mmHg) associated with acute end-organ damage (hypertensive encephalopathy).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old lady presents with a hard lump in the left breast. On examination, the lump is found to be 4 cm × 6 cm in size, not fixed to the skin, but fixed to the underlying pectoralis major muscle. The T stage of this is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. cT3

The breast lump measures 4 × 6 cm, so its largest dimension is 6 cm.

Breast cancer T staging by tumor size:

• T1: ≤2 cm
• T2: >2 cm to ≤5 cm
• T3: >5 cm
• T4: Tumor of any size with extension to the chest wall and/or skin

Although the tumor is fixed to the pectoralis major muscle, involvement of the pectoralis muscle alone does not qualify as chest-wall invasion for T4 staging.

Therefore:

• 6 cm tumor + no skin involvement/chest-wall invasion → cT3

Why not the other options?

• (a) cT4a: Requires invasion of the chest wall; pectoralis muscle involvement alone is not sufficient.
• (b) cT3 — Correct: Tumor >5 cm without T4 features.
• (c) cT4b: Requires features such as ulceration, satellite skin nodules, or edema/peau d’orange.
• (d) cT2: Tumor is >5 cm, so it exceeds the T2 range.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following is considered as a specific laboratory finding in neonatal sepsis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Neutropenia

Neutropenia is the most specific laboratory finding suggestive of neonatal sepsis. It occurs due to rapid consumption of neutrophils at the site of infection and depletion of bone marrow reserves. Although leukocyte counts may vary, neutropenia has greater specificity than leukocytosis for neonatal sepsis.

Why not the other options?

• B. Leukocytosis: Common but nonspecific; can occur with stress, crying, or other conditions.
• C. Thrombocytopenia: Frequently seen, especially in late or severe sepsis, but not specific.
• D. Raised CRP: Useful for diagnosis and monitoring, but CRP is an acute-phase reactant and is not specific for neonatal sepsis.
questions.learning: Neutropenia Neutropenia is the most specific laboratory finding suggestive of neonatal sepsis. It occurs due to rapid consumption of neutrophils at the site of infection and depletion of bone marrow reserves.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following explains the difference in biphasic blood flow between the right and left coronaries?
options: Low pressure developed during right ventricular systole
High pressure developed during right ventricular systole
Reversal of flow during end of atrial systole
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Low pressure developed during right ventricular systole

Coronary blood flow differs between the left and right coronary arteries because of differences in the pressure generated by the ventricles during systole. The right ventricle develops much lower systolic pressure than the left ventricle, resulting in less compression of the intramyocardial coronary vessels. Consequently, right coronary artery blood flow occurs during both systole and diastole (biphasic flow), whereas left coronary artery flow occurs predominantly during diastole.

• Low right ventricular systolic pressure causes minimal compression of right coronary vessels, allowing continued systolic perfusion.

Why not the other options?

• B. High pressure developed during right ventricular systole: Incorrect. The right ventricle generates much lower systolic pressure than the left.
• C. Thick right ventricular wall: Incorrect. The right ventricular wall is thinner, not thicker.
• D. Reversal of flow during end of atrial systole: Incorrect. Not responsible for the biphasic flow pattern.
questions.learning: Low pressure developed during right ventricular systole Coronary blood flow differs between the left and right coronary arteries because of differences in the pressure generated by the ventricles during systole.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Arrange the following international health organizations in the correct sequence shown in the video.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. WHO – UNICEF – NLEP – ICDS

The video shows the logos in the following order:

1. WHO (World Health Organization): United Nations' specialized agency for international public health.
2. UNICEF (United Nations Children's Fund): Focuses on child health, nutrition, immunization, education, and welfare.
3. NLEP (National Leprosy Eradication Programme): Government of India programme aimed at eliminating leprosy.
4. ICDS (Integrated Child Development Services): India's flagship programme providing supplementary nutrition, immunization, preschool education, and health services to children under 6 years and pregnant/lactating women.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 25-year-old woman presented with hearing loss that developed shortly after her first pregnancy. Her audiometry report is given below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Otosclerosis

The clinical scenario describes a patient with post-pregnancy hearing loss. The audiogram shows conductive deafness along with Carhart's notch (dip in bone conduction at 2000 Hz). These findings are highly suggestive of otosclerosis.

Ototoxicity, Meniere’s disease, and noise-induced hearing loss cause sensory neural hearing loss (SNHL) and not conductive hearing loss.

Otosclerosis is caused by bony overgrowth involving the enchondral layer of the bony otic capsule. It presents with bilateral progressive conductive hearing loss and tinnitus. It has an autosomal dominant inheritance and can worsen with stress and hormonal changes like during pregnancy and menopause.

Stapedial otosclerosis is the most common type of otosclerosis. Here the lesion starts just in front of the oval window in an area called fistula ante fenestrae.

The presence of a reddish hue on the promontory through the tympanic membrane, known as the Schwartze sign, suggests an active focus. PTA shows loss of air conduction with air-bone gap, more for lower frequencies and Carhart's notch may be seen. Tympanometry shows an As type of tympanogram in which there is reduced compliance at or near the ambient air pressure.

Medical management with sodium fluoride is used in the active stage. Definitive treatment is stapedectomy/stapedotomy with the placement of a prosthesis. Carhart notch usually disappears after a successful stapedectomy.

Other options:

Option A: Ototoxicity causes SNHL and shows a high-frequency hearing loss in the SNHL curve.

Option B: In Meniere's disease, pure tone audiometry shows an SNHL pattern with a rising curve in the early stages (as lower frequencies are involved first) and as the disease progresses higher frequencies are involved, the curve becomes flat or a falling type.

Option D: Noise-induced hearing loss is SNHL and PTA shows a characteristic acoustic dip at 4000 Hz both for air and bone conduction.
questions.learning: Otosclerosis — The clinical scenario describes a patient with post-pregnancy hearing loss. The audiogram shows conductive deafness along with Carhart's notch (dip in bone conduction at 2000 Hz).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What does the presence of painless sores on the vulval area indicate?
questions.explanation: The presence of painless sores in the vulval area is characteristic of condyloma lata, which are lesions seen in secondary syphilis caused by Treponema pallidum. These lesions are typically broad-based, flat, moist, and highly infectious, often found in warm, moist areas such as the vulva, perineum, or perianal region. Their painless nature is a key diagnostic clue. Why other options are wrong: (A) Genital herpes causes painful vesicles and ulcers, often with burning sensation (B) Condylomata acuminata (HPV-related) are cauliflower-like warts, usually not described as sores (C) Gonococcal vulvovaginitis presents with discharge and inflammation, not painless sores
questions.learning: The presence of painless sores in the vulval area is characteristic of condyloma lata, which are lesions seen in secondary syphilis caused by Treponema pallidum.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following conditions shown in the given CT is associated with the Holman-Miller sign?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Juvenile nasopharnygeal angiofibroma

The given CT showing the Holman-Miller sign is associated with nasopharyngeal angiofibroma.

Nasopharyngeal angiofibroma is a benign but locally invasive tumor predominant in adolescent males aged 10-20 years. It arises from the posterior part of the nasal cavity, close to the superior margin of the sphenopalatine foramen. These patients have a hamartomatous nidus of vascular tissue in the nasopharynx that grows to form angiofibroma under the influence of testosterone. Therefore, it is thought to be testosterone-dependent.

Angiofibroma can extend into the nasal cavity causing obstruction, epistaxis, paranasal sinuses, pterygomaxillary fossa, infratemporal fossa, cheek, orbits causing proptosis, frog-face deformity, and cranial cavity. The clinical features include:

* Profuse, recurrent, spontaneous epistaxis - most common; Internal maxillary artery is the most common source artery of nasal bleeding followed by ascending pharyngeal artery and external, internal, and common carotid arteries.

* Progressive nasal obstruction and denasal speech - due to mass in the postnasal space

* Conductive hearing loss and otitis media with effusion - due to obstruction of the eustachian tube

* Sessile, lobulated, or smooth mass in the nasopharynx

* Other clinical features include the broadening of the nasal bridge, proptosis, cheek swelling, involvement of IInd, IIIrd, IVth, and VIth cranial nerves

Diagnosis typically involves contrast-enhanced CT scans, which reveal the tumour's size and any bony destruction, along with characteristic signs such as anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus known as the Antral sign or Holman-Miller sign (shown in the image below). Biopsy of the mass is generally avoided due to the risk of severe bleeding.

Surgical excision remains the mainstay of treatment, with various approaches depending on tumour extent. Common surgical techniques include:

* Transpalatine approach

* Lateral Rhinotomy

* Endoscopic Techniques: minimally invasive

* Maxillary Swing Approach: larger tumours.

* Intracranial-Extracranial Approach: significant intracranial extension

Other Options:

Option A: Haller cells are a type of ethmoidal cells that are situated on the roof of the maxillary sinus. Sometimes they may enlarge and block the opening of the maxillary sinus leading to maxillary sinusitis.

Option C: Antrochoanal polyp is a type of non-neoplastic nasal polypoidal masses of edematous nasal or sinus mucosa which arises from the mucosa of the maxillary antrum near its accessory ostium. The clinical features include unilateral nasal obstruction, mucoid nasal discharge, and a hyponasal voice.

Option D: Unilateral obstruction of the nasal cavity due to the presence of mass and nasal bleeding is suggestive of the diagnosis of rhinosporidiosis. Rhinosporidiosis is a chronic granulomatous disease caused by Rhinosporidium seeberi. It is most prevalent in rural districts, among persons bathing in public ponds or working in stagnant water, such as rice fields.
questions.learning: Juvenile nasopharnygeal angiofibroma — The given CT showing the Holman-Miller sign is associated with nasopharyngeal angiofibroma. Nasopharyngeal angiofibroma is a benign but locally invasive tumor predominant in adolescent males aged 10-20 years.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following procedures is done with the instrument shown below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Endometrial sampling

Pipelle aspirator (a) and Vabra (b) aspirator are shown in the image above which are used to obtain endometrial sampling.

Endometrial sampling using Pipelle aspirator - aspiration of the uterine cavity and sending the sample for histopathological examination. It is used as a screening test in menopausal women on HRT or tamoxifen.

Postmenopausal bleeding is defined as bleeding from the genital tract, more than 12 months after the last menstrual period in a woman not on hormone replacement. All postmenopausal women with unexpected uterine bleeding should be evaluated for endometrial malignancy since age is a significant risk factor for this.

Transvaginal ultrasound(TVS) is the first-line investigation.

Endometrial sampling is indicated if:

* Transvaginal ultrasound is unable to provide a distinct image of the endometrium.

* Endometrium thickness is >4mm

* Areas of heterogeneous echogenic pattern are present

* Ongoing bleeding in a woman may indicate endometrial cancer, regardless of endometrial thickness.

The image below gives a summary of the evaluation of postmenopausal bleeding, as per the FOGSI guidelines.

Leech-Wilkinson cannula is used to inject dye in hysterosalpingography. The image below is that of a Leech-Wilkinson cannula.

The instrument shown below is a Sim's uterine curette, used for endometrial curettage.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 6-year-old child with a history of repeated, multiple, long bone fractures is diagnosed with osteogenesis imperfecta. Which of the following structures contains the type of collagen that is defective in this disease? * Tendon * Basement membrane * Elastic cartilage * Skin * Sclera
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 4, 5

Osteogenesis imperfecta(OI) is a connective tissue disorder that occurs due to abnormal type 1 collagen production. Type 1 collagen is also present in the skin, tendons, and sclera (1, 4, 5) apart from bones.

OI also called brittle bone disease, is an autosomal dominant disorder. There are 8 types of osteogenesis imperfecta. It occurs most commonly due to mutation in the COL1A and COL2A genes. These mutations lead to the replacement of glycine amino acid with another amino acid resulting in an abnormal triple helix of collagen. This results in the abnormal formation of type 1 collagen.

The defining clinical features of OI include:

* Osteopenia

* Recurrent Fractures

* Laxity of Ligaments

* Bluish Discoloration of The Sclerae

* Dentinogenesis Imperfecta ("Crumbling Teeth")

Note:

* Type I collagen is seen in the bone, dermis, tendon, ligaments, fibrocartilage, and sclera of the eyeball.

* Type II collagen is seen in hyaline and elastic cartilage (Option 3) and the vitreous body of the eye.

* Type III collagen is seen in reticulin fibers, smooth muscle, endoneurium, arteries, uterus, kidney, spleen, and liver.

* Type IV collagen is seen in epithelial and endothelial basal laminae and basement membranes. (Option 2)

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 28-year-old man presents in a disoriented state with bradycardia (heart rate 50/min), hypotension (80/60 mmHg), marked respiratory depression (7 breaths/min), hypothermia (95°F), and pinpoint pupils. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with the classic "opioid toxidrome" triad: CNS depression (disorientation), respiratory depression (7 breaths/min), and pinpoint pupils (miosis). Other supporting clinical signs include bradycardia (50 bpm), hypotension (80/60 mmHg), and hypothermia (95 F). Benzodiazepine overdose (Option A) also causes CNS and respiratory depression but typically results in normal or dilated pupils. Cocaine intoxication (Option B) is a sympathomimetic syndrome characterized by tachycardia, hypertension, and dilated pupils (mydriasis). Opioid withdrawal (Option C) presents with symptoms opposite to intoxication, such as agitation, tachycardia, diarrhea, and dilated pupils. The presence of pinpoint pupils is a highly specific marker for opioid toxicity, necessitating immediate airway support and the administration of Naloxone. Therefore, opioid intoxication is the definitive diagnosis for this clinical presentation
questions.learning: The patient presents with the classic "opioid toxidrome" triad: CNS depression (disorientation), respiratory depression (7 breaths/min), and pinpoint pupils (miosis).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient presented with a history of multiple episodes of vomiting. He was given an intravenous drug, and later, he developed abnormal movements. Which of the following can be used to treat him?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Benzhexol

Benzhexol should be used in the management of this patient. The development of abnormal movements following an anti-emetic injection suggests that the antiemetic used in this case is probably metoclopramide.

Metoclopramide is a dopamine receptor antagonist used as a prokinetic and anti-emetic agent. It can produce extrapyramidal side effects and dystonia is seen acutely following intravenous injections. Anticholinergics like benzhexol (trihexyphenidyl) are used in the management of these side effects. Benzhexol is a centrally-acting anticholinergic agent. It acts by restoring the cholinergic balance in the striatal interneurons.

Extrapyramidal side effects of metoclopramide are commonly seen in children and young adults with higher doses. Acute dystonia occurs after intravenous administration, while parkinsonian-like symptoms develop weeks after therapy. It is managed with the discontinuation of metoclopramide and with anticholinergics or antihistaminics. Irreversible tardive dyskinesia can occur with chronic treatment.

Other adverse effects:

It can cause galactorrhea by its dopamine antagonism. Methemoglobinemia can occur if used in infants.

Other options:

Option A: Hyoscine (scopolamine): It is a muscarinic receptor antagonist used in the management of motion sickness and vomiting.

Option B: Cyproheptadine is an H1 receptor antagonist used in the management of various allergy-related conditions like allergic rhinitis, anaphylaxis, urticaria, etc.

Option C: Levodopa is the precursor of dopamine and it is given in combination with carbidopa for the management of parkinsonism.
questions.learning: Benzhexol Benzhexol should be used in the management of this patient. The development of abnormal movements following an anti-emetic injection suggests that the antiemetic used in this case is probably metoclopramide.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A worker in an industry for the last 20 years develops dry cough and chest tightness. He had the following finding in his pulmonary biopsy. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Asbestosis

Long-term occupational exposure with dry cough and chest tightness suggests an interstitial pneumoconiosis.

Pulmonary biopsy in asbestosis classically shows ferruginous (asbestos) bodies—iron-coated fibers within macrophages.

Silicosis shows silicotic nodules, anthracosis is carbon deposition, and berylliosis causes non-caseating granulomas.

| Option | Exposure | Pathology | When it is Correct | Why NOT Correct Here | Exam Pearl

| ------ | -------- | --------- | ------------------ | -------------------- | ----------

| A. Silicosis | Mining, sandblasting | Nodular fibrosis (upper lobes) | Eggshell calcification | ❌ No silica nodules mentioned | ↑ TB risk

| B. Anthracosis | Coal dust/pollution | Carbon pigment in macrophages | Usually asymptomatic | ❌ No fibrosis, mild disease | “Black lung” (mild form)

| C. Berylliosis | Aerospace/electronics | Non-caseating granulomas | Mimics sarcoidosis | ❌ No granulomas described | Patch test positive

| D. Asbestosis ✅ | Shipyard, construction | Ferruginous bodies + fibrosis | ✔ Chronic exposure + ILD | ✔ Correct | Lower lobe fibrosis

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the condition shown in this picture?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rupture of biceps tendon

The image shows Popeye sign and it is seen in rupture of proximal tendon of biceps.  Proximal tendon of biceps refers to both long head and short head of biceps.

Popeye sign: On flexing the elbow there is an extremely prominent bulge of the muscle belly as its unrestrained fibers contract.

The proximal biceps tendon makes up 90-97% of all biceps tendon ruptures. In isolation, it has little effect on the upper limb function

The 4 most common areas of tendon rupture include:

* Quadriceps

* Achilles

* Rotator cuff (most commonly, the supraspinatus)

* Biceps.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the type of hernia:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Amyand

An Amyand hernia is an inguinal hernia that contains the appendix within the hernia sac. It’s typically right-sided and may present with features of appendicitis masquerading as hernia pain. Management depends on appendix status—normal vs inflamed—along with hernia repair. Littre hernia contains a Meckel’s diverticulum, Grynfeltt hernia is a superior lumbar hernia through the Grynfeltt triangle, and Gibbon hernia refers to a rare interparietal/lateral ventral hernia variant.

| Hernia | Contents

| ------ | --------

| Amyand hernia | Appendix within inguinal hernia sac

| Littre hernia | Meckel’s diverticulum in hernia sac

| Richter hernia | Only part of bowel wall (antimesenteric border) trapped

| Maydl hernia | Two bowel loops forming W configuration; strangulation occurs in intra-abdominal loop

| Garengeot hernia (often confused in notes) | Appendix within femoral hernia

| Gibbon hernia | Hernia containing ileocecal segment

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman at 17 weeks of gestation presents with hypertension, with blood pressure readings of 140/94 mmHg initially and 144/90 mmHg four hours later. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Hypertension in pregnancy is classified based on the timing of onset. Hypertension that is diagnosed before 20 weeks of gestation is defined as chronic hypertension. Since this patient is at 17 weeks with sustained blood pressure readings above 140/90 mmHg, chronic hypertension is the most likely diagnosis. Gestational hypertension (Option A) and pre-eclampsia (Option D) are conditions that characteristically develop after 20 weeks of pregnancy. Pre-eclampsia also requires the presence of proteinuria or end-organ dysfunction. Acute on chronic hypertension (Option C), often termed "superimposed pre-eclampsia," refers to the development of pre-eclampsia features in a patient with known chronic hypertension. Patients with chronic hypertension require close monitoring for fetal growth restriction and the later development of pre-eclampsia, as they are at significantly higher risk for these complications compared to the general obstetric population
questions.learning: Hypertension in pregnancy is classified based on the timing of onset. Hypertension that is diagnosed before 20 weeks of gestation is defined as chronic hypertension.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In which of the following conditions is ovarian drilling commonly indicated?
questions.explanation: Laparoscopic Ovarian Drilling (LOD) is a specialized surgical procedure indicated for women with Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome (PCOS) who suffer from infertility and have not responded to medical treatments like clomiphene citrate. The procedure involves using heat or a laser to destroy small portions of the ovarian stroma. This reduces the production of excessive androgens, which often restores regular ovulation and improves pregnancy rates. Ovarian tumors (Option A) require resection or staging surgery, not drilling. Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (Option C) is a medical complication of IVF that requires fluid management, as surgery can be dangerous. Endometriosis (Option D) is treated via laparoscopic ablation of implants or cystectomy for endometriomas, not stromal drilling. Therefore, ovarian drilling is a specific second-line treatment for the management of anovulatory infertility in PCOS patients
questions.learning: Laparoscopic Ovarian Drilling (LOD) is a specialized surgical procedure indicated for women with Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome (PCOS) who suffer from infertility and have not responded to medical treatments like clomiphene citrate.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A researcher is investigating the restriction (R) point, the first major checkpoint of the cell cycle that determines whether a cell will commit to DNA synthesis or exit the cell cycle into a quiescent (G₀) state. This checkpoint is located immediately before which phase of the cell cycle?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. S phase

The G₁/S checkpoint (Restriction point or R point) is the first and most important checkpoint of the cell cycle. It occurs in late G₁ phase, immediately before the S phase, where the cell decides whether to:

• Proceed to DNA replication (S phase), or
• Exit the cell cycle and enter the quiescent G₀ phase

Once a cell crosses this checkpoint, it is committed to completing the cell cycle, even if external growth factors are withdrawn.

The checkpoint assesses:

• Cell size
• Nutrient and energy availability
• Growth factor stimulation
• DNA damage

It is regulated by:

• Cyclin D–CDK4/6
• Cyclin E–CDK2
• Retinoblastoma (Rb) protein
• p53 (via p21 in response to DNA damage)

Why not the other options?

• A. G₂ phase: Incorrect. The G₂/M checkpoint occurs after DNA replication, ensuring DNA has been completely and accurately replicated before mitosis.
• B. M phase: Incorrect. The spindle assembly checkpoint occurs during metaphase, ensuring proper chromosome attachment before anaphase.
• C. S phase: ✅ Correct. The restriction point is located immediately before the S phase.
• D. G₀ phase: Incorrect. G₀ is not a phase that follows the checkpoint; rather, cells exit from G₁ into G₀ if they do not receive the signals required to pass the checkpoint.

High-yield pearl

| Cell cycle checkpoint | Location | Function

| --------------------- | -------- | --------

| G₁/S (Restriction point) | End of G₁, before S phase | Determines commitment to DNA replication; checks DNA damage, nutrients, growth factors

| G₂/M checkpoint | End of G₂ | Ensures DNA replication is complete and DNA is undamaged before mitosis

| Spindle checkpoint | Metaphase | Ensures all chromosomes are attached to spindle fibers before anaphase

Exam tip:

The G₁/S checkpoint is the commitment checkpoint of the cell cycle:

• Pass → Enter S phase and replicate DNA
• Fail → Cell arrests for repair or exits into G₀.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: In a patient with stroke who exhibits homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing, which part of the visual (optic) pathway is most likely involved by the lesion?
questions.explanation: "Homonymous hemianopia" is a visual field defect where the same half of the visual field is lost in both eyes. When this defect specifically "spares the macula" (central 5–10 degrees), it is highly characteristic of a lesion in the primary visual cortex of the occipital lobe. Macular sparing occurs because the macular region of the visual cortex is located at the occipital pole and has a dual blood supply from both the middle cerebral artery (MCA) and the posterior cerebral artery (PCA). Option C (Optic radiation) lesions usually cause complete hemianopia without macular sparing. Option D (Optic chiasma) lesions cause bitemporal hemianopia. Option A is a visual area, not a lesion site. This finding is most common after a PCA stroke; even if the artery is occluded, the MCA can often maintain perfusion to the macular representation in the cortex. Recognizing macular sparing is a critical localizing sign in clinical neurology

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A patient was undergoing a hysteroscopic removal of a submucosal fibroid, in which a fluid deficit of 2000 mL is estimated in a patient. What is the immediate complication of this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pulmonary edema

Hysteroscopy is commonly used for removal of:

• Submucosal fibroids
• Polyps
• Adhesions (Asherman syndrome)

To visualize the uterine cavity, distension fluids are used. Distension media used include:

• Normal saline
• Glycine
• Sorbitol

During the procedure, these fluids can be absorbed into systemic circulation.

Large amount of fluid absorbed

↓

Increased intravascular volume

↓

Fluid overload

↓

Pulmonary congestion

↓

Pulmonary edema

Fluid deficit >2000 mL during hysteroscopy → risk of pulmonary edema.

A large fluid deficit implies significant intravascular absorption of distension medium → acute volume overload. This can precipitate pulmonary edema with respiratory compromise. ATN, DIC, and thromboembolism are not the immediate expected complication here.

Complications of Excess Fluid Absorption

| Complication | Mechanism

| ------------ | ---------

| Pulmonary edema | Fluid overload

| Hyponatremia | Hypotonic fluid absorption

| Cerebral edema | Severe hyponatremia

| Cardiac failure | Volume overload

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following proteins functions as a pro-apoptotic factor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. BAX

Cell stress / DNA damage

↓

BAX / BAK activation

↓

Mitochondrial membrane permeabilization

↓

Cytochrome c release

↓

Caspase activation

↓

Apoptosis

BAX is a pro-apoptotic member of the BCL-2 family that promotes mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization. It facilitates release of cytochrome c from mitochondria, activating the intrinsic apoptotic pathway.

This leads to caspase activation and programmed cell death.

BCL-2, BCL-XL, and MCL-1 are anti-apoptotic proteins that inhibit mitochondrial apoptosis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the Battle sign?
questions.explanation: In clinical forensic and trauma surgery, the Battle sign is a pathognomonic physical indicator of a basilar skull fracture, specifically involving the petrous portion of the temporal bone. It is defined as mastoid ecchymosis (bruising over the mastoid process behind the ear) (Option A). This bruising results from blood tracking along the path of the posterior auricular artery. Periorbital hematoma (Option B), also known as "Raccoon eyes," is a different sign indicating a fracture of the anterior cranial fossa. Bezold abscess (Option C) is a complication of mastoiditis, involving an abscess in the sternocleidomastoid muscle. Perichondritis (Option D) is an infection of the ear cartilage. Because the Battle sign is specifically localized to the mastoid area following head trauma, mastoid ecchymosis is the definitive answer. Its appearance may be delayed for 24–48 hours after the injury occurs
questions.learning: In clinical forensic and trauma surgery, the Battle sign is a pathognomonic physical indicator of a basilar skull fracture, specifically involving the petrous portion of the temporal bone.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding vaginal epithelium in adult female: 1. From puberty till menopause, the vaginal epithelium is devoid of any gland. 2. The basal epithelial layer contains glycogen. 3. Intermediate and superficial cells become continuous with those covering vaginal portion of cervix. 4. Unlike skin, it does not contain hair follicle. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 3 and 4

1. From puberty till menopause, vaginal epithelium is devoid of glands: Correct.

• The vagina has no glands in its epithelium.
• Vaginal lubrication mainly comes from cervical mucus and transudation through the vaginal wall.

2. Basal epithelial layer contains glycogen: Incorrect.

• Glycogen is mainly present in the intermediate and superficial cells under estrogenic influence.
• Lactobacilli metabolize glycogen to lactic acid, maintaining the acidic vaginal pH.

3. Intermediate and superficial cells become continuous with those covering the vaginal portion of cervix: Correct.

• The vaginal epithelium is non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium and is continuous with the squamous epithelium of the ectocervix.

4. Unlike skin, it does not contain hair follicles: Correct.

• Vaginal mucosa lacks hair follicles, sebaceous glands and sweat glands
questions.learning: From puberty till menopause, vaginal epithelium is devoid of glands: Correct. • The vagina has no glands in its epithelium. • Vaginal lubrication mainly comes from cervical mucus and transudation through the vaginal wall.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Where is the signaling sequence in a type 2 membrane protein located?
options: Inside the membrane at the N-terminal end
Inside the membrane at the C-terminal end
Outside the membrane at the N-terminal end
Outside the membrane at the C-terminal end
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Inside the membrane at the N-terminal end

The signaling sequence in a type 2 membrane protein is located inside the membrane (transmembrane region).

A membrane protein can be either integral protein (spans the thickness of the cell membrane) or peripheral protein (attached to the peripheral side of the membrane).

Integral membrane proteins or transmembrane proteins are embedded in the cell membrane, spanning through the entire thickness. They are anchored by hydrophobic interactions and require the use of detergent for solubility.  Examples are ligand-binding receptors for hormones or neurotransmitters, transport proteins like Na+-K+ ATPase, pores, ion channels, cell adhesion molecules, and GTP-binding proteins (G proteins).

Peripheral proteins are attached only to one surface of the cell membrane and do not penetrate all the way through. They are often attached to integral proteins. Examples are cell surface receptors, enzymes, ankyrin.

Signaling sequences are 16 to 30 amino acid residues in length and located at the N-terminal extension of the membrane proteins. After an appropriate trigger, they are either cleaved (and bind to MHC class I of the endoplasmic reticulum) or act as a membrane anchor (transporting proteins across the membrane).

Integral proteins can be divided into:

• Type I integral proteins have a cleavable N-terminal signal sequence (towards the cytosol). Examples include histocompatibility antigens, glycophorin, and membrane immunoglobulin.
• Type II integral proteins have a non-cleavable N terminal combined signal/anchor sequence. Examples include transferrin receptors and glycosyl transferases.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which part of the placenta is attached to the maternal body?
questions.explanation: The placenta is a feto-maternal organ. The maternal part of the placenta is the Decidua basalis, which is the specific portion of the modified endometrium that lies directly beneath the site of implantation and is firmly attached to the maternal body (the uterine wall). The Decidua parietalis (Option A) lines the remainder of the uterine cavity. The Chorionic plate (Option C) is the fetal surface of the placenta, from which the umbilical cord originates and the placental vessels branch. The Spiral arteries (Option D) are the maternal vessels that supply blood to the intervillous spaces but are not a "part" of the placental structure itself. This placental-decidual interface is where the critical exchange of gases, nutrients, and waste occurs. Abnormalities in this attachment lead to serious complications: placenta accreta occurs when the placenta attaches too deeply into the myometrium, and abruptio placenta occurs when the decidua basalis prematurely separates from the uterine wall

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: What is the effect of sympathetic nervous system stimulation on glomerular filtration rate (GFR)?
options: Increased GFR due to afferent arteriolar dilation
Increased GFR due to efferent arteriolar dilation
Decreased GFR due to afferent arteriolar constriction
Decreased GFR due to efferent arteriolar constriction
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Decreased GFR due to afferent arteriolar constriction

• Sympathetic stimulation (e.g., during hemorrhage, severe stress, or exercise) predominantly causes constriction of the afferent arteriole, which reduces glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure and consequently decreases GFR.
• At the same time, sympathetic activation also constricts the efferent arteriole to a degree, along with systemic vasoconstriction — but the net effect at high sympathetic tone is a reduction in renal blood flow and GFR, since afferent constriction dominates the response and reduces overall perfusion to the glomerulus.
• This is a protective mechanism to shunt blood away from the kidneys toward vital organs (heart, brain) during conditions like severe hypotension or shock.
• Options involving dilation (A, B) are incorrect, since sympathetic stimulation causes vasoconstriction, not dilation, in the renal vasculature.

| --------- | ------------ | -------------

| Sympathetic stimulation (NE) | Afferent >> Efferent constriction | ↓ GFR

| Angiotensin II | Efferent constriction (predominant) | Maintains/↑ GFR (at low doses)

| Prostaglandins (PGE2, PGI2) | Afferent dilation | Maintains GFR (protective)

| ACE inhibitors/ARBs | Efferent dilation (block AT-II) | ↓ GFR (intended in proteinuric disease)

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A patient was brought to the hospital after a road traffic accident. He had severe muscle injury and his serum K+ level was found to be 5.5 mEq/L. What change will happen to the resting membrane potential in this patient?
options: First becomes more positive, then negative
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Becomes more positive

Hyperkalemia reduces the K⁺ gradient across the cell membrane, decreasing outward K⁺ diffusion. This makes the resting membrane potential less negative (partial depolarization). As extracellular K⁺ rises, the membrane shifts toward threshold. Hence the resting membrane potential becomes more positive.

↓

↓ Concentration gradient

↓

↓ K⁺ efflux from cell

↓

Less positive charge leaving

↓

Inside becomes less negative

↓

RMP shifts toward zero (more positive)

Later - Recycling

Note: Ash from incineration of biomedical waste shall be disposed of at common hazardous waste treatment and disposal facility. However, it may be disposed of in a municipal landfill, if the toxic metals in incineration ash are within the regulatory quantities as defined under the Hazardous Waste (Management and Handling and Transboundary Movement) Rules, 2008 as amended from time to time.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Describe the structural composition of the outer nose?
options: Upper 1/2 is bony, and lower 1/2 is cartilaginous
Upper 2/3rd is bony and the lower 1/3rd is cartilaginous
questions.explanation: The structural framework of the external human nose is composed of both rigid bone and flexible cartilage. The upper one-third of the nose is supported by bone, specifically the paired nasal bones and the frontal process of the maxilla. The lower two-thirds of the nose is composed of hyaline cartilage, which includes the major alar cartilages, lateral nasal cartilages, and the cartilaginous part of the nasal septum. This arrangement provides stability at the root while allowing for flexibility and airway regulation at the tip and nostrils. Option A and Option B provide incorrect proportions for these components. Understanding this specific 1:2 ratio of bone to cartilage is essential in plastic and reconstructive surgery (rhinoplasty) and in managing nasal fractures. Fractures typically involve the upper bony bridge, whereas trauma to the lower portion often results in cartilaginous deviation or septal hematoma. Consequently, the correct anatomical description characterizes the upper third as bony and the lower two-thirds as cartilaginous
questions.learning: The structural framework of the external human nose is composed of both rigid bone and flexible cartilage. The upper one-third of the nose is supported by bone, specifically the paired nasal bones and the frontal process of the maxilla.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What level of prevention is involved when a government intends to establish tobacco control regulations?
questions.explanation: Primordial prevention is the level of prevention that targets the social, economic, and environmental factors that contribute to the emergence of risk factors. By establishing tobacco control regulations (such as bans on advertising or public smoking), the government is working to prevent the emergence of the habit in the population, effectively stopping the development of a major cardiovascular and oncological risk factor before it even starts. Primary prevention (Option B) focuses on individuals who already have the risk factor (e.g., advising a current smoker to quit) to prevent the disease. Secondary prevention (Option C) involves early diagnosis (e.g., screening for lung cancer). Tertiary prevention (Option D) focuses on rehabilitation after a disease has occurred. Primordial prevention is considered the most cost-effective and population-wide strategy for managing non-communicable diseases. It targets the "causes of the causes," aiming to change the underlying societal norms and environments to promote a tobacco-free lifestyle for future generations
questions.learning: Primordial prevention is the level of prevention that targets the social, economic, and environmental factors that contribute to the emergence of risk factors.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 56-year-old man presents with an 18-month history of gradually progressive weakness affecting both his upper and lower limbs. He has difficulty buttoning his shirt, climbing stairs, and walking long distances. Examination reveals marked muscle wasting with fasciculations in the upper limbs, spasticity, brisk deep tendon reflexes, and bilateral extensor plantar responses. Sensory examination is completely normal. A few months later, he develops dysarthria and dysphagia. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)

The patient has the classical features of Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS), a progressive motor neuron disease characterized by simultaneous involvement of:

• Upper motor neurons (UMN)
• Lower motor neurons (LMN)

with no sensory deficits.

Key clinical clues

• Progressive weakness
• LMN signs

• Muscle wasting
• Fasciculations
• Weakness

• UMN signs

• Hyperreflexia
• Spasticity
• Extensor plantar (Babinski) response

• Bulbar involvement

• Dysarthria
• Dysphagia
• Tongue wasting and fasciculations (later)

• Sensory examination is normal

The coexistence of UMN + LMN signs with preserved sensation is the hallmark of ALS.
questions.learning: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) — The patient has the classical features of Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS), a progressive motor neuron disease characterized by simultaneous involvement of: • Upper motor neurons (UMN) • Lower motor neurons (LMN)…

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: An infant is being evaluated for recurrent seizure episodes, and EEG findings reveal hypsarrhythmia. Which medication is preferred for the management of this condition?
questions.explanation: The finding of hypsarrhythmia on an EEG is pathognomonic for infantile spasms, also known as West syndrome. This is a severe epileptic encephalopathy occurring in infants. The first-line pharmacological treatment is adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), which is highly effective in stopping the spasms and improving the EEG pattern. Vigabatrin (Option B) is also an effective treatment and is considered the first-line choice specifically for cases associated with tuberous sclerosis, but ACTH remains preferred for idiopathic or other symptomatic cases. Valproate (Option C) is a broad-spectrum anticonvulsant but is less effective for this specific syndrome. Carbamazepine (Option D) is not indicated and may actually worsen the condition in infants with West syndrome. Therefore, ACTH is the gold standard for the initial management of hypsarrhythmia
questions.learning: The finding of hypsarrhythmia on an EEG is pathognomonic for infantile spasms, also known as West syndrome. This is a severe epileptic encephalopathy occurring in infants.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with diminished night vision and the following finding was seen on fundoscopy. Which of the following statements is not true regarding the condition?
options: Dystrophy of rods more common than that of cones
ERG shows decreased amplitude of A and B waves
Sometimes patients present in later stages with loss of peripheral vision.
Night blindness is a late feature
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Night blindness is a late feature

Diminished night vision along with fundoscopy features point to the diagnosis of retinitis pigmentosa. Option D is not true regarding retinitis pigmentosa. Night blindness is an early feature.

Retinitis pigmentosa is retinal dystrophy that results in degeneration of photoreceptors(rods more than cones). It can be inherited (autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, or X-linked recessive) or acquired due to sporadic mutation in the rhodopsin gene. Fundoscopy shows bilateral, mid-peripheral intraretinal perivascular 'bone-spicule' changes and atrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium

Patients present with worsening night blindness initially. However, patients do not often notice night blindness and may present after much disease progression. They also develop tunnel vision, which manifests as difficulty performing activities of daily living such as reading, walking, and driving.

Ocular examination reveals normal visual activity and central vision (though central vision will be involved later in disease progression). Fundoscopy shows bilateral, mid-peripheral intraretinal perivascular 'bone-spicule' changes and atrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium. There is severe peripheral pigmentation, arteriolar narrowing, and pallor of the disc.

Retinitis pigmentosa can lead to posterior subcapsular cataracts, open-angle glaucoma, keratoconus, and posterior vitreous detachment as possible complications.

There is no specific treatment for retinitis pigmentosa

Option B:Electroretinography (ERG) is the record of changes in the resting potential of the eye induced by a flash of light.

Waves of normal ERG

• a-wave: negative wave possibly arising from the rods and cones
• b-wave: large positive wave which is generated by Muller cells, but represents the activity of the bipolar cells
• c-wave: positive wave representing the metabolic activity of pigment epithelium

In retintis pigmentosa, it is abnormal and shows reduced scotopic, subnormal responses in early disease and becomes completely extinguished in advanced disease.
questions.learning: Night blindness is a late feature Diminished night vision along with fundoscopy features point to the diagnosis of retinitis pigmentosa. Option D is not true regarding retinitis pigmentosa.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 25-year-old patient presents to the surgical OPD with a painless left inguinal reducible mass. On examination cough impulse is positive. After further investigations, the patient is diagnosed with an inguinal hernia. What is the surgical management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hernioplasty

The given clinical scenario suggestive of inguinal hernia which is managed with Lichtenstein mesh repair which is a type of hernioplasty.

Inguinal hernias can either be direct or indirect. The contents of a direct hernia protrude medially to the inferior epigastric artery. Whereas, the contents of an indirect hernia protrude laterally to the inferior epigastric artery. Despite the differences in origin, the management of both hernias is done by a Lichenstein repair.

A Lichtenstein mesh repair is currently one of the most frequently used methods for treating an inguinal hernia. It is done for the reconstruction of the inguinal floor in adults. It is an anterior tension-free mesh repair that reduces the chances of recurrence of a hernia. A piece of prosthetic nonabsorbable mesh is used to fit the canal to bridge the defect in this repair.

Other surgical methods used for the repair of a hernia are:

* Bassini repair - It is done for the reconstruction of the inguinal floor in adults. In this method, a mesh is not used. It is associated with a high recurrence and is not used frequently now. It is used only in cases of hernial strangulation and peritonitis where the use of a mesh is not preferred. It is performed by suturing the transversus abdominis and internal oblique musculoaponeurotic arches/conjoined tendon to the inguinal ligament.

* Shouldice repair - It is a multilayered repair, where the posterior wall of the inguinal canal is strengthened by continuous sutures. It involves double-breasting of the transversalis fascia. It is associated with a very low recurrence rate.

* Gilbert repair (plug and patch repair) - It is an extension of Lichtenstein’s original mesh repair and has now become the most commonly performed primary anterior inguinal hernia repair. In this technique, a cone-shaped plug of polypropylene mesh is used. It is deployed like an upside-down umbrella when inserted into the internal inguinal ring to occlude the hernia

* McVay repair (Cooper's ligament repair) is used for the correction of direct inguinal hernia, large indirect hernia, recurrent hernia, femoral hernias (particularly suited for strangulated femoral hernias). In this method, the transversus abdominis aponeurosis is approximated to Cooper's ligament.

* Stoppa-Rives repair - It is used for the repair of large, recurrent, or bilateral hernias. In this method, a sub-umbilical midline incision is given to place a large mesh into the preperitoneal space.

* Herniotomy - It is used to treat inguinal hernia in a child which occurs due to the presence of a patent processus vaginalis. Therefore in herniotomy, the repair of the inguinal ring is not done

Pearl PF0034: Boundaries of Hesselbach’s triangle

* Lateral - inferior epigastric artery

* Medial - lateral border of rectus abdominis

* Inferior - inguinal ligament

Direct inguinal hernia emerges through Hesselbach’s triangle (Hence situated medial to inferior epigastric artery)

Indirect inguinal hernia enters deep inguinal ring (Hence it is lateral to inferior epigastric artery)
