questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child with diarrhea is eager to drink, but the skin pinch returns slowly. According to IMNCI guidelines, into which category does this child fall?
questions.explanation: Under the Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness (IMNCI) guidelines, the classification of dehydration is based on specific clinical signs. A child who is eager to drink (thirsty) and has a skin pinch that goes back slowly (less than 2 seconds) meets the criteria for "Some Dehydration", which is coded as the Yellow category. The Pink category (Option A) is for "Severe Dehydration," characterized by lethargy, inability to drink, and a skin pinch that goes back very slowly (more than 2 seconds). The Green category (Option C) is for "No Dehydration," where the child has none of these signs. Management for the Yellow category involves "Plan B" rehydration—providing oral rehydration solution (ORS) in the health facility over a 4-hour period while monitoring the child’s progress. This standardized color-coded system allows health workers to rapidly identify the severity of illness and initiate life-saving treatment protocols in resource-limited settings
questions.learning: Under the Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness (IMNCI) guidelines, the classification of dehydration is based on specific clinical signs.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: After sustaining trauma to the anatomical snuff box—a triangular depression on the lateral aspect of the wrist just below the thumb—a patient is assessed for an underlying fracture. Given the anatomical importance of this region and its association with specific carpal bones, which bone is most likely to be fractured in such an injury?
questions.explanation: The scaphoid is the bone most commonly fractured in the carpal region, especially following trauma where tenderness is localized in the anatomical snuff box. The scaphoid forms the floor of this triangular space, making it directly accessible to palpation. A fall on an outstretched hand (FOOSH) is the typical mechanism of injury that leads to this fracture. The lunate (Option B, often called lunar) is frequently involved in dislocations but less commonly fractured in the snuff box. The cuboid (Option C) is a tarsal bone in the foot, not the hand. While the trapezius (Option D, referring to the trapezium bone) also contributes to the floor of the snuff box distally, the scaphoid is significantly more prone to clinical fractures. Recognition of snuff box tenderness is vital because scaphoid fractures carry a high risk of avascular necrosis due to their retrograde blood supply
questions.learning: The scaphoid is the bone most commonly fractured in the carpal region, especially following trauma where tenderness is localized in the anatomical snuff box.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 60-year-old woman presented with post-menopausal bleeding. Ultrasonography revealed a mass with feeding vessel as shown in the image below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Endometrial polyp

Visualization of a mass with a single feeding vessel on a color Doppler is characteristic of an endometrial polyp.  In contrast, submucous leiomyomas often receive blood flow from multiple vessels (option A).

Endometrial polyps are soft, fleshy growths within the uterus that consist of endometrial glands, fibrous stroma, and surface epithelium. Risk factors for endometrial polyps include increasing age, obesity, and tamoxifen use.

They are usually asymptomatic. When symptomatic, they present with heavy menstrual bleeding, prolonged bleeding, intermenstrual bleeding, or infertility.

The main diagnostic tools for endometrial polyps include transvaginal ultrasound (TVS) with applied color Doppler, saline infusion sonography, and hysteroscopy.

The risk factors for the malignant transformation include postmenopausal status, age older than 60, and abnormal bleeding. Other factors such as larger polyp size (>1.5 cm), tamoxifen use, diabetes, and obesity may also contribute to a higher risk.

Hysteroscopic polypectomy may be considered most effective for symptomatic women or those with risk factors for malignant transformation.
questions.learning: Endometrial polyp Visualization of a mass with a single feeding vessel on a color Doppler is characteristic of an endometrial polyp. In contrast, submucous leiomyomas often receive blood flow from multiple vessels (option A).

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A patient was brought to the emergency department following a road traffic accident. During an autopsy, apparent bleeding was seen on the surface of his brain. Which type of hemorrhage would not be washed away under direct running water?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Subarachnoid hemorrhage

Subarachnoid haemorrhage will persist when washed under running water during an autopsy.

Subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) is bleeding in the space between the brain and the arachnoid membrane which is the subarachnoid space. During an autopsy, the blood from a subarachnoid haemorrhage is not easily washed away by running water. This is because it is located in this deep layer, which can trap the blood within the brain's sulci and gyri.

While doing the autopsy, there is typically some fresh blood present. However, it cannot be washed off because the blood is situated beneath the very thin and transparent arachnoid layer.

This makes the blood from a SAH less likely to be displaced compared to haemorrhages located in other regions, such as epidural or subdural spaces. Thus, despite running water during an autopsy, the blood from a subarachnoid haemorrhage often remains in place, making it detectable even after washing.
questions.learning: Subarachnoid hemorrhage Subarachnoid haemorrhage will persist when washed under running water during an autopsy. Subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) is bleeding in the space between the brain and the arachnoid membrane which is the subarachnoid space.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 10-year-old boy is brought to the hospital with symptoms of an inguinal hernia. During the operation, the surgeon observes a segment of necrotic bowel in the hernial sac. What is the appropriate course of action for resection and anastomosis of a necrotic bowel seen during surgery?
options: The surgeon must use chromic catgut.
The surgeon must not include the submucosa in the sutures.
The surgeon must use the single layer, extramucosal suture technique.
The surgeon must use the single-layer seromuscular suture technique.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. The surgeon must use the single layer, extramucosal suture technique.

Single-layer extramucosal intestinal anastomosis is the preferred technique for bowel resection and anastomosis because it incorporates the submucosa—the strongest layer of the bowel wall—while minimizing tissue ischemia, luminal narrowing, and foreign-body reaction.

• Submucosa is the holding layer of the intestine and must be included in the sutures for a secure anastomosis.
• Extramucosal (serosubmucosal) sutures approximate the bowel edges without penetrating the mucosa.
• A single-layer anastomosis is associated with:

• Comparable or superior strength to two-layer techniques
• Reduced tissue trauma and ischemia
• Shorter operative time
• Lower risk of luminal narrowing

Why the Other Options Are Incorrect

• A. Use chromic catgut → Not mandatory; modern intestinal anastomoses commonly use absorbable synthetic sutures (e.g., polyglactin, PDS).
• B. Must not include the submucosa → Incorrect. The submucosa must be included because it provides the greatest tensile strength.
• D. Single-layer seromuscular technique → Does not reliably include the submucosa and is therefore less ideal.
questions.learning: The surgeon must use the single layer, extramucosal suture technique. Single-layer extramucosal intestinal anastomosis is the preferred technique for bowel resection and anastomosis because it incorporates the submucosa—the strongest layer of the bowel…

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is an example of a longitudinal observational and analytical study?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cohort Study

Cohort study is an example of a longitudinal observational and analytical study.

A cohort study is a type of analytical study, which progresses from cause to effect, as exposure has occurred but not disease. It is also known as a forward-looking study, incidence study, prospective study, and longitudinal study. A well-designed cohort study is considered the most reliable means of showing an association between a cause or suspected risk factor and subsequent disease (or effect).

Types of epidemiological studies:

• Observational studies - allow nature to take its course, the investigator measures but does not intervene.

1. Descriptive studies - limited to the description of the occurrence of a disease in a population- (hypothesis formulation).
2. Analytical studies - go further by analyzing the relationship between health status and other variables- (hypothesis testing).

• Ecological studies
• Cross-sectional studies
• Case-control studies
• Cohort studies

• Experimental studies or intervention studies involve an active attempt to change a disease determinant or the progress of a disease and are similar in design to experiments in other sciences- (hypothesis confirmation).

1. Randomized controlled trials
2. Field trials
3. Community trials

Other options:

Option A: Although case-control studies are inherently analytical, they are not longitudinal. Longitudinal studies involve the collection of variables about a subject over an extended duration.

Option C: A randomized control trial is an experimental study in which an intervention is given to a group of patients participating in the study and compared to another group of patients with similar characteristics who are not given that intervention to be studied. It uses patients as the unit of study.

Option D: An ecological study is a type of analytical study that analyzes the health status and its relation with other variables. It is also called a correlational study, and it uses the population as a unit of study. Longitudinal studies involve the collection of variables about a subject over an extended duration.
questions.learning: Cohort Study Cohort study is an example of a longitudinal observational and analytical study. A cohort study is a type of analytical study, which progresses from cause to effect, as exposure has occurred but not disease.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Minimum number of antenatal visits according to WHO is ______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 8

According to WHO, the minimum number of antenatal visits should be 8.

Ideal number of antenatal visits is 12-14.

The ideal number of antenatal visits should be:

* Monthly visits upto 28 weeks

* Two weekly visits between 28-36 weeks

* Weekly visits from 36 weeks onwards

This means a total of 12-15 visits.

In the Indian scenario, according to MCH the suggested schedule is as follows and requires minimum of 4 visits:

* 1st visit: within 12 weeks preferably as soon as pregnancy is suspected, for the registration of pregnancy and 1st antenatal check-up.

* 2nd visit: between 14-26 weeks

* 3rd visit: between 28-34 weeks

* 4th visit: between 36 weeks and term

A booked case is one that has at least 3 antenatal visits, with two visits in the third trimester.
questions.learning: 8 According to WHO, the minimum number of antenatal visits should be 8. Ideal number of antenatal visits is 12-14.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is least likely to cause mucormycosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Broad spectrum antibiotics

Among the given options, the condition least likely to cause mucormycosis is the use of broad-spectrum antibiotics.

Mucormycosis is an opportunistic mycosis. It is typically seen in patients with diabetes mellitus and immunocompromised patients. Mucormycosis recently emerged as an important superinfection in COVID-19 patients, especially in India. The surge in cases is most likely due to diabetes mellitus and steroid use.

Risk factors for the infection include the following:

* Uncontrolled diabetes

* Acidosis (especially diabetic ketoacidosis)

* Steroid treatment

* Lymphomas and leukemias

* Immunodeficiencies

* Severe burns

The rhino-orbital-cerebral is the most common form of mucormycosis. Patients present with rhinitis, eye or facial pain, and facial numbness followed by the onset of conjunctival suffusion and swelling along with blurry vision.

Patients can have local tissue destruction with blackish nasal discharge typically resembling the presentation of invasive mucormycosis. The blackish discoloration is due to direct fungal invasion causing arterial and venous thrombosis leading to gangrene.

Diagnosis is made by biopsy with histopathologic examination. The biopsy shows characteristic wide, ribbon-like aseptate hyphal elements that branch at right angles.

The below image shows biopsy findings seen in mucormycosis.

Treatment includes intravenous administration of amphotericin B and wide excision of necrotic tissues. Along with the reversal of underlying conditions and risk factors.
questions.learning: Broad spectrum antibiotics Among the given options, the condition least likely to cause mucormycosis is the use of broad-spectrum antibiotics. Mucormycosis is an opportunistic mycosis.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Identify the edges of the lesion given in the image?
questions.explanation: The image displays a characteristic Basal Cell Carcinoma (rodent ulcer), and the defining clinical feature of its margin is a rolled-out (or "pearly, rolled") edge. These raised, semi-translucent borders are a classic hallmark of this slow-growing malignancy. Everted edges (Option A) are characteristic of squamous cell carcinoma, where the tissue is growing outward. Sloping edges (Option C) are typical of healing venous ulcers. Punched-out edges (Option D) are seen in trophic or syphilitic ulcers, which appear deep and cleanly cut. Recognizing these edge characteristics is fundamental for the clinical diagnosis of chronic skin lesions. A rodent ulcer, while locally invasive, rarely metastasizes but can cause significant tissue destruction if left untreated. It typically occurs on sun-exposed areas of the head and neck. Definitive management involves wide local excision or Mohs micrographic surgery to ensure clear margins while preserving healthy tissue
questions.learning: The image displays a characteristic Basal Cell Carcinoma (rodent ulcer), and the defining clinical feature of its margin is a rolled-out (or "pearly, rolled") edge.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which monoclonal antibody is used in cancer treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rituximab

Rituximab is an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody and is used in the treatment of lymphomas.

* Rituximab is a chimeric monoclonal antibody that targets the CD20 B-cell antigen. CD20 is found in cells from the pre–B cell stage through its terminal differentiation to plasma cells and is expressed in 90% of B-cell neoplasms.

* Monoclonal antibody binding to CD20 generates transmembrane signals that produce autophosphorylation and activation of serine/tyrosine protein kinases, induction of c-Myc oncogene expression, and expression of major histocompatibility complex class II molecules.

* Rituximab is approved as a single agent for relapsed indolent lymphomas and significantly enhances response and survival in combination with chemotherapy for the initial treatment of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma(DLBCL).

* It remains effective in patients who relapse after initial treatment with rituximab-based combinations.

* Rituximab improves response rates when added to combination chemotherapy for other indolent B-cell non-Hodgkin’s lymphomas (NHLs), including CLL, mantle cell lymphoma, Waldenström macroglobulinemia, and marginal zone lymphomas.

Note:

Monoclonal antibodies recognize the extracellular domain of the EGFR, inhibit ligand-induced signalling, and can elicit an immune response. Cetuximab is a recombinant, chimeric human/mouse IgG1 antibody that binds to EGFR and prevents ligand-dependent signalling and receptor dimerization, thereby blocking cell growth and survival signals. It is used to treat patients with metastatic colon cancers and Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma(HNSCC)
questions.learning: Rituximab Rituximab is an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody and is used in the treatment of lymphomas. * Rituximab is a chimeric monoclonal antibody that targets the CD20 B-cell antigen.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 28-year-old foreigner presents with sudden onset of profuse watery diarrhea after returning from a recent trip to Southeast Asia. He reports passing large volumes of pale, “rice-water” stools without blood or mucus. Which of the following toxins is most likely responsible for this patient’s condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cholera toxin

Vibrio cholerae causes profuse “rice-water” diarrhea through the action of cholera toxin, an A-B exotoxin. The toxin ADP-ribosylates the Gs protein, leading to persistent activation of adenylate cyclase, increased intracellular cAMP, and massive secretion of chloride and water into the intestinal lumen. The resulting diarrhea is watery, non-inflammatory, and non-bloody, causing rapid dehydration and electrolyte loss.

Why not the other options?

• A. Shigella toxin: Causes bloody diarrhea (dysentery) by invading the colonic mucosa and inhibiting protein synthesis via the 60S ribosomal subunit.
• B. Cholera toxin: ✔ Correct. Causes profuse rice-water stools by increasing cAMP without invading the intestinal mucosa.
• C. E. coli toxin: Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC) also causes watery diarrhea but is classically associated with traveler’s diarrhea, not the characteristic rice-water stools of cholera.
• D. Botulinum toxin: Produces descending flaccid paralysis by blocking acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, not diarrhea.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Hemorrhagic cystitis is a serious side effect of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cyclophosphamide

Cyclophosphamide is an alkylating agent used in the treatment of malignancies and autoimmune diseases. A major dose-limiting adverse effect is hemorrhagic cystitis, caused by its toxic metabolite acrolein, which damages the bladder urothelium. This complication can be prevented by adequate hydration and Mesna (2-mercaptoethane sulfonate).

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Leflunomide: Common adverse effects include hepatotoxicity, diarrhea, hypertension, and teratogenicity, not hemorrhagic cystitis.
• B. Mycophenolate mofetil: Mainly causes gastrointestinal upset, leukopenia, and increased risk of infections.
• D. Methotrexate: Associated with myelosuppression, mucositis, hepatotoxicity, and pulmonary fibrosis, but not hemorrhagic cystitis.
questions.learning: Cyclophosphamide Cyclophosphamide is an alkylating agent used in the treatment of malignancies and autoimmune diseases. A major dose-limiting adverse effect is hemorrhagic cystitis, caused by its toxic metabolite acrolein, which damages the bladder urothelium.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which macrovascular complication typically occurs in the later stages of diabetes mellitus?
questions.explanation: Chronic complications of diabetes mellitus are broadly categorized into microvascular and macrovascular groups. Macrovascular complications result from damage to large blood vessels due to accelerated atherosclerosis. Coronary artery disease (Option A) is the primary macrovascular complication, leading to myocardial infarction and heart failure. Other macrovascular diseases include stroke (cerebrovascular disease) and peripheral artery disease. Nephropathy (Option C) and retinopathy (Option D) are microvascular complications, meaning they involve the damage of small capillaries in the kidneys and eyes, respectively. A foot ulcer (Option B) is a complex complication usually resulting from a combination of microvascular neuropathy and macrovascular peripheral artery disease, but it is not classified purely as a macrovascular disease. Because CAD involves the major arteries of the heart, it is the classic example of diabetic macrovascular pathology
questions.learning: Chronic complications of diabetes mellitus are broadly categorized into microvascular and macrovascular groups. Macrovascular complications result from damage to large blood vessels due to accelerated atherosclerosis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following carries the lowest risk of developing invasive ductal carcinoma?
questions.explanation: Breast lesions are categorized by their risk of malignant transformation. Squamous metaplasia (Option D) of the lactiferous ducts is a benign, reactive change often associated with inflammation or abscesses; it carries no increased risk (lowest risk) for the development of invasive ductal carcinoma. In contrast, florid epithelial hyperplasia (Option A) and intraductal papilloma (Option B) are proliferative lesions that carry a mildly increased risk (roughly 1.5 to 2 times baseline). Atypical hyperplasia (Option C), whether ductal or lobular, is a high-risk precursor lesion carrying a significantly elevated risk (4 to 5 times baseline) of progressing to invasive cancer. Understanding this hierarchy is essential for managing patients with benign breast disease. While metaplasia sounds complex, it is essentially a structural adaptation to irritation and lacks the proliferative or atypical characteristics that drive oncogenesis. Therefore, squamous metaplasia is the correct choice for the lesion with minimal oncogenic potential

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Thyroid hormone acts via which among the following receptor?
options: Transmembrane receptor linked to tyrosine kinase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Nuclear receptor

The thyroid hormone receptors belong to nuclear receptors.

The nuclear receptor is a broad term that includes receptors located in both the nucleus and cytoplasm. This is because even for the receptors that are located in the cytoplasm, the end effect is seen via the nucleus.

Pearl PF0103: Classification of Hormones by Mechanism of Action

A) Hormones that bind to intracellular receptors

* Cytoplasmic receptors

* Steroids such as glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids and androgens

* Nuclear receptors

* Thyroid hormones

* Vitamins A and D

B) Hormones that bind to cell surface receptors

* GPCR - G protein-coupled receptors

* Gs - stimulation of the 2nd messenger cAMP

* Examples: ACTH, CRH, TSH, LH, FSH hCG, Catecholamines (β receptors), Vasopressin (V2 receptors), Secretin, Somatostatin, and Glucagon.

* Gi - inhibition of the 2nd messenger cAMP

* Examples: Catecholamines (ɑ2 receptors), Acetylcholine (M2, M4), Somatostatin

* Gq - The 2nd messenger is Phospholipase C (IP3 DAG Ca2+)

* Examples: Parathyroid hormone, GnRH - Gonadotropin-releasing hormone, GHRH - Growth hormone releasing hormone, TRH, Catecholamines (ɑ1 receptors), Vasopressin (V1 receptor), Gastrin, Cholecystokinin and Oxytocin.

* cGMP as the 2nd messenger

* Examples: Atrial natriuretic factor, Nitric oxide

* Tyrosine kinase receptors such as those that employ Janus kinase (JAK-STAT pathway) or MAP kinase pathway

* Growth hormone, Growth factors (GFs) - eg: IGF, VEGF, FGF, PDGF etc, Erythropoietin, Insulin and Prolactin.

Note: Even though the cytoplasmic receptors are present in the cytoplasm, once the hormone-receptor complex is formed it moves to the nucleus for its actions.
questions.learning: Nuclear receptor — The thyroid hormone receptors belong to nuclear receptors. The nuclear receptor is a broad term that includes receptors located in both the nucleus and cytoplasm.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the smallest diameter of the true pelvis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Sacrocotyloid diameter

The sacrocotyloid diameter is the shortest oblique diameter of the pelvic inlet and extends from the sacral promontory to the iliopectineal eminence (cotyloid region) on one side.

Important pelvic diameters:

• Diagonal conjugate → measured clinically from sacral promontory to inferior pubic symphysis
• True conjugate (obstetric conjugate) → narrowest anteroposterior diameter through which the fetal head passes
• Interspinous diameter → narrowest transverse diameter of the midpelvis
• Sacrocotyloid diameter → smallest diameter of the true pelvis

| Diameter | Measurement

| -------- | -----------

| Interspinous (bispinous) | 10.5 cm

| Diagonal conjugate | 12.5 cm

| True (obstetric) conjugate | 10 cm

| Obstetric conjugate | 10 cm

| Sacrocotyloid diameter | 9–9.5 cm ← smallest

Sacrocotyloid diameter = distance from sacral promontory → iliopectineal eminence (cotyloid notch) bilaterally

• Represents the posterior sagittal diameter of the pelvic brim
• At 9–9.5 cm, it is the smallest diameter of the true pelvis
• Clinically significant in flat/platypelloid pelvis — head engagement affected
questions.learning: Sacrocotyloid diameter — The sacrocotyloid diameter is the shortest oblique diameter of the pelvic inlet and extends from the sacral promontory to the iliopectineal eminence (cotyloid region) on one side.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The major thyroxine-binding protein is _____.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Thyroxine-binding globulin

Thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG) is the major protein that binds to thyroxine and tri-iodothyronine.

Thyroid hormones bind to transthyretin and albumin to a much lesser extent than TBG.

Hormones and their Binding Proteins

* T4  and T3  bind to thyroxine-binding globulin  (TBG), albumin, and thyroxine-binding pre-albumin (TBPA)

* Cortisol binds to cortisol-binding globulin (CBG);

* Androgen and estrogen bind to sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG);

* IGF-I and -II bind to multiple IGF-binding proteins (IGFBPs);

* GH interacts with GH-binding protein (GHBP), a circulating fragment of the GH receptor extracellular domain;

* Activin binds to follistatin.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 21-year-old patient Suyash came to OPD with history of fall on hand. Now he is having pain at hand region. X-ray of patient is given. Which of the following joint has been shown in his X-ray?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ellipsoid joint

The X-ray indicates the radiocarpal (wrist) joint, which is a condyloid/ellipsoid synovial joint. Articulating surfaces:

• Proximally: Distal end of radius and articular disc of distal radioulnar joint
• Distally: Scaphoid, lunate, and triquetrum (proximal carpal bones)

Because it is an ellipsoid joint, it allows biaxial movement:

• Flexion
• Extension
• Abduction (radial deviation)
• Adduction (ulnar deviation)
• Circumduction (combination of above)

Comparison with other options:

• Hinge joint: elbow, interphalangeal joints
• Ball-and-socket: shoulder, hip
• Saddle joint: first carpometacarpal joint of thumb

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Ingestion of an unknown substance results in tachycardia and the perception of a red-colored halo. Which substance is most likely responsible for these findings?
questions.explanation: LSD (Lysergic acid diethylamide) is a potent hallucinogen. Its clinical effects include profound sensory distortions, such as synesthesia (crossing of senses) and the perception of red-colored halos or trails around objects. LSD also triggers a sympathetic response, leading to tachycardia, pupil dilation (mydriasis), and hypertension. Cannabis (Option A) classically causes "red eyes" (conjunctival injection) and increased appetite but not the specific halo-hallucinations of LSD. Crack/Cocaine (Option B) is a pure stimulant that causes extreme tachycardia and euphoria but not primarily visual hallucinations. Heroin (Option D) is an opioid that characteristically causes "pinpoint" pupils, respiratory depression, and bradycardia—the opposite of tachycardia. LSD "trips" can be intensely pleasant or terrifying ("bad trip"), often requiring supportive care in a quiet environment. Recognizing these specific drug-induced visual symptoms is a key part of the psychiatric and forensic assessment of substance abuse
questions.learning: LSD (Lysergic acid diethylamide) is a potent hallucinogen. Its clinical effects include profound sensory distortions, such as synesthesia (crossing of senses) and the perception of red-colored halos or trails around objects.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following statements about mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) of HIV is incorrect? (NEET PG 2016)
options: Transmission most commonly occurs during early gestation
Majority of fetuses are not infected even without any intervention
The risk of mother-to-child transmission can be reduced by elective cesarean section
The risk is related to the status of infection in the mother
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Transmission most commonly occurs during early gestation

Mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) of HIV can occur:

• In utero (during pregnancy)
• Intrapartum (during labor and delivery) — most common
• Postnatally through breastfeeding

Therefore, the statement that transmission most commonly occurs during early gestation is incorrect.

Risk factors for MTCT:

• High maternal viral load
• Advanced maternal HIV disease
• Prolonged rupture of membranes
• Breastfeeding without ART

Prevention strategies:

• Maternal antiretroviral therapy (ART)
• Elective cesarean section in selected patients with high viral load
• Avoidance or modification of breastfeeding depending on guidelines

Without intervention:

• Most fetuses are still not infected
• Transmission risk is approximately 15–45%
• With proper ART, risk can be reduced to <2%

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following studies progresses from cause to effect?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cohort Study

A cohort study is a type of analytical study, which progresses from cause to effect, as exposure has occurred but not disease. It is also known as a forward-looking study, incidence study, prospective study, and longitudinal study. A well-designed cohort study is considered the most reliable means of showing an association between a cause or suspected risk factor and subsequent disease (or effect).

Types of epidemiological studies:

* Observational studies - allow nature to take its course, the investigator measures but does not intervene.

* Descriptive studies - limited to the description of the occurrence of a disease in a population- (hypothesis formulation).

* Analytical studies - go further by analyzing the relationship between health status and other variables- (hypothesis testing).

* Ecological studies

* Cross-sectional studies

* Case-control studies

* Cohort studies

* Experimental studies or intervention studies involve an active attempt to change a disease determinant or the progress of a disease and are similar in design to experiments in other sciences- (hypothesis confirmation).

* Randomized controlled trials

* Field trials

* Community trials

Other options:

Option A: Although case-control studies are inherently analytical, they are not longitudinal. Longitudinal studies involve the collection of variables about a subject over an extended duration.

Option C: A randomized control trial is an experimental study in which an intervention is given to a group of patients participating in the study and compared to another group of patients with similar characteristics who are not given that intervention to be studied. It uses patients as the unit of study.

Option D: An ecological study is a type of analytical study that analyzes the health status and its relation with other variables. It is also called a correlational study, and it uses the population as a unit of study. Longitudinal studies involve the collection of variables about a subject over an extended duration.
questions.learning: Cohort Study — A cohort study is a type of analytical study, which progresses from cause to effect, as exposure has occurred but not disease. It is also known as a forward-looking study, incidence study, prospective study, and longitudinal study.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: McCall's Culdoplasty is a surgical procedure targeted towards preventing or correcting:
questions.explanation: McCall’s culdoplasty is a specialized gynecological procedure performed during a vaginal hysterectomy to provide support to the vaginal vault and obliterate the cul-de-sac (Pouch of Douglas). Its primary clinical goal is to prevent or correct an enterocele, which is the herniation of the small intestine into the upper vagina. By suturing the uterosacral ligaments together and attaching them to the posterior vaginal vault, the surgeon creates a robust support structure that closes the potential hernial space. While other procedures address a ureterocele (Option B) or a cystocele (Option C), McCall's technique specifically targets the apical support needed to prevent enterocele formation. A cystocele (bladder prolapse) is typically corrected via anterior colporrhaphy rather than culdoplasty. Therefore, in the management of pelvic organ prolapse, McCall's culdoplasty remains a foundational technique for maintaining the depth and integrity of the posterior vaginal wall and preventing the descent of abdominal contents into the vaginal canal
questions.learning: McCall’s culdoplasty is a specialized gynecological procedure performed during a vaginal hysterectomy to provide support to the vaginal vault and obliterate the cul-de-sac (Pouch of Douglas).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is an oral factor Xa inhibitor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rivaroxaban

Rivaroxaban is an oral direct factor Xa inhibitor. They represent a new class of oral anticoagulant drugs that do not require monitoring.

This group of drugs inhibit factor Xa in the final common pathway of clotting [conversion of Prothrombin (Factor II) to thrombin (Factor IIa)]. They are given as fixed doses and have a rapid onset of action.

Oral direct factor Xa inhibitors are indicated in:

• Prevention of embolic stroke in patients with atrial fibrillation (without valvular heart disease)
• Venous thromboembolic disease (VTE)
• Postoperative thromboprophylaxis in patients undergoing hip and knee arthroplasty
questions.learning: Rivaroxaban Rivaroxaban is an oral direct factor Xa inhibitor. They represent a new class of oral anticoagulant drugs that do not require monitoring.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Which skeletal bone is regarded as the most reliable indicator for sex determination in forensic examination?
questions.explanation: In forensic osteology, the Pelvis is the most reliable bone for sex determination, with an accuracy of over 95%. This reliability stems from the anatomical adaptations in the female pelvis for childbearing. Key features used include the subpubic angle (wider in females), the greater sciatic notch (wider in females), and the overall shape of the pelvic inlet (circular/oval in females vs. heart-shaped in males). The Skull (Option A) is the second most reliable structure, with about 80% accuracy, using markers like the mastoid process and supraorbital ridges. Long bones (Option C), such as the femur, and the Sternum (Option D) are much less reliable and are used as secondary evidence when the pelvis or skull is unavailable. Forensic anthropologists prioritize the pelvis because its sexual dimorphism is the most pronounced due to functional biological requirements. Therefore, for the definitive identification of biological sex from skeletal remains, the pelvis remains the gold standard
questions.learning: In forensic osteology, the Pelvis is the most reliable bone for sex determination, with an accuracy of over 95%. This reliability stems from the anatomical adaptations in the female pelvis for childbearing.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following is not a contraindication to the use of morphine?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Acute myocardial infarction

Acute myocardial infarction is not a contraindication for morphine use.

Morphine is the opioid of choice for myocardial infarction as it relieves anxiety, chest pain, and myocardial oxygen demand.

Contraindications to the use of Morphine:

• Bronchial asthma: Histamine release can cause bronchoconstriction and precipitate attacks of asthma.
• Renal failure: Morphine-6-glucuronide (metabolite) can accumulate and lead to prolonged respiratory depression.
• Emphysema: Respiratory depression and decreased response to hypoxia can cause hypercapnia in patients with COPD
• Head injury: Hypercapnia due to respiratory depression can increase ICP. Miosis, vomiting, and effect on wakefulness make interpreting the signs of head injury difficult.
• Biliary colic: Constriction of sphincter of Oddi can worsen biliary spasm
• Hypotension and shock
questions.learning: Acute myocardial infarction Acute myocardial infarction is not a contraindication for morphine use. Morphine is the opioid of choice for myocardial infarction as it relieves anxiety, chest pain, and myocardial oxygen demand.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the procedure shown in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pancreaticojejunostomy

The image shows the resection of the tail of pancreas followed by longitudinal pancreaticojejunostomy i.e. Puestow procedure which is a treatment modality for chronic pancreatitis.

When chronic pancreatitis is accompanied by intractable pain, it is best treated with side-to-side Roux-en-Y pancreaticojejunostomy, also known as the modified Puestow procedure or lateral pancreaticojejunostomy.

Note:

Duval procedure is outdated and not in use due to low improvement rates. Restenosis and segmental obstruction of the pancreas is common due to progressive scarring. It is now only used in resectable tumors of the body or the tail of the pancreas.

Pearl PF0325: Drainage procedures for chronic Pancreatitis

Duval procedure: Distal pancreatectomy with Roux-en-Y pancreaticojejunostomy

Puestow procedure: Resection of tail followed by longitudinal pancreaticojejunostomy

* Partington and Rochelle modification of Puestow procedure: Elimination of resection of pancreatic tail

* A longitudinal pancreatotomy typically discloses segmental stenosis of the pancreatic duct and the presence of intraductal calculi in a patient with chronic calcific pancreatitis.

* Following mobilization of a Roux limb of jejunum, a longitudinal pancreaticojejunostomy is performed to permit extensive drainage of the pancreatic duct system.

Pearl PF0333: Resection and Hybrid Surgical Procedures for Chronic Pancreatitis

Beger’s procedure: Duodenum-preserving pancreatic head resection (DPPHR)

* The completed resection after transection of the pancreatic neck and subtotal removal of the pancreatic head, with preservation of the distal common bile duct and duodenum (Marked A).

* Completion of the reconstruction of the anastomosis to the distal pancreas and to the proximal pancreatic rim by the same Roux limb of the jejunum.

Frey’s procedure:

* The local resection of the pancreatic head with longitudinal pancreaticojejunostomy (LR-LPJ) provides complete decompression of the entire pancreatic ductal system. Reconstruction is performed with a side-to-side Roux-en-Y pancreaticojejunostomy.

Warren’s modification of Beger’s procedure:

Berne modification (Beger + Frey) involves excavation of the central portion of the head without formal division of the neck.

(image below)

Hamburg modification of Frey’s procedure

Note:

Surgical treatments for chronic pancreatitis

Resection

* Pancreaticoduodenectomy (Kausch–Whipple procedure)

* Pylorus-preserving pancreaticoduodenectomy (Traverso–Longmire)

* Beger procedure

* Near-total or total pancreatectomy

Decompression/Drainage

* Duval procedure

* Puestow–Gillesby procedure

* Partington–Rochelle procedure (Puestow)

* Izbicki procedure

Hybrid (resection+decompression)

* Frey procedure

* Hamburg modification

* Berne modification
questions.learning: Pancreaticojejunostomy — The image shows the resection of the tail of pancreas followed by longitudinal pancreaticojejunostomy i.e. Puestow procedure which is a treatment modality for chronic pancreatitis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman, one week after delivering a healthy full-term baby, presents to the obstetrics and gynecology clinic with complaints of a pale brownish vaginal discharge that has a fishy odor. What is the nature of this discharge?
questions.explanation: The vaginal discharge seen during the first few weeks postpartum is called lochia. Based on the timing (one week ago) and appearance (pale brownish or pinkish), the discharge is classified as Lochia Serosa, which characteristically occurs between days 5 and 9 of the puerperium. It is composed of wound exudate and mucus and often has a fishy smell. Regarding the distractors, Lochia Rubra (Option A) is red, contains blood, and is seen only in the first 1–4 days. Lochia Alba (Option C) is pale white or yellowish and is seen after the 10th day. Leukorrhea (Option D) is a profuse white discharge usually associated with vaginitis or subinvolution rather than normal postpartum recovery. Thus, the specific one-week timing and brownish color definitively identify the discharge as lochia serosa

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is seen in low insulin:glucagon ratio?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Activation of hormone-sensitive lipase

Low insulin:glucagon ratio occurs in the fasting state. Since insulin has an inhibitory effect on hormone-sensitive lipase (lipolytic hormone), low insulin:glucagon ratio results in the activation of hormone-sensitive lipase.

In adipose tissues, decreased insulin results in the inhibition of lipogenesis and activation of intracellular hormone-sensitive lipase. The stored triglycerides are broken down (lipolysis) by hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) into free fatty acids (FFAs) and glycerol. In the fasting state, glucose is spared for the brain and glycerol is used as a substrate for gluconeogenesis.

In diabetic patients, low insulin level corresponds to an increase in HSL activity, promoting the breakdown of lipids and the release of FFAs from adipose tissue. HSL activity is accelerated by hormones like epinephrine, norepinephrine, glucagon, ACTH, TSH, GH, ADH, and melanocyte-stimulating hormones (MSH).

Well-fed state (Insulin)
During fasting (Glucagon)

Lipogenesis increased
Lipogenesis inhibited

Lipolysis inhibited
Lipolysis increased

Insulin inhibits HS-lipase
Glucagon activates HS-lipase

Lipoprotein lipase active
Lipoprotein lipase inactive

Other options:

Option A: Activation of lipoprotein lipase (LPL) is promoted by insulin, not low insulin: glucagon ratio. LPL is involved in the breakdown of triglycerides and is active in the well-fed state. In low insulin: glucagon ratio, lipoprotein lipase activity is reduced, leading to decreased hydrolysis of triglycerides.

Option B: Activation of glycogen synthase is promoted by insulin. In low insulin: glucagon ratio, glycogen synthase activity is reduced, leading to decreased glycogenesis. Instead, glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis are promoted to maintain blood glucose levels.

Option C: Activation of phosphofructokinase 1 (PFK1) is promoted by insulin. PFK1 is a rate-regulating enzyme in glycolysis. In low insulin: glucagon ratio, glycolysis is downregulated, and gluconeogenesis is upregulated to maintain blood glucose levels.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 26-year-old man reports a respiratory tract infection four weeks ago, followed by gradually progressive weakness that began in the lower limbs and later involved the upper limbs, making standing and walking difficult for the past two weeks. Examination reveals absent reflexes with preserved pain sensation and proprioception. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS) is an acute, immune-mediated polyneuropathy that often follows a viral or bacterial respiratory or gastrointestinal infection (classically Campylobacter jejuni). The hallmark of GBS is symmetric, "ascending" muscle weakness that starts in the lower extremities and moves upward. The most critical diagnostic clinical findings are "areflexia" (lack of reflexes) and the relative sparing of sensory functions, as seen in this patient. Myasthenia gravis (Option B) presents with fatigable weakness, mostly affecting ocular and bulbar muscles, and does not typically follow an ascending pattern. Polymyositis (Option C) causes subacute proximal muscle weakness and would not present with areflexia. Multiple sclerosis (Option D) is a central nervous system disorder that typically presents with patchy, non-symmetric neurological deficits (like optic neuritis or sensory changes) rather than global ascending paralysis. The most dangerous complication of GBS is respiratory failure due to diaphragmatic weakness. Diagnosis is confirmed by "albuminocytologic dissociation" in the CSF (high protein, normal cell count)
questions.learning: Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS) is an acute, immune-mediated polyneuropathy that often follows a viral or bacterial respiratory or gastrointestinal infection (classically Campylobacter jejuni).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: ASEPSIS wound scoring takes all of the following into consideration except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Induration

ASEPSIS wound score does not take induration into consideration. Instead, the I in ASEPSIS stands for the isolation of bacteria from the wound.

ASEPSIS wound score and Southampton wound score are used to determine the severity of the surgical site wound infection (SSI).

ASEPSIS score includes:

• Additional treatment

• Antibiotics for wound infection
• Drainage of pus under local anesthesia
• Debridement of the wound under general anesthesia

• Serous discharge
• Erythema
• Purulent exudate
• Separation of deep tissue
• Isolation of bacteria from the wound
• Stay as inpatient prolonged over 14 days as a result of wound infection

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 30-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a history of penetrating chest trauma. On examination, marked tracheal deviation is noted. What is the immediate step in management?
questions.explanation: Severe tracheal deviation following penetrating chest trauma is a pathognomonic sign of a tension pneumothorax. This occurs when air trapped in the pleural space shifts the mediastinum and compresses the heart and opposite lung, leading to rapid obstructive shock. Immediate needle decompression using a large-bore cannula (typically in the 5th intercostal space, mid-axillary line) is mandatory and life-saving. Waiting for a chest X-ray (Option B) or performing an E-FAST ultrasound (Option C) is dangerous because it delays critical intervention in a clinically diagnosed emergency. While 100% oxygen (Option D) is part of general stabilization, it will not relieve the mechanical pressure causing the tracheal shift and circulatory collapse. Once the pressure is relieved by a needle, a definitive intercostal chest drain (ICD) must be placed. Thus, clinical diagnosis and immediate decompression are the priorities

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: What is the most common cause of seizures in a 2-year-old child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Febrile seizures

The most common cause of seizures in the said age group is febrile seizures.

Febrile seizures are defined as seizures that:

Occur between the age of 6 to 60 months
Associated with a temperature of ≥38°C (100.4°F)
Do not occur as a result of central nervous system infections or any metabolic imbalance.
Occur without a history of afebrile seizures in the past.

Depending on the duration and recurrence of the febrile seizure, they are classified as follows:

Simple febrile seizure
Complex febrile seizures
Febrile status epilepticus

Generalised, tonic-clonic seizure
Focal seizure
Febrile seizure

Last for ≤15 minutes, without another episode in 24 hours
Lasts >15 minutes and/or recurs in 24 hours
Duration of >30 minutes

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 32-year-old woman diagnosed with diarrhoea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome presented to the casualty with severe abdominal pain. She was prescribed a drug that exerts a direct spasmolytic effect on the smooth muscles of the gastrointestinal tract. Which drug could it be?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dicyclomine

Dicyclomine is a weak muscarinic receptor antagonist with non-specific direct spasmolytic effects on the smooth muscle of the gastrointestinal tract.

Other options:

Option B: Scopolamine exerts spasmolytic activity indirectly through its antimuscarinic action. It is not preferred due to its adverse effects like drowsiness, dryness, and blurred vision.

Option C and D: Galantamine and rivastigmine are central cholinesterase inhibitors and do not possess spasmolytic activity.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 55-year-old woman presents with chronic mucopurulent discharge from her left eye and swelling near the medial canthus, suggestive of nasolacrimal duct obstruction. What is the most appropriate treatment for this condition?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with symptoms of chronic dacryocystitis (mucopurulent discharge and swelling at the medial canthus) caused by a permanent obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct. The gold-standard surgical treatment for this condition in an adult is Dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR). This procedure involves creating a new permanent drainage pathway between the lacrimal sac and the nasal cavity by bypassing the obstructed duct. Dacryocystectomy (DCT, Option B) involves the total removal of the lacrimal sac; while it cures the infection, it leaves the patient with permanent tearing (epiphora) and is usually reserved for patients with sac tumors or those unsuitable for DCR. Conjunctivo-cysto rhinostomy (Option C) is a more complex bypass used only when the canaliculi are also obstructed. Balloon catheter dilation (Option D) is occasionally used for partial obstructions but is much less effective for established chronic cases than a formal DCR. Therefore, DCR is the definitive curative procedure to restore tear drainage and eliminate the source of infection
questions.learning: The patient presents with symptoms of chronic dacryocystitis (mucopurulent discharge and swelling at the medial canthus) caused by a permanent obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the most common cause of puberty menorrhagia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anovulation

The most common cause of puberty menorrhagia is anovulatory cycles.
Anovulatory cycles → unopposed estrogen → endometrial hyperplasia → prolonged and heavy periods.

Other causes

Endocrine dysfunction:

• Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS
• Hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism.

Hematological:

• Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura
• Von-Willebrand’s disease  leukaemia.

Pelvic tumors:

• Fibroid uterus
• Sarcoma botryroides
• Estrogen producing ovarian tumor

Pregnancy complications (abortion)

Treatment:

Reassurance and psychological support. Rest and correction of anemia is done.In refractory cases, progestogens, such as medroxyprogesterone acetate or norethisterone 5 mg thrice daily is given till bleed- ing stops. Usually, the bleeding is controlled within 3–7 days. Medication is continued for 21 days. The condition usually becomes normal following 2–3 courses and then normal cycles resume. In emergency, conjugated equine estrogen 20–40 mg IV is given every 6–8 hours. Once the bleeding is controlled, combined oral pills are started.

Regular menstrual cycle will be established once the hypothalamo-pituitary-ovarian axis is matured.
questions.learning: Anovulation — The most common cause of puberty menorrhagia is anovulatory cycles. Anovulatory cycles → unopposed estrogen → endometrial hyperplasia → prolonged and heavy periods.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following conditions are transmitted as a recessive, sex-linked trait? I. Retinitis pigmentosa II. Colour blindness III. Cystic fibrosis IV. Duchenne muscular dystrophy Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. I, II and IV

X-linked recessive disorders are caused by mutations on the X chromosome. They predominantly affect males, while females are usually carriers. Affected fathers do not transmit the disease to their sons, but all daughters become carriers.

• X-linked recessive disorders:

• Colour blindness
• Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD)
• Hemophilia A & B
• G6PD deficiency
• Bruton agammaglobulinemia
• Lesch-Nyhan syndrome
• Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency

• Retinitis pigmentosa can be inherited as autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, or X-linked recessive; therefore, an X-linked recessive form exists.
• Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the CFTR gene (chromosome 7) and is not X-linked.
questions.learning: I, II and IV X-linked recessive disorders are caused by mutations on the X chromosome. They predominantly affect males, while females are usually carriers.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient following a crush injury is passing red color urine due to myoglobinuria. Which of the following will most likely be seen in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hyperkalemia

In this clinical scenario, a patient with a crush injury develops red-colored urine due to myoglobinuria from rhabdomyolysis. This process results in the release of intracellular potassium, leading to hyperkalemia, and also contributes indirectly to the development of acute kidney injury (AKI).

Rhabdomyolysis is defined as a pathological condition of skeletal muscle cell damage leading to the release of toxic intracellular material into the blood circulation. The causes of rhabdomyolysis include:

* Crush injury

* Hypothyroidism (precipitated by exertion, alcohol, infection)

* Electric shock

* Prolonged seizures

* Malignant hyperthermia

* Exertion

* Drugs like fibrates, statins

* Polymyositis / Dermatomyositis

* McArdle's disease (GSD-5) causes recurrent rhabdomyolysis.

Rhabdomyolysis is a cause of AKI due to myoglobin release from injured muscle due to excessive strenuous exercise, heat stroke, or traumatic crush injuries. Pathogenic factors for AKI due to endogenous toxins include intrarenal vasoconstriction, direct proximal tubular toxicity, and mechanical obstruction of the distal nephron lumen. Patients often present with muscle pain and high-colored urine(myoglobinuria). The following features are also seen:

* High serum creatinine kinase (> 5 times normal)

* High serum myoglobin

* High serum LDH

* Hyperkalemia

* Hypermagnesemia

* Hyperphosphatemia

* Hypocalcemia

* Hyperuricemia

* Once AKI develops, high serum creatinine and urea

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is not used to treat PCOD?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tamoxifen

Tamoxifen is the best answer as it is not commonly used in the treatment of polycystic ovarian disease (PCOD). Tamoxifen is a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM).

Treatment of PCOD:

• Weight reduction alone is beneficial in mild hirsutism.
• Lifestyle changes, such as smoking cessation, are recommended.
• Fourth-generation oral contraceptive pills (OCP) containing ethinyl estradiol and drospirenone are used for treating menstrual abnormalities, reducing acne, and hirsutism.
• OCP with cyproterone acetate is prescribed for PCOS patients with hirsutism.
• Patients with PCOD are prone to developing insulin resistance, which can be controlled with metformin. Acarbose can be used as an alternative if metformin is contraindicated.
• Drugs used in the management of infertility in women with PCOS include letrozole and clomiphene citrate. FOGSI, in 2024, updated letrozole as the first-line drug for induction of ovulation in patients with PCOS. However, the FDA approval for the same is still pending.

Surgical options include laparoscopic ovarian drilling or puncture of not more than four cysts in each ovary. This is done either by laser or by unipolar electrocautery. It restores endocrine levels and improves fertility. Surgery is indicated only if:

• Medical therapy fails
• Hyperstimulation occurs
• Infertile women
• Previous pregnancy losses

Note: In cases where clomiphene and dexamethasone fail to induce ovulation, tamoxifen can be considered as an alternative treatment for infertility associated with PCOD. However, it is not recommended as the initial choice. It's important to note that tamoxifen carries a significant risk of endometrial hyperplasia and can also result in unexpected pregnancy with potential teratogenic effects when used for induction.
questions.learning: Tamoxifen Tamoxifen is the best answer as it is not commonly used in the treatment of polycystic ovarian disease (PCOD). Tamoxifen is a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: All of the following can be done to transport a polytrauma patient who is conscious except?
options: Strap their thorax, abdomen and lower limbs on a stretcher
Place in prone position to prevent aspiration
Put patient on lateral position and shift him immediately
Roll the patient onto a hard board
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Put patient on lateral position and shift him immediately

Patients with polytrauma are shifted into a supine or prone position (not in a lateral position) by laying them over a firm surface to restrict spinal movement.

As per ATLS guidelines, in patients with trauma, airway management is first done along with cervical spine stabilization. All trauma patients until proven otherwise are considered to have an injured vertebral column.

The patients are placed supine on a firm surface without rotating or bending the spinal column and a rigid cervical collar (philadelphia collar) is applied. Aspiration can be prevented by putting the patient in the prone position and strapping can be done to provide further stabilization.

Long spine boards with straps are helpful in the rapid transport of the patient from one place to another. The patient can be put on the long spine board by log-rolling (a technique where four people hold the patient and roll the patient like a log without allowing rotation or bending of the spine).

Conscious and alert patient indirectly means that they don’t need intubation and their airway is patent. If the patient is unconscious always check the airway and if needed, endotracheal intubation must be done immediately by various methods. Preferably by direct laryngoscopy and intubation.
questions.learning: Put patient on lateral position and shift him immediately Patients with polytrauma are shifted into a supine or prone position (not in a lateral position) by laying them over a firm surface to restrict spinal movement.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient presents with hip pain and true shortening of the affected limb and is diagnosed with tuberculosis of the hip. Based on these clinical features, which stage of the disease is the patient currently in?
questions.explanation: Tuberculosis of the hip progresses through four clinical stages. In the "Stage of Synovitis" (Option B), there is joint effusion and the limb is in an abducted/externally rotated position ("apparent lengthening"). In the "Stage of Early Arthritis" (Option A), the limb becomes adducted and internally rotated, leading to "apparent shortening." The hallmark of the "Stage of Advanced Arthritis" (Option C) is the presence of "true shortening" of the limb. This occurs because the acetabulum and femoral head have undergone significant destruction, leading to subluxation or dislocation ("wandering acetabulum"). Option D is incorrect as "arthritis without subluxation" describes earlier phases before significant structural collapse. Advanced TB hip is a debilitating condition that often results in fibrous ankylosis. Management involves the multi-drug anti-tubercular regimen (AKT), traction to maintain joint space, and sometimes surgical intervention (arthrodesis or arthroplasty) to restore function or stabilize the joint
questions.learning: Tuberculosis of the hip progresses through four clinical stages. In the "Stage of Synovitis" (Option B), there is joint effusion and the limb is in an abducted/externally rotated position ("apparent lengthening").

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 4-year-old child is brought with a gradually enlarging, tender mass in the flank region noticed over the past few weeks. On examination, the child appears otherwise well. The mass is firm, non-fluctuant, non-mobile, and not associated with overlying skin changes or signs of inflammation. No other systemic symptoms are present. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A large, firm, flank mass in a 4-year-old child is the classic presentation for Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma), the most common primary renal malignancy of childhood. Crucially, the mass in Wilms tumor is typically smooth and characteristically does not cross the midline, which differentiates it from neuroblastoma. Neuroblastoma (Option D) often presents in younger children (average age 2), feels "knobby" or irregular, and characteristically crosses the midline. Angiomyolipoma (Option A) is a benign renal tumor rare in early childhood unless associated with tuberous sclerosis. Renal cell carcinoma (Option C) is extremely rare in the first decade of life. While Wilms tumor mass is often described as painless, large tumors can cause discomfort or tension in the flank region. Management involves a combination of surgery (nephrectomy) and chemotherapy, with excellent survival rates for localized disease
questions.learning: A large, firm, flank mass in a 4-year-old child is the classic presentation for Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma), the most common primary renal malignancy of childhood.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which one of the following terms correctly denotes the mechanism and phenotypic changes that are not a result of variation in the underlying DNA sequence, but are caused by secondary modifications of DNA or histones in response to other heritable or environmental influences?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Epigenetics

Epigenetics refers to heritable changes in gene expression and phenotype that occur without alteration of the underlying DNA sequence. These changes can result from modifications such as:

• DNA methylation
• Histone modification
• Chromatin remodeling
• Regulatory non-coding RNAs

Why not other options?

• A. Pleiotropy: One gene produces multiple phenotypic effects.
• B. Epigenetics: Correct. Changes in gene expression without changing the DNA sequence.
• C. Co-dominance: Both alleles are expressed simultaneously in the heterozygous state.
• D. Epistasis: One gene masks or modifies the expression of another gene.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 14-day-old neonate brought to the outpatient department is found to have bilateral conjunctivitis. Chest X-ray done showed lung infiltrates. Which of the following organisms is most likely responsible for the infection?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chlamydia trachomatis

Chlamydia trachomatis is most likely responsible for the infection.

Chlamydia trachomatis inclusion conjunctivitis usually manifests 1 week after birth. It is usually a venereal infection derived from the cervix or urethra of the mother during delivery.

On examination, the conjunctiva is swollen and edematous. The discharge is initially watery, later becomes purulent or bloody.

Newborns with suspected chlamydia infection should have samples drawn from both the conjunctivae and oropharynx. Since it is an obligate intracellular organism, swabs should also include conjunctival epithelial cells if possible. Subsequent Giemsa staining shows characteristic intracellular inclusion bodies formed by Chlamydia oculogenitalis.

Treatment involves administration of suspension of erythromycin ethylsuccinate 50 mg/kg daily in four divided doses before feeds for 2–3 weeks.

If left untreated, associated systemic diseases such as chlamydial otitis and pneumonia may develop later. In all cases, both parents must receive appropriate treatment for genital infection.

Neonatal conjunctivitis, also called ophthalmia neonatorum, typically presents during the first month of life. The age of the neonate is an important clue towards the etiology of the infection.

Age
Cause of conjunctivitis

First 24 hours
Chemical causes- erythromycin/gentamycin drops,

24 to 48 hours
Neisseria gonorrhea (most common), Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus, coliforms

5 to 14 days
Chlamydia trachomatis, Herpes keratoconjunctivitis

5 to 18 days

Neonates are at higher risk of conjunctivitis due to predisposing factors such as:

• Decreased tear production
• Absence of IgA in tears
• Decreased immune function
• Absence of lymphoid tissue in the conjunctiva
• Decreased lysozyme activity.

Other risk factors for developing neonatal conjunctivitis are premature rupture of membranes, prolonged delivery, prematurity, poor prenatal care, mechanical ventilation, poor hygiene conditions, and history of midwife interference.

Other options :
Option B: Hemophilus influenza is one of the most common causes of acute bacterial conjunctivitis in children < 6 years of age and is responsible for causing conjunctivitis-otitis syndrome where conjunctivitis is followed by acute otitis media.

Option C: Streptococcus usually manifests 48-72 hours after birth. It is a common cause of acute bacterial conjunctivitis in children.

Option D: Mycoplasma, specifically M.genitalium can cause conjunctivitis due to contamination of the eye with genital infections in adults.
